ranges.en: Partners building a dividing wall in a shared courtyard place it centrally, using the material local custom prescribes.
Gevil wall: each partner contributes three handbreadths, giving a six-handbreadth thickness.
Gazit wall: each partner contributes two and a half handbreadths, giving a five-handbreadth thickness.
Kefisin wall: each partner contributes two handbreadths, giving a four-handbreadth thickness.
Leveinin wall: each partner contributes one and a half handbreadths, giving a three-handbreadth thickness.
If such a shared wall falls, its site and stones are jointly owned and divided equally.
Gardens: where customary to wall them, the court can compel a neighbor to share in building the partition.
Open fields: where customary not to wall them, a neighbor cannot be compelled to build a partition.
Without consent, a builder must set the wall on his own land, facing outward, with a border mark.
A wall built solely by one party that falls belongs only to him, as the border mark shows.
With mutual consent, partners build on the property line with border marks on both sides.
A jointly consented wall that falls is jointly owned, with its site and stones divided equally.
The Gemara asks what the term meḥitza, used in the Mishnah, actually means.
The term means a wall, a barrier separating the properties.
A baraita on a vineyard fence breached repeatedly, with the owner ordered to rebuild, illustrates the meaning of meḥitza.

2b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A vineyard owner who gives up on an unfenced vineyard makes its produce forbidden and is liable for it.
The reason for compulsion is mutual consent; without both partners agreeing, no one can be forced to build.
It follows that being exposed to another's sight is not considered damage.
Objection: perhaps meḥitza here means division rather than a partition.
A verse from Numbers, where the congregation's division refers to shares of the spoil, supports the meaning division.
If a wall may be built against one partner's will, then exposure to sight must count as damage.
If so, the mishna should have said 'who wished to divide,' not 'who wished to make a partition'.
What then is the meaning of meḥitza?
It means a wall.
If the mishna means a wall, it should have said 'build it,' not 'build the wall'.
Had it said 'it,' one might think pegs suffice; the wording teaches that a real wall must be built.
Quoted mishna: partners build the dividing wall in the middle of the courtyard.
Is it not obvious that a jointly agreed wall stands in the middle?
No: the rule is needed where one partner initiated the wall and persuaded the other.
What is the concern? The Gemara seeks the purpose of the ruling.
The persuaded partner could claim he agreed only to use of the airspace, not the courtyard ground.
The mishna teaches that the persuaded partner must still yield ground for the wall.
Is exposure to sight then really not called damage?
Mnemonic for the proofs that follow: garden, wall, compels, divide, windows, Rav Naḥman.
Come and hear a source that may contradict the claim that sight is not damage.
The mishna on a garden: the court compels a neighbor to share in building a partition.
A garden differs: Rav's ruling bars standing in another's field, so the concern is an evil eye, not sight.
But the mishna says 'and similarly,' linking the garden rule to the stone materials used for a courtyard wall.
Mishna: a fallen courtyard wall must be rebuilt by compulsion up to four cubits.
A fallen wall is different, since a wall already stood there before.
Why would the questioner ask at all, given that the mishna clearly concerns a fallen wall?
The latter clause is needed: above four cubits no one is compelled to rebuild, since privacy is then secured.
Mishna: residents may compel co-owners to fund a gatehouse and door for the courtyard.
Conclusion: exposure to sight is called damage.
Public exposure to the street differs from an individual's gaze; the mishna concerns the public.
Come and hear another source.
Mishna: a courtyard is divided only if each share can contain four by four cubits.
Implied inference: if there is space enough for both shares, the courtyard is divided.
Isn't the division then made by a wall?
No, the division is made by a mere partition of pegs.
Come and hear the ruling on windows.
Mishna: a window must be four cubits from a neighbor's wall, whether above, below, or opposite.
Baraita: the distances guard against peeking from above, looking from below, and blocking light opposite.
Damage from a window into one's own house is different.
Come and hear.
Rav Naḥman citing Shmuel: a roof adjoining a neighbor's courtyard requires a four-cubit parapet.
The roof case differs: the courtyard owner uses his yard regularly, so the roof owner cannot know when it is used.

3a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The speaker's closing words: he will withdraw so that the other cannot see him when he comes.
Introduces a different version of the discussion, one that reads meḥitza differently.
The Gemara asks what the term meḥitza means in the Mishnah.
It means division, not a partition.
The verse in Numbers about the congregation's division of the spoil supports reading meḥitza as division.
If they build against one partner's will, then sight-damage must be counted as damage.
Let us say instead: what does meḥitza mean?
It means a wall.
A baraita on a breached vineyard fence, with the owner ordered to rebuild, shows meḥitza as a partition.
Inference: the reason for compulsion is mutual desire, so sight-damage is not called damage.
If the mishna means a wall, it should say 'build it,' not 'build the wall.'
Then what does the term mean?
It means division.
If meḥitza means division, the mishna should say 'who wished to divide,' not 'who wished to make a partition.'
The phrasing mirrors ordinary speech, as when people say: come, let us make a division.
If sight-damage counts as damage, why does the mishna specify 'if both wished'? Even if not, should compulsion apply?
Rabbi Asi, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan: the mishna concerns a courtyard not subject to the division rule, where both wish to divide.
What, then, is the tanna teaching us?
Proposed lesson: without a division rule, if both partners wish to divide, they divide the courtyard.
Mishna: where both partners wish to divide, they divide even when the courtyard is smaller than the usual minimum.
Had we learned only that, we would think mere pegs suffice; this mishna teaches that a real wall is required.
Why not teach only this mishna and omit the other one, since this one contains more detail?
The other mishna is needed for its final clause: jointly owned sacred writings are not divided even when both wish.
Alternative version: if both wished and then changed their minds, what follows? Can one retract?
Rav Asi, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan: the mishna concerns a case where each partner acquired from the other, so neither may retract.
Why not teach a case where the division rule applies even without mutual desire?
Teaching only that case would suggest that without the division rule, neither can be compelled; so the mishna teaches compulsion in both cases.
But the latter clause of the earlier mishna already says this, so how can you claim it?
Mishna's latter clause: when both wish to divide, they divide even if the courtyard is smaller than usual.
Does this not mean that either partner can compel a wall?
No, it refers only to a partition of mere pegs, not to an actual wall.
Again: why not teach only this mishna and omit the other, which has more detail?
The other mishna is needed for its final clause on jointly owned sacred writings. This concludes the alternative version.
To what case did you assign the mishna?
To a case where the courtyard is not subject to the division rule.
If there is no division rule, then if they wished to divide, what follows? Can they not retract?
Rabbi Asi, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan: they acquired each other's portions, so neither may retract.
But even a mutual acquisition is merely verbal, so what is its effect?
They acquired concrete directions, fixing which specific plot each receives.
Rav Ashi's example: each partner walked through and asserted possession of his designated portion.
Quoted mishna: the wall is built with the material customary in that place, such as gevil, gazit, kefisin, or leveinim.
Gevil is unplaned stone; gazit is planed stone.
A verse in Kings describes costly stones measured as chiseled (gazit) stones, showing gazit means planed stone.
Kefisin are small bricks; leveinim are large bricks.
Rabba bar Rava challenges Rav Ashi: how do you know gevil means unplaned stone?
Alternative: gevil may be planed stone of half gazit's thickness, with the extra handbreadth being the space between two rows.
The known tradition that kefisin are small bricks, with an extra handbreadth for the space between two rows, supports that reading.
Rav Ashi replies: both identifications are learned as traditions, not derived from the reasoning.
Rav Aḥa bar Avya challenges Rav Ashi: how do you know kefisin are small bricks rather than unplaned stones?
Alternative: kefisin are unplaned stone, with the extra handbreadth covering the protruding edges.
Gevil is unplaned and gazit planed, with the extra handbreadth for protruding edges, supporting the alternative.
Rav Ashi replies: that gevil is unplaned is a tradition, and kefisin being small bricks is likewise a tradition.
Abaye concludes: the space between two rows is a handbreadth, when filled with mortar; more is needed for gravel.
Others say the reverse: the handbreadth rule holds for gravel fill, while mortar needs less space.
Does this mean a chiseled-stone wall stands if its thickness is five handbreadths per four cubits of height?
But the one-cubit wall separating the Holy of Holies stood thirty cubits high with only six handbreadths of thickness.
That wall had an extra handbreadth, which let it stand at that height.
Why did the Second Temple not build a one-cubit partition as the First Temple did?
A six-handbreadth partition stands only up to thirty cubits, and the Second Temple was taller.
How do we know the Second Temple was taller than the First?
Haggai's verse: the glory of this latter house will be greater than the former.
Rav and Shmuel, or Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Elazar, disagree on the verse: one reads it as greater structure, the other differently.

3b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Both readings hold: the Second Temple was taller and also lasted longer than the First.
If the Second Temple was taller, why not build a thirty-cubit wall and hang a curtain above it?
A thirty-cubit wall of six handbreadths stands only because the ceiling and plaster hold it up; without them it falls.
Then build the tallest wall that can stand alone and a curtain for the rest?
Abaye: tradition requires the divider be wholly wall or wholly curtain, as in the First Temple or the Tabernacle, never a mix.
Dilemma: do the stated measurements include the plaster, or apply to the bare material?
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: the measurements include the plaster, which seems the reasonable reading.
If the measures excluded plaster, the mishna would have listed the plaster's measure, so they must include it.
Rejoinder: the measures may well exclude plaster, and the reasoning does not establish otherwise.
A plaster layer under one handbreadth is simply not taught, so the omission proves nothing.
Objection: the mishna itself gives one and a half handbreadths, so it does list amounts under a full handbreadth.
Those half-handbreadths are listed only because they can combine into a full handbreadth.
Eiruvin mishna: a beam must be wide enough to hold a small brick, half a large brick of three handbreadths.
The Eiruvin mishna refers to full three-handbreadth bricks, while this mishna covers slightly smaller ones, plaster included.
Rav Ḥisda: never demolish a synagogue before building its replacement, either from negligence or to avoid disrupting prayer.
What practical difference lies between these two explanations?
They differ where another synagogue exists: the concern of negligence still applies to rebuilding.
Mareimar and Mar Zutra alternated summer and winter synagogues so the community was never without one.
If the money for a new synagogue is already collected, may the old one be demolished first?
Even with money collected, it may be diverted to redeem captives, leaving the community without a synagogue.
If the bricks, boards and beams are ready, may the old synagogue be demolished?
Even then, materials may be sold to redeem captives, so the building must not be razed.
If so, even a completed synagogue could be sold for captives, so no synagogue should ever be razed.
People do not sell their homes, and certainly not their synagogues.
The earlier rule applies only without visible cracks; with cracks the old building may be razed first.
Rav Ashi saw cracks in the Mata Meḥasya synagogue and demolished it at once.
He moved his bed onto the site and stayed until the new building was finished and fitted with drainpipes.
How could Bava ben Buta advise Herod to raze the Temple and rebuild it, given the rule about synagogues?
But Rav Ḥisda says one must not demolish a synagogue before its replacement is built.
Either the Temple showed cracks, or the government is different, since a government never retracts its decisions.
Shmuel: if the government says it will uproot mountains, it uproots them and does not retract.
Herod had been a slave in the Hasmonean household.
Herod set his eyes on a young girl of the Hasmonean house.
Hearing a heavenly voice that a rebellious slave would now succeed, Herod rose up and killed all his masters, sparing only her.
When the girl saw that he wanted to marry her, she climbed to the roof.
She called out that any man claiming Hasmonean descent was a slave, since only she remained of that house.
Hearing this, the girl leapt from the roof and fell to the ground.
Herod preserved her body in honey for seven years.
Some hold that Herod had relations with her corpse, while others deny it.
Motive per each view: to satisfy desire, or to be said to have married a king's daughter.
Herod reasoned from Deuteronomy 17:15 that the Sages expounded it to require a king of Jewish roots.
Herod killed all the Sages but spared Bava ben Buta to take counsel with him.

4a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Herod sets a porcupine-hide garland on Bava ben Buta's head, and Herod then visits him incognito to test him.
Herod, unidentified, reports the 'evil slave Herod' and asks what he is doing.
Bava ben Buta asks what he should do to him.
Herod replies that the Master should curse him.
Bava cites Ecclesiastes: do not curse a king, even in thought.
Herod objects that he is not a king, since he rules illegally.
Bava replies that even a rich man may not be cursed.
Bava cites Ecclesiastes: do not curse a rich person in your bedchamber.
Bava adds that even a mere leader may not be cursed.
Bava cites Exodus: you shall not curse a leader of your people.
Herod argues that the rule covers only a leader who acts as your people do, which he does not.
Bava replies that he is afraid of Herod.
Herod notes that no one is present to report the remark, since they are alone.
Bava cites Ecclesiastes: a winged creature will carry the sound.
Herod admits he is the man and regrets killing the Sages, had he known they were so cautious.
What is that man's remedy for his sins?
Bava advises him to occupy himself with the light of the world, the Temple, citing Proverbs' lamp and Isaiah's light.
Isaiah: all nations will flow to the Temple; the word alludes to light.
Some report that Bava put the advice differently.
In that version he advises Herod to restore the eye of the world, the Temple, citing Numbers 15:24.
Ezekiel: I will desecrate My Temple, the delight of your eyes.
Herod objects that he fears the Roman government.
Bava advises sending a messenger who takes a year to go, stay, and return, so the Temple can be demolished meanwhile.
Rome's reply: do not demolish, or do not rebuild, and calls Herod a slave who made himself free, not a king.
The letter describes Herod as a slave who made himself a freeman.
What does reikha mean?
Samuel II: today I am tender and anointed king, showing reikha denotes royalty.
Alternatively the meaning can be learned from another verse.
Genesis: they cried before Joseph, avrekh, applied to the viceroy.
Those who have not seen Herod's building have never seen a beautiful building.
With what did Herod build it?
Rabba: with white and green marble.
Others say blue, white, and green marble.
Alternate rows project and recede, so the plaster holds.
Herod wanted to cover it with gold, but the Sages told him it looks more beautiful like sea waves.
How did Bava ben Buta give Herod such advice?
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, or R. Yehoshua ben Levi, holds that Daniel was punished for advising Nebuchadnezzar.
For what reason was Daniel punished?
Because he advised Nebuchadnezzar.
Daniel 4:24: let my counsel be acceptable; redeem your sins with charity.
Daniel 4:25-26: all this came upon Nebuchadnezzar, and at the end of twelve months, showing the advice was heeded.
A slave like Herod is obligated in mitzvot, so Bava had to help him repent; or the Temple was otherwise unbuildable.
From where do we know Daniel was punished?
Esther 4:5: she called Hatach; Hatach is Daniel.
Rav's identification: Hatach is Daniel.
This works if Daniel was cut down from his greatness.
But if Hatach means all governmental matters were decided by his word, what punishment remains?
He was thrown into the lions' den.
Quoted mishna: everything follows the regional custom.
What does the word 'everything' add?
It adds a place where walls are built of palm and laurel branches.
Quoted mishna: if the wall falls, the site and stones belong to both partners equally.
Isn't it obvious, since both partners built the wall?
No: it is needed for a wall that fell wholly into one partner's domain, or where one cleared the stones into his own.
Lest one say the party claiming a share bears the burden of proof.
The mishna teaches that both are presumed partners, so neither needs further proof.
Quoted mishna: a garden in a place where walls are customary, the court compels the neighbor to share construction.
This seems to conflict with the implication that where there is no custom, the court does not compel.
The latter clause on fields, read as inference, seems to conflict with the garden reading.
If the garden silence implies no compulsion, why is the field case needed at all?
Abaye: the tanna means that an ordinary garden and a custom-field both compel construction.
Rava objects: then why does the mishna say 'but' before the field case?
Rava: the ordinary garden is treated like a custom place and compels; an ordinary field is treated like a no-custom place and does not.
Quoted mishna: a partner building alone must withdraw onto his own land and make a border mark facing outward.
What is the meaning of the border mark?
Rav Huna: the builder bends the edge of the wall outward.
Why not mark inside? The neighbor could claim the wall as both theirs.
Such a cut or addition is noticeable, so the deception would not succeed.
A variant: Rav Huna bends the edge inward, and the outward alternative is open to the neighbor's deception.
Likewise, an added mark would be noticeable, so the deception would fail.
But the mishna teaches that the mark is made on the outside, which is a difficulty.
Rabbi Yoḥanan said:

4b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The builder smears clay on the outer face of the wall, up to a cubit, as a border mark.
Suggestion: he could smear on the inside, but then the neighbor could smear outside and claim the wall too.
Objection: if deception is a concern, the neighbor could peel off the outer clay and claim the wall as both theirs.
Peeling clay is noticeable, so the deception will not succeed.
How does one make a border mark on a partition of palm branches?
Rav Naḥman: the builder directs the tips of the branches outward.
Suggestion: he could direct them inward, but then the neighbor could direct his own outward and claim it.
Objection: the neighbor could cut off the outward tips and claim the partition as both theirs.
Counsel: the builder smears clay on the tips of the palm branches.
The neighbor could peel the clay off and claim the partition.
Peeling is noticeable, so the deception fails.
Abaye: a palm-branch partition has no remedy for proving who built it, except a written document.
Quoted mishna: if both partners agreed to build, they build it in the middle, each marking his side.
Rava of Parzika proposes that neither partner should make a border mark.
Rav Ashi: it is needed where one partner marks first, so that the other's silence leaves the wall his, a remedy against swindlers.
Rava of Parzika counters: the former clause also provides a remedy against swindlers, so why does the latter repeat it?
Rava: the former clause teaches a legal rule and incidentally a remedy, but the latter clause would then teach only a remedy.
Ravina: the latter clause concerns palm-branch barriers, excluding Abaye's view, and teaches that a border mark suffices.
Quoted mishna: for one surrounding another on three sides, the inner owner need not contribute to the three walls; R. Yosei requires the fourth side too.
Shmuel: the halakha follows R. Yosei, that the inner owner pays for all partitions if the fourth side is built.
It makes no difference whether the surrounded or the surrounding party built the fourth side.
Amoraic dispute: Rav Huna says he pays by what the other spent; Ḥiyya bar Rav says by a cheap reed-fence valuation.
The first clause of the mishna: no obligation for the first three sides, so the fourth side implies obligation.
Latter clause of the mishna: R. Yosei requires payment for all partitions when the fourth side is built, which seems to match the first tanna.
Per Rav Huna: the tanna requires only a reed-cost valuation, while R. Yosei requires actual expenditure.
Restating Ḥiyya bar Rav's view: payment is by reed-fence value.
If the tanna and R. Yosei both use reed value, what difference remains, and what does the tanna then pay?
Difference: the tanna grants a watchman's wage; R. Yosei also grants the reed-value share of the partition.
Second difference: the tanna pays only for the fourth-side partition, while R. Yosei pays for all three.
Third difference: the tanna requires payment only when the surrounded owner built the fourth side, not the surrounding owner.
R. Yosei: it makes no difference who built the fourth side; the inner owner pays for all partitions.
Alternative version: the tanna requires payment for the fourth side even if the surrounding owner built it, while R. Yosei differs.
R. Yosei: the inner owner pays only if he built the fourth side, which shows acceptance; if the surrounding owner built it, nothing is paid.

ranges.en: Ronya's field is enclosed on all sides by Ravina's fields.
Ravina demands half the cost of the partitions he built; Ronya refuses to pay.
Ravina lowers the demand to a share based on the cheaper price of reeds; Ronya still refuses.
Ravina asks for a watchman's wage instead, and Ronya still does not pay.
Once, while Ronya was harvesting dates, Ravina's situation and the date harvest are set out.
Ravina tells his sharecropper to take a cluster of dates from Ronya's field.
The sharecropper goes to fetch the dates and Ronya protests loudly.
Ravina argues that Ronya's protest shows he approves of the partitions and their protection.
Ravina argues that even a goat would make the field need guarding against eating the dates.
Ronya replies that a goat only needs to be chased away, so no partition is required.
Ravina counters that someone would have to chase the goat, so Ronya owes a watchman's wage.
Ravina brings the dispute before Rava to decide.
Rava rules that Ronya should appease Ravina with a watchman's wage, or else pay half the partition cost per Rav Huna and Rabbi Yosei.
Ronya bought land adjoining Ravina's property, raising a neighbor's right of first refusal issue.
Ravina wants to remove Ronya from the land under the halakha of a neighbor's preemptive right.
Rav Safra, son of Rav Yeiva, objects with a proverb that a small plot still bordering the parcel gives Ronya the right to stay.
Mishnah: a fallen partition wall in a shared courtyard must be rebuilt to four cubits with the partner, and his payment is presumed unless disproved.
Mishnah: a reluctant partner cannot be forced above four cubits, but one who builds against the higher wall must pay for all of it, and the roof is treated accordingly.
Mishnah: a builder's claim of non-payment is presumed true unless the neighbor brings proof that he paid.
Reish Lakish teaches that a borrower who claims early repayment within the set time is not believed, since lenders expect repayment on time.
Abaye and Rava disagree, holding that people often repay early when they happen to have the money, so their claim is credible.

5b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara states the purpose of the rule, so the claimant is not repeatedly troubled over the money.
The Gemara cites the Mishna's rule that a partner is presumed to have paid unless proof shows otherwise, as support for Abaye and Rava.
The Gemara asks what the case is: did the borrower say he repaid on the due date, or before it?
If he claimed early repayment, the Mishna would imply that people do repay before the due date, supporting Abaye and Rava.
The Gemara answers that this case differs, because each row's payment falls due on its own completion, so the time is different.
The Gemara brings a Mishna continuation as proof for Reish Lakish, that a neighbor is not believed about early repayment.
The Gemara asks again about the case: why would the claim of paying on the due date not be believed?
If the borrower claimed early payment and was disbelieved, that implies people do not repay before the due date, supporting Reish Lakish.
The Gemara answers that the neighbor's case differs, since he disputes that the Rabbis will obligate him to pay for the wall.
Rav Pappa and others acted per Abaye and Rava, Mar bar Rav Ashi per Reish Lakish, and the halakha follows Reish Lakish.
Even for orphans' property, the presumption applies: a person is not apt to repay within the due time, so no oath is needed.
A dilemma: if a lender demands payment after the due date and the borrower says he repaid early, is he believed?
The Gemara asks whether a claim against a presumption is believed, since the borrower could have lied and claimed on-time payment instead.

6a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether, where a presumption cuts against the claimant, the borrower may not argue that he would not lie.
Brings the Mishna's rule that a partner is presumed to have paid unless proof says otherwise, as a proof.
Asks what the case is: did the claimant demand payment after the due date and was told it was paid on time or early?
If the borrower claimed early repayment, the implication is that presumptions do not bar a defendant's claim that he would not lie.
Distinguishes this case: each row's payment falls due on its own completion, so the claim is effectively on-time payment.
Cites a further Mishna continuation about a reluctant neighbor and the presumption of non-payment as another proof.
Asks again what the case is, as the dispute concerns payment demanded after the due date and the reply that it was paid on time.
Concludes from the Mishna that a claim against a presumption is not believed, implying the borrower cannot argue he would not lie.
Rejects the proof: the reluctant neighbor disputes that the Rabbis will obligate him to pay for the added wall.
Rav Aha, son of Rava, asks Rav Ashi to consider a Mishna in Shevuot as a proof, introducing the case of a debt admitted in witnesses' presence.
The Mishna in Shevuot rules that if the borrower says he already paid he is exempt, but if he denies any money is owed he is liable.
Asks whether the first answer means repayment on time and the second means early repayment, which the Mishna still holds liable, implying no such presumption.
Rejects the inference: the second answer means the loan never happened, so it is a denial of borrowing, not of repayment.
Explains that one who denies borrowing is treated as one who denies repayment, and since he admitted the loan, he is liable.
Restates the Mishna on the reluctant neighbor building beside the high wall, and Rav Huna explains that a half-length or half-height extension counts as the whole.
Rav Naḥman disagrees: he built close only where he actually built, so the payment obligation covers only the corresponding portion.
Rav Huna concedes that a corner attachment is not treated as building against the whole wall, while Rav Naḥman concedes for beam supports; Rav Huna rules no presumption arises from openings.
Explains that the builder made openings in advance, expecting the neighbor would later want beams, so the openings do not imply payment.
Rav Naḥman rules that a right to place thin beams on a neighbor's wall does not include thick beams, but a thick-beam right includes thin beams.
Rav Yosef holds that a thin-beam right also includes thick beams, opposing Rav Naḥman's ruling.
Some report Rav Naḥman's ruling the other way, that thin-beam rights include thick, and that this version agrees with Rav Yosef.
Rav Naḥman rules on drainage: a right to drip water includes a drainpipe, but a drainpipe right does not include dripping.
Rav Yosef holds that a drainpipe right also includes dripping, contrary to Rav Naḥman.
Another version of Rav Naḥman's ruling reverses the drainage rule, so that the two rights include each other.
The rule differs for a hut with a willow-branch roof, which is not covered by a drainage right.
Rav Yosef holds that even a willow-branch hut's drainage right is included.
Rav Yosef acted on his view in a case involving a willow-branch hut, permitting the water to drip from it.
Rav Naḥman says that Rabba bar Avuh holds that one who rents a room to another

6b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A renter of a large building may use its projections and wall cavities up to four cubits from his room, and the wall's thickness where customary.
He may not use the front garden, though Rav Naḥman permits it; the rear yard is excluded, though Rava permits it.
Rava holds that even the rear yard of the houses may be used.
Ravina sets time limits on a neighbor's beam: thirty days for a beam, seven days for a festival sukka, and immediate privilege if fixed with clay.
Abaye rules that two houses across a public domain must each build a fence over half their roofs, staggered so neither can see the other's roof.
Asks why Abaye specifies a public domain, since the same rule would apply across a private domain.
Abaye mentions the public domain because a neighbor might argue he must hide from the public anyway, so the other cannot compel him to build.
Abaye replies that the public sees him only by day, while the neighbor is visible day and night, standing or sitting, and from living opposite.
Restates Abaye's ruling on the two-house fences, which the Gemara then questions as possibly obvious.
Asks whether the rule about each owner building half the fence is so obvious that it needs no teaching.
Answers that the rule is needed where one owner built a fence on half his roof first, so the other owner is not compelled to share the cost.
Asks what purpose the proposed compensation for expense serves, lest one neighbor claim the other must pay for the whole fence.
Explains that the neighbor who built half the fence may say the added weight would damage his own foundation as well, so he need not build the rest.
Shmuel says a roof adjoining a neighbor's courtyard needs a four-cubit fence, but roof-to-roof needs no fence, and Rav Naḥman agrees partly.
Rav Naḥman's own view: no four-cubit fence on the roof, only a partition of ten handbreadths.
Asks for what purpose Rav Naḥman requires the partition: prevention of exposure needs four cubits, catching a thief needs only pegs, and stopping goats needs less.
The partition is meant to catch the neighbor as a thief, since a peg partition allows an excuse of stretching, but ten handbreadths does not.
Objects to Rav Naḥman from a baraita: if a courtyard is higher than a neighbor's roof, the owner need not attend to it at all.
Explains the baraita means no four-cubit partition is required, though a ten-handbreadth partition is, as Rav Naḥman holds.
Amoraim disagree on two adjoining courtyards at different levels: Rav Huna has the lower owner build from his level up and the upper owner from his level up.
Rav Ḥisda holds the upper owner assists by building from below, including the part opposite the lower courtyard.
A baraita supports Rav Ḥisda: the upper owner must build from below, and if a courtyard is above a roof, he need not build a partition.
Recounts a two-story building whose lower story collapsed, and the lower owner proposes that they demolish and rebuild the whole structure together.
The upper owner replies that he lives comfortably and is under no obligation to rebuild the lower residence.

7a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The lower owner proposes to dismantle the structure and rebuild it.
The upper owner objects that he has no place to live during the renovation.
The lower owner offers to rent the upper owner a place to live for the duration.
The upper owner refuses to move, and tells the lower owner to crawl in and out of his apartment, since the damage is not his problem.
Rav Ḥama rules that the upper owner can legally prevent the rebuilding, except where the supports sink below ten handbreadths, which belong to the lower owner.
The Gemara qualifies the ruling: if they stipulated to rebuild together if the house sinks, they must dismantle and rebuild.
Asks to what extent the ceiling must drop before the stipulation is triggered.
Cites a Mishna on building a house without stated dimensions, where the height equals half the length plus half the width, to answer the question.
Rabba rejects this attribution to Rav Naḥman, warning against putting foolish opinions in his name.
Rabba states Rav Naḥman's actual view: the ceiling need only be high enough for normal living.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua defines the minimum height as high enough to bring in reed bundles from Meḥoza and turn around.
A man builds a wall outside his neighbor's windows, and the neighbor says it blocks his light and darkens his house.
The neighbor complains that the wall darkens him.
The builder offers to seal the windows and make new windows above his wall in the neighbor's wall.
The neighbor objects that this will damage his wall.
The builder offers to demolish the wall to the window level, rebuild it, and make windows above his wall.
The neighbor objects that an old lower wall with a new upper part will not endure.
The builder offers to demolish the wall to the ground and rebuild it, then make windows above his wall.
The neighbor objects that a new wall in an old house will not endure.
The builder offers to demolish the whole house and put windows in the new structure he will erect.
The neighbor objects that he would have no place to live in the meantime.
The builder offers to rent the neighbor a place to live.
The neighbor declines, not wanting to bother with moving.
Rav Ḥama rules that by law the neighbor can prevent the building of the wall, and the Gemara notes the two cases are alike.
Asks why the second case is needed, since it is identical to the first.
Teaches that even if the neighbor uses the house only for straw and wood, blocking light still counts as damage that he can prevent.
Two brothers divide their father's estate: one takes a hall and the other a garden, and the garden owner builds a wall in front of the hall's opening.
The hall owner complains that the wall blocks his light and darkens his house.
The garden owner replies that he is building on his own property.
Rav Ḥama rules that by right he may say that, since he is permitted to build there.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi how this differs from a baraita on brothers dividing an estate.
Cites the baraita: where one brother takes a vineyard and the other a field, the vineyard owner gets four cubits of the field, as the division was on that condition.
Rav Ashi replies that there they assessed the value of the fields, including the work area, but here they did not.
Ravina asks what happened here: did they not assess values, or are the brothers fools to divide without assessing?
Rav Ashi replies that they assessed the bricks, beams and boards, but not the airspace, so each retains full rights to his airspace.
Suggests the hall owner could say the former bright hall has become a small dark room.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi says the seller gave only a place that is called a hall by name, though it is no longer used that way.
Rav Ashi cites a baraita: a sale of a beit kor of dirt is valid even if it is only a letekh, since only the name was sold.
Qualifies the baraita: the rule applies only if the land is actually called a beit kor.
The baraita continues with the same rule for an orchard lacking pomegranates and a vineyard lacking grapevines, each qualified by the name of the land.
Rejects the analogy: the seller can say he sold only the name, but the hall owner can say his share was taken on the condition of living there as the fathers did.
Begins an objection to Rav Ḥama's ruling that the brother may build in front of the hall; the text breaks off here.

7b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Neharde'ans follow their own line; Rav Ḥama ruled like Shmuel that brothers who divide an estate have no right-of-way against each other.
Shmuel continues that brothers have no rights of windows, ladders, or water channels against each other, and that these are fixed halakhot.
Rava disagrees and holds that brothers do have all these rights.
Rav Ḥama rules that orphans' promissory note cannot be used to collect, nor can it be torn up, where a receipt was produced.
Explains that the note must not be torn because the orphans may later prove the receipt was forged.
Rav Aḥa son of Rava asks Ravina what the halakha is in this case.
Ravina rules that the halakha follows Rav Ḥama in all cases except the receipt, since witnesses are not presumed liars.
Mar Zutra son of Rav Mari holds the halakha follows Rav Ḥama here too, since the receipt was never produced when the father lived, suggesting forgery.
Mishna: residents of a courtyard may compel each member to share the cost of a gatehouse and door.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees: not every courtyard needs a gatehouse, so each must be judged by its needs.
Mishna: residents of a city may compel each member to share the cost of a wall, double doors, and a crossbar.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees again: not every town needs a wall.
Mishna: one who lives in the city twelve months, or buys a residence there, is considered a townsman for these obligations.
Asks whether a gatehouse is truly beneficial, citing the pious man who built one and whom Elijah stopped speaking with.
Resolves the conflict: the mishna's gatehouse is inside the courtyard, while the pious man's is outside, blocking the poor.
Alternative resolution: both gatehouses are outside, but only one has a door that prevents the poor from being heard.
Alternative resolution: both have doors, but only one needs a key, which the poor cannot reach.
Alternative resolution: both need keys, but one is kept inside the courtyard and the other outside.
The Gemara restates the mishna's rule that residents may compel each member to contribute to a courtyard gatehouse and door.
A baraita: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says only a courtyard adjoining the public domain needs a gatehouse.
Explains that even a courtyard not adjoining the public domain sometimes receives people pressed in by crowds, so the Rabbis require it generally.
Restates the rule on compelling city residents to build a wall, and a baraita adds double doors and a crossbar for the city.
A baraita: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says only a city adjoining the border needs a wall.
The Rabbis reply that invading troops sometimes reach even inland cities, so every city benefits from a wall.
Rabbi Elazar asks Rabbi Yoḥanan whether wall costs are collected by the number of persons or by their net worth.
Rabbi Yoḥanan replies that costs are collected by net worth, an established halakha Elazar must follow.
Variant: Rabbi Elazar asks whether wall costs are collected by proximity of houses to the wall or by net worth.
Rabbi Yoḥanan replies that costs are collected by proximity of houses to the wall.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia imposed the wall tax even on the Sages.
Reish Lakish objects that the Sages do not require protection.
Reish Lakish cites Psalms 139:17-18 on how precious and numerous God's beloved ones are, as support.
Asks whom the verse refers to, since the righteous cannot outnumber the grains of sand that Genesis describes for all Israel.
Explains the verse means the deeds of the righteous, not the righteous themselves, are more numerous than sand.
Reish Lakish argues a fortiori: if sand protects the shore from the sea, the more numerous deeds of the righteous protect them.
Rabbi Yoḥanan asks why Reish Lakish did not cite the verse about the wall and towers from Song of Songs.
Cites Song of Songs 8:10: I am a wall refers to the Torah, and my breasts are like towers.

8a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gemara identifies the towers in the verse by following Reish Lakish's reading, which matches Rava's exposition.
Rava's proof from the Song of Songs verse about the wall and towers, read as Israel and its houses of study.
The towers are explained as synagogues and study halls.
Rav Naḥman bar Rav Ḥisda imposed the poll tax even on the Sages.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak objects that this violates the Torah, Prophets and Writings.
Support from the Torah verse in Deuteronomy about the holy ones.
Continuation of the Deuteronomy verse, cited as the Torah's teaching against taxing scholars.
Moses asks God that even when God loves the nations, the holy ones stay in God's hand.
The rest of the Deuteronomy verse is cited to show scholars sit at God's feet.
Rav Yosef glosses the verse: these are scholars who travel from city to city to study Torah.
The phrase about receiving words is glossed as discussing and teaching the words of God.
The Gemara moves from the Torah verse to the same idea in the Prophets.
Support from the Hosea verse, cited as a prophetic source.
The Hosea verse on gathering Israel despite hired lovers and the burden of kings.
Ulla explains that this verse is partly written in Aramaic.
Ulla's Aramaic reading: the word for hired means learning, so the verse concerns Torah study.
Support from the Ezra verse, cited as a Writings source.
The Ezra verse says tribute, impost and toll may not be imposed on them.
Rav Yehuda explains each term in the verse as a specific tax: king's portion, head tax, and arnona.
Rav Pappa imposed a tax on orphans to dig a new cistern.
Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi objects that the water may never be found, so the money is wasted.
Rav Pappa replies that he will collect the money and return it if the well fails.
Rav Yehuda: all residents pay for city gates, including orphans, but Sages are exempt since they need no protection.
All residents pay for cisterns, including Sages, since they too need water.
This applies only when money is collected rather than a mass labor effort; when people must dig themselves, Sages are exempt.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi opens his storehouses in a drought and admits only those who study Bible, Mishna, Talmud and halakha and aggada.
Ignoramuses are told not to enter.
Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram, unknown to Rabbi, pushes in and enters.
Rabbi Yonatan asks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to sustain him.
Rabbi asks whether he has read the Bible.
He replies that he has not.
Rabbi asks whether he has studied Mishna.
He again replies no.
Rabbi asks by what merit he should sustain him.
Sustain me like a dog and a raven, which are fed without learning anything.
After he leaves, Rabbi sits down.
Rabbi is distressed and says he regrets giving bread to an ignoramus.
Rabbi Shimon suggests that the man may be Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram, his disciple who refused to profit from Torah honor.
They check, find it so, and Rabbi says everyone may enter, since others may hide being scholars.
Rabbi's consistent view: suffering comes to the world only because of ignoramuses.
The story of the crown tax imposed on Tiberias, brought before Rabbi.
The city leaders ask that the Sages contribute along with them.
Rabbi says no, the Sages are exempt.
The leaders threaten to run away, leaving the Torah scholars with the entire burden.
Rabbi tells them to run away as they wish.
Half the city flees, and the authorities reduce the tax; the remaining half come to Rabbi.
The remaining residents ask that the Sages contribute along with them.
Rabbi again says no, the Sages are exempt.
The remaining residents threaten to run away too.
Rabbi tells them to run away, and they all flee.
Only one launderer remains and is taxed, then he flees, and the crown tax is canceled.
Rabbi concludes that suffering comes to the world only because of ignoramuses.
The mishna teaches how long one must live in a city to be treated as one of its people.
A baraita about a caravan that lodged in an idolatrous city seems to conflict with the mishna's thirty-day rule.
Rava says there is no difficulty: the twelve months apply to citizens, the thirty days to residents of a city that is being taken.
A baraita on vows, showing that a vow about a city's people uses twelve months or thirty days by its wording.
The Gemara asks whether twelve months is required for all matters.
A baraita listing the periods for each charitable fund: thirty days, three months, six months, nine, and twelve for city columns.
Rabbi Asi says Rabbi Yoḥanan explains that the mishna's twelve months applies only to the city's columns.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says all must contribute to the city's columns, even orphans, but the Sages are exempt.
Rav Pappa: orphans pay for the city wall, the city horseman and the armory guard, but Sages do not.
The general principle: orphans pay for anything from which they benefit.
Rabba imposed a charitable levy on the orphans of the house of bar Maryon.
Abaye objects with a baraita: no charity may be imposed on orphans, even to redeem captives.
Rabba replies that he did it to honor them as benefactors, not to help the poor.
The mother of King Shapur sends Rav Yosef a purse of dinars and says it should be used for a great mitzva.
Rav Yosef sits and considers the condition.
What is the great mitzva she meant?
Abaye answers that, based on the baraita, the money cannot be given to orphans and should be used for captives' ransom.

8b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Redeeming captives is a great mitzva, as the Sages taught.
Rava asks Rabba bar Mari where the Sages derive that redeeming captives is a great mitzva.
Rabba bar Mari answers with Jeremiah 15:2 listing death, sword, famine and captivity.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says the last punishment listed in that verse is the most severe of them.
The sword is worse than death.
Rabbi Yoḥanan's point can be derived from a verse or from logical reasoning.
Logic: the sword mutilates the body while natural death does not.
Psalm 116:15 proves that the death of the pious is precious, so death is better than the sword.
Famine is worse than the sword, shown by logic that the famine victim suffers more.
Lamentations 4:9 proves that famine is worse than the sword, and captivity includes all of them.
A baraita: the charity fund is collected by two people and distributed by three, like a court.
Charity platter food is collected and distributed by three people because it is handled daily.
Platter food goes to any poor person, the fund only to the city poor, and uses may be changed as needed.
Residents may set local measures, prices and wages, and fine violators.
The Gemara restates the baraita: no authority is given to fewer than two people.
The Gemara asks where these rules are derived from.
Rav Naḥman derives it from Exodus 28:5, where the plural they implies two collectors.
Authority is the concern, not trust; one person may be trusted, which supports Rabbi Ḥanina.
Rabbi Ḥanina's report that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi appointed two brothers to the charity fund.
What is the authority associated with collecting charity?
Collectors may seize collateral for charity, even on Shabbat eve, according to Rav Naḥman citing Rabba bar Avuh.
The objection from Jeremiah 30:20 and Rav's teaching that even charity collectors will be punished as oppressors.
Reply: the collectors may force only the rich; Rava compelled Rav Natan bar Ami to give four hundred dinars.
Daniel 12:3 is cited about those who are wise and shine like the firmament.
The wise who shine are interpreted as a judge who issues a true judgment.
Daniel 12:3 continues: those who turn the many to righteousness shine like stars.
Those who turn the many to righteousness are the charity collectors.
A baraita reads the same verse as referring to judges, charity collectors, and schoolteachers.
Asking which schoolteachers are meant, since not every teacher merits this praise.
Rav says Rav Shmuel bar Sheilat is an example of such a teacher.
Rav found Rav Shmuel bar Sheilat standing in a garden.
Rav asks whether he abandoned his trust and neglected his students.
He replies that he has not seen his garden for thirteen years and his thoughts remain with the children.
What did Ravina say about the Sages?
Judges 5:31 is cited: those who love God shine like the sun in its might.
A baraita: charity collectors may not separate from each other when they are out of sight of one another.
One collector may go to the gate while another goes to a shop, provided they can see each other.
If a collector finds coins in the market, he must put them in the charity purse, not his pocket.
He may take them home later from the purse, to avoid suspicion.
Likewise, if a collector is repaid a debt of a mina in the market, the same rule applies.
He must deposit it in the charity purse and only later take it home.
Collectors with no poor to serve may exchange coins for others, but not for themselves.
Platter collectors with no poor to serve may sell food to others, but not to themselves.
Charity coins are counted one by one, not two by two.
Abaye says Rabba used to avoid sitting on mats bought with charity funds.
Rabba changed his view after hearing the baraita that residents may change the use of charity.
Abaye says Rabba used to keep two purses, one for the poor of the world, one for the poor of his city.
Rabba changed to one purse after hearing Shmuel say so to Rav Taḥalifa bar Avdimi.
Shmuel instructed Rav Taḥalifa bar Avdimi to use only one purse.

9a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ashi also made a single purse and stipulated with the townspeople about how it is to be used.
Rav Ashi adds that no stipulation is needed, since donors trust his discretion over the money.
Two butchers agreed on schedule penalties; one violated it, and Rava ordered him to compensate the other.
Rav Yeimar bar Shelamya objects that the city may fine violators of its ordinances, which seems to conflict with Rava's ruling.
Rava does not respond to the objection.
Rav Pappa defends Rava's silence: the rule applies only where no prominent person is in the city.
Where a prominent person is present, the residents cannot make binding regulations without his approval.
A baraita: one does not reckon accounts with charity collectors or with Temple treasurers.
II Kings 12:16 is cited as a hint that treasurers are trusted without reckoning, since they act in good faith.
Rabbi Elazar: even a trusted household treasurer should be counted, as the Temple scribes counted the money in II Kings 12.
Rav Huna: collectors check the need of one asking for food but not for clothing.
Rav Huna's distinction is reasoned logically: someone in rags is exposed to shame, while a hungry person is not.
Isaiah 58:7 is read with a shin as paros, meaning examine, and the clothing clause shows the reverse.
Rav Yehuda reverses the rule: collectors examine the one seeking clothing but not the one seeking food.
Rav Yehuda's logic: the hungry suffers while the one in rags does not suffer in the same way.
Isaiah 58:7 read with a samekh means share immediately, and the clothing clause means once the need is clear.
A baraita is taught in accordance with Rav Yehuda's view.
The baraita: a poor man asking for clothing is examined, but one asking for food is not.
The mishna in Peah: a traveling poor man receives a loaf of set value and lodging provisions, and three meals on Shabbat.
A baraita: a poor man who goes door to door need not be attended to.
A poor man going door to door came before Rav Pappa, who did not attend to him.
Rav Sama objects that if the Master does not help, no one will, and he will die of hunger.
Rav Pappa cites the baraita that one need not attend to a door-to-door beggar.
Rav Sama replies that the baraita means no large gift is required, but a small gift is.
Rav Asi: one should never hold back from giving at least a third of a shekel a year.
Nehemiah 10:33 is cited for the annual third-of-a-shekel obligation.
Rav Asi: charity is equal to all the other mitzvot combined, as the verse uses the plural mitzvot.
The plural mitzvot in the verse is read as a sign that charity outweighs all of them.
Rabbi Elazar: one who causes a good deed is greater than one who does it himself.
Isaiah 32:17 is cited: the causing of righteousness brings lasting peace and assurance.
If one merits, he gives wholeheartedly; if not, he is compelled to house poor soldiers.
Rava urges the people of Meḥoza to act charitably toward one another to keep peace with the government.
Rabbi Elazar: while the Temple stands, a shekel contribution brings atonement.
Now that the Temple is gone, charity is the means of atonement; otherwise the nations will take money by force.
Even money taken by force from them is counted to them as charity.
Isaiah 60:17 is cited: your oppressors will be counted as charity.
Rava says Ulla told him this matter.

9b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Elazar's teaching is introduced as the source of the nickname of the infant who perverted his mother's ways.
What is meant by the verse describing God donning charity like a coat of mail?
Just as each scale of the armor combines into one large coat, each peruta given combines into a great sum.
Rabbi Ḥanina derives the same idea from a different verse.
Isaiah 64:5 is cited: each thread of a garment combines, so each peruta of charity combines into a large sum.
Why was Ulla called the infant who perverted his mother's ways?
Rav Aḥadvoi bar Ami asked Rav Sheshet a question on leprosy and impurity.
Rav Aḥadvoi asks from where we know that a leper renders a person impure during his days of counting.
Rav Sheshet answers that since he renders garments impure, he also renders people impure.
Rav Aḥadvoi objects that connected impurity may be different, as carrying a carcass impures clothes but not people.
Rav Sheshet asks how we know a creeping animal's carcass impures a person, if not because it impures garments.
Rav Aḥadvoi cites Leviticus 22:5, which explicitly says that touching a creeping animal impures a person.
Rav Sheshet asks how we know that semen impures a person, if not by analogy to garments.
Rav Aḥadvoi cites Leviticus 22:4 and expounds the extra word or to include one who touches semen.
Rav Aḥadvoi replied mockingly, Rav Sheshet was offended, and Rav Aḥadvoi became mute and forgot his learning.
His mother wept before Rav Sheshet, reminding him she had nursed him; he prayed and Rav Aḥadvoi was healed.
The Gemara asks where we derive that a leper impures a person during his days of counting.
A baraita from Rabbi Shimon bar Yoḥai derives the leper's impurity from the repeated wording about washing garments.
Rabbi Elazar: one who gives charity in secret is greater than Moses our teacher.
Deuteronomy 9:19 describes Moses fearing anger and wrath.
Proverbs 21:14 describes charity given in secret pacifying anger, though a bribe brings fierce wrath.
This disagrees with a statement of Rabbi Yitzḥak.
Rabbi Yitzḥak: a secret gift pacifies anger but not fierce wrath, as the verse shows.
Another version: any judge who takes a bribe brings fierce wrath upon the world.
Rabbi Yitzḥak: one who gives a peruta to a poor man gets six blessings, and one who comforts him gets eleven.
Isaiah 58:7 is cited as the source of the six blessings for giving to the poor.
The eleven blessings for comforting a poor person are introduced.
Isaiah 58:10-12 lists the blessings promised to one who comforts the afflicted.
Rabbi Yitzḥak then asks about a further verse.
What is the meaning of Proverbs 21:21 about one who pursues charity finding life and honor?
God supplies money to anyone who pursues charity so he can perform charity.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: God sends him deserving people to whom he can give.
The rule is meant to exclude Rabba's different derivation.
What does the exclusion of Rabba's interpretation mean?
Rabba expounds Jeremiah 18:23, where Jeremiah asks God to make his enemies stumble.
Jeremiah asks that those seeking to give charity be made to stumble among undeserving people, so they get no reward.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: one who habitually gives charity merits sons who are masters of wisdom, wealth and aggada.

10a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Proverbs 21:21 is glossed: pursuing charity brings life, wealth, and honor, paralleling the wisdom and aggada verses.
A baraita: Rabbi Meir says one can answer a critic who asks why God does not sustain the poor Himself.
The critic asks: if your God loves the poor, why does He not sustain them Himself?
God commands us to sustain the poor so we are saved from the judgment of Gehenna through that charity.
Turnus Rufus asks Rabbi Akiva the same question about God and the poor.
Rabbi Akiva gives the same answer about being saved from Gehenna through charity.
Turnus Rufus rejects the answer: charity actually condemns Jews to Gehenna.
Turnus's parable of a king who angered his slave, whom others feed, showing that defying the decree is an offense.
Leviticus 25:55 is cited: the children of Israel are God's slaves.
Rabbi Akiva's counter-parable of a king who angered his son, and a gift is sent to the one who fed him.
Deuteronomy 14:1 is cited: you are the children of the Lord your God.
Turnus says Jews are sons only when they do God's will and slaves when they do not, so his parable fits now.
Rabbi Akiva replies by citing the verse that follows.
Isaiah 58:7 is cited: when are the poor brought into houses? Now, when billeting soldiers is imposed.
Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Shalom: a person's livelihood and losses are allocated from Rosh HaShana, and the verse shows which applies.
A story: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai's nephews gave away most of their money after a dream, and the government took the rest.
Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai reassures them and reveals the dream.
The nephews ask how he knew.
He says he saw the dream about them.
The nephews ask why he did not tell them the dream in advance.
He did not want them to give for the wrong reason, so the mitzva would be done purely for its own sake.
Rav Pappa slipped on a ladder and said that haters of Israel are punished like Shabbat violators and idolaters.
Ḥiyya bar Rav of Difti suggests Rav Pappa may have failed to sustain a poor person, which caused this near-punishment.
A baraita: one who averts his eyes from charity is treated as if he worshipped idols.
Deuteronomy 15:9 and 13:14 are compared to show that a base thought is treated like idol worship.
The comparison makes a base thought of refusing charity equal to idolatry.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei: acts of charity bring great peace and advocates before the Father in Heaven.
Jeremiah 16:5 is cited, with kindness and mercy read as kind deeds and charity.
Rabbi Yehuda: great is charity, which brings the redemption closer.
Isaiah 56:1 is cited: uphold justice and do charity, for My salvation is near.
Ten strong things in the world are each overcome by a stronger one, with death the strongest.
Proverbs 10:2 is cited: charity delivers from death.
Rabbi Dostai son of Rabbi Yannai: a human gift to a king is uncertain to be accepted, but God is not like that.
Psalms 17:15 is cited: one who gives a peruta to a poor person merits seeing God's face.
Rabbi Elazar would give a peruta to a poor person before praying, citing the same verse.
What is the meaning of being satisfied with the likeness when one awakes?
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: these are Torah scholars who forgo sleep in this world and are satisfied with God's radiance in the World to Come.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: Proverbs 19:17 would be impossible to say if not written, since giving to the poor is lending to God.
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba reports Rabbi Yoḥanan's point.
Proverbs 11:4 and 10:2 seem to contradict each other on whether charity delivers from death.
The two verses refer to two kinds of charity: one saves from an unnatural death, the other from Gehenna.
Zephaniah 1:15 is cited, with the day of wrath linked to Gehenna.
The charity that saves from an unnatural death is identified.

10b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Describes giving charity anonymously, excluding the practices of Mar Ukva and Rabbi Abba.
How then should one give charity so that neither party knows the other?
A baraita on how to get sons suggests that giving to the charity box is not always preferred, which seems to conflict.
Rabbi Abbahu: Moses asked God how Israel's horn would be exalted, and God answered through giving in Exodus 30:12.
Solomon was asked how far charity's power reaches, and he cites David's verse in Psalms 112:9.
Isaiah 33:16 is cited: his bread is given and his water is sure, so he dwells on high.
Rabbi Abbahu: Solomon was asked who is destined for the World to Come.
Solomon answers: those honored before their elders, as Isaiah 24:23 says.
Yosef son of Rabbi Yehoshua, when ill, reports seeing an inverted world where the high were low.
Rabbi Yehoshua calls it a clear world, the true standard of worth.
How did Yosef see the Torah scholars in that world?
They are important there just as they are important here.
Yosef heard that in the World to Come people say happy is the one who arrives with his learning.
Yosef heard that those executed by the government have such status that no one can stand in their section.
Who are these martyrs? Not Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues, but perhaps the martyrs of Lod.
A baraita: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai asked his students about Proverbs 14:34 on righteousness exalting a nation.
Rabbi Eliezer: the righteous nation is Israel.
II Samuel 7:23 is cited: who is like Your people Israel, one nation on earth.
Nations' charity is a sin for them, since they do it only to be exalted.
Ezra 6:10 is cited: the nations offer sacrifices for the king's sake, so it is not full charity.
A baraita says one who gives a sela to be credited with his children's life and the World to Come is fully righteous.
Resolution: the baraita refers to a Jew, while the other refers to a gentile.
Rabbi Yehoshua answers the same verse: Israel is righteous and gentile charity is sin.
Gentile charity is a sin because they do it only to prolong their kingdom.
Daniel 4:24 is cited: Nebuchadnezzar was told to atone through charity to extend his serenity.
Rabban Gamliel answers likewise, citing Israel as the nation exalted.
II Samuel 7:23 is cited again.
Gentile charity is sin because they do it only to show off.
One who is haughty falls into Gehenna, and wrath means Gehenna.
Zephaniah 1:15 is cited: that day is a day of wrath.
Rabban Gamliel says we still need to hear Rabbi Eliezer HaModa'i's view.
Rabbi Eliezer HaModa'i gives the same reading.
Israel is the nation exalted by righteousness.
II Samuel 7:23 is cited once more.
Gentile charity is sin, since they do it only to mock Israel.
Jeremiah 40:3 is cited: Nebuzaradan says the disaster comes because of sin.
Rabbi Neḥunya ben HaKana: righteousness and kindness belong to Israel, and sin to the nations.
Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai says Rabbi Neḥunya's view is more precise than the others.
What was Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai's own interpretation?
Just as a sin offering atones for Israel, so charity atones for the nations.
Ifera Hurmiz sent four hundred dinars to Rabbi Ami, who refused, and Rava accepted them for peace with the kingdom.
Rabbi Ami was angry at Rava's acceptance.
Isaiah 27:11 is cited: when the boughs are withered, they shall be broken off and burned.
Rava and Rabbi Ami both acted for peace with the kingdom, but Rabbi Ami thought the money should go to gentile poor.
Rava gave the money to gentile poor, and Rabbi Ami was angry.

11a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Those who reported the story to Rav Ami did not finish it, so he never learned Rava gave the money to gentile poor.
A baraita introduces a story about Binyamin the righteous, the supervisor of the charity fund.
During a drought a woman came to Binyamin and asked him to sustain her.
She asks him directly to sustain her.
He replies that the charity fund has nothing left in it.
She warns that without his help she and her seven sons will die.
He stood up and sustained her from his own funds.
Later he fell gravely ill, and the ministering angels pleaded with God.
The angels cite God's saying that whoever saves one life in Israel saves a world, so Binyamin should not die young.
They tore up his sentence.
A Sage taught that twenty-two years were added to his life.
King Munbaz gave away his treasures and his ancestors' treasures in a drought, and his brothers protested.
Munbaz replied that his ancestors stored treasures below where hands can reach, while he stores them above, citing Psalms 85:12.
Psalms 89:15 is cited: righteousness and justice are the foundation of God's throne.
His ancestors stored something unproductive, while he stored something that yields fruit.
Isaiah 3:10 is cited: the righteous shall eat the fruit of their deeds.
His ancestors stored money.
He stored up souls instead.
Proverbs 11:30 is cited: the fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and the wise win souls.
His ancestors stored for others, while he stored for himself.
Deuteronomy 24:13 is cited: it shall be righteousness to you.
His ancestors stored for this world, while he stored for the World to Come.
Isaiah 58:8 is cited: your righteousness goes before you, the glory of the Lord your rearguard.
A mishna: buying a residence in the city makes one a citizen immediately.
The mishna disagrees with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says any land purchase suffices.
A different baraita attributes to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that only land suitable for a residence suffices, which contradicts the first.
The two baraitot are two tanna'im disagreeing about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view.
Mishna: a courtyard is divided only if each share has four by four cubits, and a field only with room for nine kav of seed each.
The nine kav requirement for a field is restated.
Rabbi Yehuda requires room for nine half-kav of seed each for a field.
A garden requires room for a half-kav of seed each.
Rabbi Akiva says half that amount, a quarter kav, suffices.
Other properties, such as a hall, drawing room, dovecote and bathhouse, are divided only if each part keeps its use.
The general rule: divide if each part keeps the name of the original item; otherwise do not.
Division is at the request of both owners, and sacred scrolls are never divided.
Rabbi Asi says Rabbi Yoḥanan: the four cubits are in addition to the space in front of house entrances.
A baraita: a courtyard is divided only if there are eight cubits for each.
The mishna says four cubits, which seems to contradict the baraita, so the baraita must follow Rabbi Asi.
Some raise the baraita as a contradiction to the mishna and reconcile it with Rabbi Asi's explanation.
Rabbi Asi explains that the four cubits are beyond the space for entrances.
Rav Huna: a courtyard is divided according to its entrances.
Rav Ḥisda: four cubits are given for each entrance, and the rest divided equally.
A baraita is taught in accordance with Rav Ḥisda.
Illustration: one entrance gets four cubits and two entrances get eight, and the rest is split evenly.
A wide entrance of eight cubits takes eight cubits in front and four cubits in the courtyard.
What is the purpose of the four cubits in the courtyard here?
Abaye explains: he takes a strip four cubits wide along the length of the courtyard.
Ameimar: a pit for animal feed has four cubits on every side for the animals.
This applies only when the pit has no special entrance and is accessed from all sides.

11b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Only four cubits in front of the entrance are granted when the owner has his own entrance to the pit.
Rav Huna: a portico opening onto a courtyard gets no adjoining four cubits, since one can unload inside it.
Rav Sheshet objects from a baraita that gates of porticos do get four cubits.
That baraita refers to a study hall portico, which is closed and not used for unloading.
A baraita: a gatehouse, portico and balcony get four cubits, but five houses on one balcony share only one set.
Rabbi Yoḥanan asks Rabbi Yannai whether a chicken coop with a staircase gets four cubits.
Rabbi Yannai: the four cubits are for unloading animals, which chickens do not need.
Rava asks Rav Naḥman about a house half roofed and half open: does it get four cubits?
Rav Naḥman: no, since the owner can unload inside even when the roof covers the outside part.
Rav Huna asks Rabbi Ami whether residents of an alleyway can block a resident from moving his entrance to another alleyway.
Rabbi Ami: yes, they can block him.
Rav Huna asks whether a king's billeting burden is divided by number of people or number of entrances.
Rabbi Ami: it is divided by the number of people in each household.
A baraita: dung in a courtyard is divided by entrances, while billeting is divided by household size.
Rav Huna: residents can prevent a neighbor from sealing an area by the entrance, since it would lengthen the way.
A baraita on five courtyards opening onto an alleyway seems to contradict this ruling.
The two baraitot are a dispute between tanna'im, with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar differing.
Why does the baraita mention courtyards at all, when it is about alleyways?
The baraita is incomplete and teaches the same point in terms of Rabbi Yehuda's view of the outermost courtyard.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: all five courtyards may use the alleyway.
The Master's statement: a sealed entrance may be reopened without objection from the alleyway residents.
Rava: this applies only if the doorposts were left intact; if they were broken, the residents can object.
Abaye says a baraita supports Rava's view.

12a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A house with a sealed entrance keeps its four cubits; breaking its doorposts negates them.
Baraita: a sealed grave impurifies only opposite its entrance; broken doorposts make it impure all around.
The same contrast for a house: a sealed entrance limits impurity, a broken one spreads it all around.
Rabbi Yohanan rules that residents of the destination city may prevent locals from sealing alleys leading to it.
Clarifies that this applies even when the destination has another route, not only when no other route exists.
Rav's principle that a public path may not be ruined, supported by Rav Giddel's statement about established routes.
Shmuel rules that residents of alleys opening onto a public thoroughfare may be prevented from installing doors.
Some infer that Shmuel's rule covers only four cubits, based on Rabbi Zeira's report of Rav Nahman.
Rejects that inference: the four-cubit rule concerns impurity only, while crowds may enter far past four cubits.
Mishna: a field is not divided unless each share can sow nine kav; Rabbi Yehuda's measure is nine half-kav.
Gemara reconciles the two views: each Sage ruled according to the custom of his own locale.
What is the practice in Babylonia, where the Mishna was not taught?
Rav Yosef: in Babylonia, a field is a parcel whose size equals one day's plowing.
Does 'day's plowing' mean a day in the planting season or the plowing season? Either reading yields an unfair payment.
Two resolutions: plowing before sowing is repeated afterward, or rocky ground takes longer to plow in the plowing season.
Rav Nahman: a joint water cistern is divided only if each share supplies a day's irrigation work.
Shmuel's father: an orchard is divided only if each share is large enough to sow three kav.
Baraita setup: one tells another he is selling him part of a vineyard without specifying how much.
Sumakhos: the seller may not give less than an area sowable with three kav.
Rabbi Yosei: Sumakhos's ruling is mere prophecy, not grounded in reasoning.
What is the measure in Babylonia for this matter?
Rava bar Kisna: three rows of twelve vines, the amount a person can hoe in one day.
Rabbi Avdimi of Haifa: since the Temple's destruction, prophecy was taken from prophets and given to Sages.
Does this mean a Sage is not a prophet?
Prophecy was taken from the prophets but was not taken from the Sages.
Ameimar: a Sage is greater than a prophet.
Psalm 90:12 speaks of a prophet with a heart of wisdom; comparisons run from lesser to greater, so wisdom ranks higher.
Abaye: the Sages still enjoy the prophetic gift, as shown by how their rulings recur.
A statement of a great man is cited in another great man's name in accordance with his view.
Rava objects: perhaps both sages were born under the same constellation and so reach the same conclusions.
Rava's alternative: the Sages still have prophecy, as a statement of a great man is cited in another's name.
Proof: a great man's statement is cited by a later great man in accordance with his view.

12b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ashi's claim that the first Sage's view matches Rabbi Akiva's, so it must have come through prophecy.
Rav Ashi's question: perhaps both were born under the same constellation and so reached the same view.
Rav Ashi: rather, know that a great man's statement is later cited as a halakha transmitted from Sinai.
A great man's statement is cited as a Sinai tradition in accordance with his view, showing prophetic insight.
Objection: perhaps he reached the view by chance, like a blind man finding a skylight.
Rabbi Yohanan: since the Temple's destruction, prophecy was taken from prophets and given to fools and children.
In what way was prophecy given to fools?
Example: Mar bar Rav Ashi overheard a fool in Mehoza mention an appointment to the yeshiva.
Mar bar Rav Ashi concluded the fool's words signaled his own success and went to Mata Mehasya.
The Sages sent delegations that he detained until a quorum of ten; then he taught and was appointed head of the yeshiva.
Rav Aha of Difti applied the aphorism to himself: one treated poorly will not soon be treated well.
In what way was prophecy given to children?
The daughter of Rav Hisda, asked whom she wants as a husband, answers that she wants both of them.
Rava says he will be the last; this came to pass as she later married Rami bar Hama and then Rava.
Rabbi Avdimi of Haifa: before eating one has two hearts; after eating one has only one heart.
Proof from Job 11:12 on a hollow man and Exodus 27:8, where nevuv is read as hollow with planks.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua: wine opens the mind even of one closed like a virgin.
Proof from Zechariah 9:17, where yenovev means opens.
Rav Huna: it is obvious that a firstborn takes a double portion along one boundary, like any other son.
Does a yavam also receive his two portions along one boundary?
Abaye: this case equals that one, since the Torah calls the yavam a firstborn.
Rava: regarding the inheritance he is like a firstborn, but not regarding how the estate is distributed.
Proof from Deuteronomy 25:6: and it shall be the firstborn, the verse makes him firstborn only in his inheritance.
Anecdote: a man bought land on his father's boundary, then asks his brothers to give him that parcel as his share.
Rabba: in such a case the court compels people to refrain from conduct characteristic of Sodom.
Rav Yosef objects: the brothers can justify refusing by calling the field especially valuable, like the house of bar Maryon.
The halakha follows Rav Yosef.
Rabba: with two parcels by two water channels, the court compels giving the brother the field adjoining his own.
Rav Yosef objects: the other brother may have a valid reason, since one channel flows well and the other does not.
The halakha follows Rav Yosef.
Rav Yosef: when one brother owns an adjoining field, the court compels giving him the parcel next to it.
Abaye objects: the other brother may want more sharecroppers, which is a valid reason to refuse.
The halakha follows Rav Yosef; the argument about sharecroppers is not a real reason.

13a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A field with a water channel on one side and a river on the other is divided diagonally so each heir reaches both.
Mishna continuation: a hall or drawing room is not divided unless each portion can still be used as before.
If neither portion is large enough for either brother's use, what is the halakha?
Rav Yehuda: there is a rule of 'you set the price or I will', so one partner may force a buyout.
Rav Nahman: there is no such rule of forced buyout; the partnership simply continues.
Rava objects to Rav Nahman: if no buyout rule exists, how would a firstborn and a brother divide a slave and an animal?
Rava's example: how are the firstborn and the ordinary brother to divide a slave and a non-kosher animal?
Rav Nahman: the brother works for one day and the firstborn for two days.
Objection from the mishna on a half-slave half-freeman: Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai differ on his service and marriage options.
Beit Shammai's point proved from Isaiah 45:18 that the world was created for procreation.
The court compels the master to free the slave's other half, with a bill for half his value; Beit Hillel retracted to Beit Shammai's view.
It is different here: the slave can say set the price, but cannot offer to sell himself, so only procreation justifies the compelled buyout.
Come and hear: a mishna on two brothers and an inherited bathhouse shows the rich brother cannot compel commercial use.

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna's example: a rich brother tells a poor one to take servants to the bathhouse or olives to the press.
