Reply: there, the rich brother can say set a price and buy my share, since the poor brother cannot buy out the rich one.
Come and hear: a baraita where a co-owner accepts less of a small courtyard, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rejects the buyout.
What are the circumstances of the baraita? If it is as taught, what is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning?
Proposed emendation: the baraita is incomplete and the dispute concerns only the buyout option.
Under that reading, all agree the court listens to the one offering less, and the buyout option is then disputed.
Rejects the emendation: the baraita stands as taught and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rejects the buyout.
What is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reason for rejecting the buyout?
The other partner has no money to pay the difference, and a gift is unwelcome to him.
Proof from Proverbs 15:27: he who hates gifts shall live.
Abaye: Rav Yehuda's rule is actually Shmuel's view, as the mishna on sacred writings shows.
The mishna rules that sacred writings held jointly are not divided even if both want to.
Shmuel: the rule applies only to one scroll; when the writings are in two scrolls, they may be divided.
If there is no buyout rule, why limit the rule to one scroll? Even two scrolls should not be divided unevenly.
Rav Shalman's reading: the mishna addresses a case where both partners want to divide.
Ameimar: the halakha follows Rav Yehuda; a buyout rule exists.
Rav Ashi asks Ameimar about Rav Nahman's contrary view.
Ameimar: I have not heard that view; I do not hold it.
Challenge: the sons of Ravin and Rav Dimi divided two maidservants, and that case shows the buyout principle at work.
They brought the case to Rava, who ruled there is no buyout rule.
It is different there: each brother wanted both maidservants, so a split is not a buyout case.
Objection: sacred writings both partners want should be divisible, yet Shmuel requires two scrolls.
Rav Shalman's interpretation: the mishna means both partners want to divide, and then two scrolls allow division.
Baraita: Rabbi Meir permits attaching Torah, Prophets, and Writings into one scroll.
Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages require each book, or each section, to be a separate scroll.
Rabbi Yehuda: Baitos ben Zunin attached eight prophetic books into one scroll with Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's approval.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: they brought a combined scroll before him and he ruled like Rabbi Meir.
Spacing rules: four blank lines between Torah books, three between the Twelve Prophets, and a finished book may start mid-column.
Baraita: one may attach the three parts into one scroll, leaving blank parchment at the start and end for winding.

14a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If one wishes to cut a scroll, one may cut it, provided the next book begins at the top of the next column.
Contradiction with another baraita on how much parchment to leave for winding around the pole or the circumference.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak: the tanna teaches disjunctively, leaving parchment for either the pole or the circumference as needed.
Rav Ashi: the second baraita refers to a Torah scroll, which is wound from both ends toward the middle on two poles.
Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Tzadok: this is how the scribes of Jerusalem made their scrolls.
Baraita: a Torah scroll's length should not exceed its circumference when rolled, nor its circumference exceed its length.
The Sages ask Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi what the proper size of a Torah scroll is.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: six handbreadths on gallnut-treated hide; he does not know the measure for ordinary parchment.
Anecdote: Rav Huna wrote seventy scrolls and only once achieved equal length and circumference; Rav Aha bar Yaakov's scroll was jealousy-inducing.
The Sages report that Rabbi Ami wrote four hundred Torah scrolls.
Rav Hamnuna: perhaps he wrote the verse Moses commanded us the Torah four hundred times, not four hundred scrolls.
Rava challenges Rabbi Zeira: Rabbi Yannai planted four hundred vineyards.
Rava: perhaps they were the smallest vineyards that halakha recognizes, two vines facing two plus a tail.
Objection from a baraita on the Ark's measurements: 2.5 by 1.5 by 1.5 cubits, a cubit of six handbreadths.
The baraita's calculation of the tablets' space in the Ark, leaving two handbreadths for a Torah scroll.
Proof from I Kings 8:9: nothing in the Ark except the two tablets Moses put there.
What does the repeated restriction nothing except teach?
It includes a Torah scroll placed in the Ark.
Baraita continues with the width: two handbreadths left, so the scroll can go in and out without being pressed; Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda's variant: a five-handbreadth cubit, giving different dimensions and leftover space.
Continuing the Ark's width: the remaining space held silver columns beside the tablets.
Proof from Song of Songs 3:9-10, a palanquin with silver columns, understood as alluding to the Ark.
The Philistines' chest of gifts was placed beside the Ark, and the Torah scroll rested upon it.
Proof from Deuteronomy 31:26: place the scroll at the side of the Ark, not inside it.
How, on Rabbi Meir's view, do I reconcile the verse nothing except the tablets with something else in the Ark?

14b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection: a six-handbreadth circumference yields a two-handbreadth diameter, too small for the Torah scroll and broken tablets in the Ark.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov: the Temple courtyard scroll was wound only to its beginning, so its circumference was two handbreadths.
How does a two-handbreadth item fit into a space of exactly two handbreadths?
Rav Ashi: a small section of the scroll was wound separately and placed on top.
Where was the Torah scroll kept before the Philistines' chest arrived, according to Rabbi Yehuda?
A shelf protruded from the Ark, and the scroll rested on it.
According to Rabbi Meir, who places the scroll inside the Ark, what does the verse at the side of the Ark teach?
It teaches that the scroll was placed inside the Ark beside the tablets, not between them.
Where were the silver columns placed, and how does Rabbi Meir derive that the broken tablets were kept in the Ark?
Rav Huna: the repeated name in II Samuel 6:2 teaches that broken tablets were placed in the Ark along with the second set.
What does Rabbi Yehuda derive from that verse?
Rabbi Yohanan: the verse teaches that the ineffable name and all of God's appellations were placed in the Ark.
Doesn't Rabbi Meir also need the verse for that, and from where does he derive the broken tablets' placement?
Rav Yosef's baraita on Deuteronomy 10:1-2 shows that the broken tablets were placed in the Ark with the second set.
What does Rabbi Yehuda learn from that verse?
Reish Lakish: asher shibbarta alludes to God approving Moses' breaking the tablets, saying yishar kohakha.
Baraita: the order of the Prophets is Joshua and Judges, Samuel and Kings, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, Isaiah and the Twelve.
Hosea is said to be the first prophet spoken to, yet there were earlier prophets; why does his book come first among the Twelve?
Rabbi Yohanan: Hosea was the first of four prophets prophesying together, and the book follows that order.
Hosea's prophecy is written with Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, the last prophets, so he is counted with them.
Isaiah preceded Jeremiah and Ezekiel chronologically, so why is Isaiah placed after them?
Books are grouped by theme: destruction is juxtaposed with destruction, and consolation with consolation.
Baraita: the order of the Writings is Ruth and Psalms, Job and Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Lamentations, Daniel, Esther, Ezra and Chronicles.
If Job lived in Moses' time, why not begin the Writings with Job?
We do not begin with suffering; Ruth, though about suffering, has a hopeful future.
Rabbi Yohanan: Ruth's name (reish, vav, tav) alludes to David, who sated God with songs and praises.
Baraita on authors: Moses wrote his book and Balaam's portion and Job; Joshua wrote his book and eight verses; Samuel wrote his book, Judges, and Ruth.
David wrote Psalms through ten elders, including psalms by Adam, Melchizedek, Abraham, Moses, Heman, Jeduthun, and Asaph.

15a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita continues: the psalms also include those by the three sons of Korah.

Baraita: Jeremiah wrote his book and Kings and Lamentations; Hezekiah's circle wrote Isaiah and Wisdom books; the Great Assembly wrote Ezekiel, Twelve, Daniel, Esther; Ezra wrote his book and Chronicles up to his time.
This supports Rav's view that Ezra did not go up until he recorded his genealogy; Nehemiah finished Chronicles.
Joshua wrote the last eight Torah verses, according to the view that the baraita follows.
Proof from Deuteronomy 34:5: Moses could not have written his own death, so someone else completed the Torah.
Rabbi Yehuda: Moses wrote until this point and Joshua wrote from here on; some attribute this view to Rabbi Nehemiah.
Rabbi Shimon rebuts: could a Torah scroll lack a single letter, given the verse about taking this Torah scroll?
Rabbi Shimon: until this point God dictated and Moses wrote; from Moses' death on, God dictated and Moses wrote with tears.
Proof from Jeremiah 36:18, where Baruch says he wrote the dictated words with ink, showing dictation is a Torah pattern.
Whose opinion is the rule that the last eight verses are read by one reader? Is it Rabbi Yehuda's, against Rabbi Shimon's?
Even on Rabbi Shimon's view, these verses differ in being written with tears, so they cannot be split between readers.
The baraita says Joshua wrote his own book.
Objection: the book records Joshua's death, so he could not have written it.
Eleazar son of Aaron completed the book.
Objection: the book also records the death of Eleazar son of Aaron.
Pinhas completed it.
The baraita says Samuel wrote his own book.
Objection: the book records Samuel's death.
Gad the seer and Nathan the prophet completed it.
David wrote Psalms through ten elders, as the baraita lists.
Why not count Ethan the Ezrahite among those who contributed to Psalms, since he is credited with Psalm 89?
Rav: Ethan the Ezrahite is Abraham, who came from the east.
Proof: Psalm 89:1 names Ethan the Ezrahite, and Isaiah 41:2 refers to one raised from the east, identified as Abraham.
The baraita counts both Moses and Heman among the elders, yet Rav equates Heman with Moses; how can both be included?
There were two Hemans: one was Moses, and the other was a Temple singer, a descendant of Samuel.
The baraita says Moses wrote his book, the portion of Balaam, and the book of Job.
Rabbi Levi bar Lahma: Job lived in Moses' time, shown by the unusual word eifo in Job 19:23 and Exodus 33:16.
Objection: by the same reasoning, Job could have lived in the time of Isaac, Jacob, or Joseph, since each has the word eifo.
Job 19:23 continues with veyuhaku, the inscribed words, and Moses is called the inscriber in Deuteronomy 33:21.
Rava: Job lived at the time of the spies whom Moses sent to scout the land.
Proof: Job 1:1 has the name Utz, while Numbers 13:20 has the word eitz, a tree, in the spies' account.
Is the comparison valid, since one word is Utz and the other is eitz?
Moses told the spies: Job's years are as long as a tree, and he protects his generation like a tree, hence the allusion.
A Sage before Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani argues that Job never existed and his story is only a parable.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani rebuts from Job 1:1: there was a man in the land of Utz whose name was Job, so he existed.
If 'there was' proves a real person, was Natan's parable to David about a poor man and his lamb also a real case?
If it were only a parable, why would it name the man and his city? So Job was clearly a real person.
Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Elazar: Job returned from exile at the start of the Second Temple and studied in Tiberias.
Objection from a baraita: Job's days ran from when Israel entered Egypt until they left, which contradicts the later date.

15b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita means Job's life spanned the period from Israel's entry into Egypt to its exit, without placing him in that era.
Objection: a baraita lists seven prophets to the nations, including Job, suggesting Job was not Jewish; Elihu is then argued to be Jewish from Job 32:2.
Elihu and Job are included because their main prophecies were to the nations, unlike other prophets whose main audience was Israel.
Objection: a baraita calls Job a pious gentile who came only to receive his reward and then cursed God.
This is a tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Elazar places Job in the era of the judging of the judges, as Job 27:12 implies.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha: Job lived in the days of Ahasuerus, since Job's daughters were the most beautiful women in the world.
Why not place Job in the days of David, when a beautiful maiden was sought in I Kings 1:3?
David's search was throughout the land of Israel, while Ahasuerus's search was throughout the world, as with Job's daughters.
Three views: Rabbi Natan places Job in the kingdom of Sheba, the Rabbis in the Chaldean period, and some in Jacob's time; all but the last hold Job was Jewish.
Objection: if Job were a gentile, the Divine Presence would have rested on gentiles after Moses, yet Moses asked it not to rest on them.
Rabbi Yohanan: the generation of Job was steeped in licentiousness, citing Job 27:12 on seeing.
Proof from Song of Songs 7:1 on looking upon the Shulamite, interpreted as licentious gazing.
Objection: the phrase you have seen might connote prophecy, as in Isaiah 1:1's vision.
If so, why would the verse add why have you become altogether vain? The reference must be to licentious gazing.
Rabbi Yohanan: Ruth 1:1, in the days of the judging of the judges, indicates a generation that judged its judges.
Illustration: a judge and defendant trade accusations of splinters and beams, and silver for dross and watered wine, so judges could not judge.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani citing Rabbi Yonatan: malkat Sheba means the kingdom of Sheba, not a woman.
The Satan reports to God that he found no one as faithful as Abraham, who did not complain even when Sarah's burial place was purchased.
God directs the Satan's attention to Job, a perfect and upright man with none like him on earth.
Rabbi Yohanan: the praise of Job exceeds that of Abraham, since Job's verse adds turns away from evil, comparing Genesis 22:12.
The full verse of Job 1:8 is quoted, describing Job as perfect, upright, fearing God, and turning from evil.
What is meant by and turns away from evil?
Rabbi Abba bar Shmuel: Job forgave debts, even of half a peruta.
The Satan's challenge in Job 1:9-10: does Job fear God for naught, given the protective hedge about him and his house?
What is meant by you have blessed the work of his hands?
Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak: anyone who took even a peruta from Job was blessed.
What is meant by his livestock is increased in the land?
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina: Job's livestock reversed the natural order, as the goats killed the wolves.
The Satan's challenge to touch all that Job has, and God's reply that all is in the Satan's power except Job himself.
Job's children were feasting when a messenger reported the oxen plowing and the asses feeding beside them.
What is meant by the oxen were plowing and the asses were feeding beside them?
Rabbi Yohanan: this teaches that God gave Job a taste of the calamity to come.

16a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Opening phrase comparing a situation to the World-to-Come, where plowing and harvest coincide.
Quoted verses from Job chapter one describing the messengers' reports and Job's response.
Opening of Job chapter two: God asks Satan where he has been, and Satan answers.
Satan claims he roamed the world and found no one as faithful as Abraham.
Genesis verse in which God told Abraham to walk the land, cited as evidence of Abraham's merit.
Satan adds that Abraham never questioned God even when he could not find a burial place for Sarah.
God's verse praising Job and noting that Satan moved Him against Job without cause.
Rabbi Yochanan: were the verse not explicit, one could not say God was persuaded, since it would be improper.
A baraita describing how Satan descends, misleads a person, accuses him above, and takes his soul.
Job chapter two verses on Satan's request to afflict Job's body, and the resulting affliction.
Rabbi Yitzchak: Satan's suffering exceeded Job's, illustrated by a servant told to break a barrel but save its wine.
Resh Lakish: Satan, the evil inclination and the Angel of Death are one and the same entity.
Job 2:7 cited to show that the Satan is the one who went out and struck Job.
Satan is identified as the evil inclination.
Genesis 6:5 and Job 2:6 compared through the shared word 'only', supporting the identification.
Job 1:12 cited, where God says only do not stretch out your hand.
Satan is also identified as the Angel of Death.
Job 2:6 cited: only spare his life.
Inference: Job's life apparently rests in Satan's hand, so Satan must be the Angel of Death.
Rabbi Levi: both Satan and Peninnah acted with intentions for the sake of Heaven.
Satan, seeing God favor Job, insists God would not forget Abraham's kindness, so his motive was good.
Samuel I 1:6 cited to show that Peninnah provoked Hannah in order to make her pray.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov taught this in Paphunya; Satan came and kissed his feet in gratitude.
Job 2:10 cited: Job did not sin with his lips.
Rava: Job did not sin with his lips but did sin in his heart.
The Gemara asks what Job was saying with this.
Job 9:24 quoted, where Job says the earth is given into the hand of the wicked.
Rava: Job sought to overturn the bowl, meaning he hinted at a heretical thought.
Abaye objects: Job was speaking only about the Satan, not about God.
A parallel tannaitic dispute is cited, using the same verse about the earth given to the wicked.
Rabbi Eliezer: Job sought to overturn the bowl, meaning he sought to accuse God.
Rabbi Yehoshua objects: Job was speaking only about the Satan.
Job 10:7 cited: Job claims he is not wicked and that none can deliver from God's hand.
Rava: Job tried to absolve the whole world from judgment.
Job's argument before God: You created kosher and non-kosher animals, Eden and Gehenna, righteous and wicked, so who can restrain You.
What did Job's friends reply to him?
Job 15:4 quoted as the friends' reply, saying he undermines fear and devotion before God.
God created the evil inclination but also gave the Torah as its antidote, a spice that counters it.
Rava expounded a verse about Job's charity and kindness.
What is the meaning of what is written?
Job 29:13 quoted: the blessing of the lost came upon me, and I caused the widow's heart to sing for joy.
Job would take an orphan's field, improve it, and return it; he would also spread rumors of kinship so widows got married.
Job 6:2 quoted: O that my vexation were weighed in balances.
Rav: dust should be put in Job's mouth for weighing his deeds against God's, as if he were in friendship with Heaven.
Job 9:33 quoted: there is no arbiter between us who might lay a hand on both.
Rav again: dust should be put in Job's mouth, since no servant may rebuke his master.
Job 31:1 quoted: a covenant made with the eyes, so why should he look upon a virgin.
Rava repeats the rebuke, comparing Job's conduct with that of Abraham.
Abraham did not even look at his own wife.
Genesis 12:11 cited: Abraham says that Sarai is a beautiful woman.
Inference: Abraham did not know her beauty earlier because he had not gazed at her.
Job 7:9 quoted: as a cloud vanishes, so one who goes down to Sheol does not come up.
Rava: from this it follows that Job denied the resurrection of the dead.
Job 9:17 quoted: He crushes me with a tempest and multiplies my wounds without cause.
Rabba: Job blasphemed with the word tempest and was answered with a tempest.
The phrase from Job 9:17 cited to show the word tempest was used.
Job's appeal to God: perhaps You confused Iyov with oyev, the enemy, so he was answered from a tempest.
Job 38:1 quoted: God answered Job out of the tempest.
Job 38:3 quoted: God asks Job to gird his loins and answer Him.
God's reply: each hair has its own follicle so two never share one, so God would not confuse Iyov with oyev.
Job 38:25 quoted: who has divided a channel for the torrent of rain.
God's reply: each raindrop has its own channel, so God would not confuse Iyov with oyev.
What shows that the word te'ala has the sense of a mold or channel?
Rabba bar Sheila answers that the term is used for a channel shaped like a mold.
I Kings 18:32 cited: Elijah made a channel around the altar, as large as two seah of seed.
The second half of Job 38:25 cited: a path for the lightning of thunder.
God's reply: each thunderclap has its own path, so God would not confuse Iyov with oyev.
Job 39:1 quoted about the wild goats of the rock giving birth.
The Gemara comments that this goat is cruel to her young when she crouches to give birth.

16b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: God's continued reply: a mother goat is protected by an eagle that places her kid, so one moment's difference would kill it; God would not confuse Iyov with oyev.
Job 39:1 cited about the hinds that calve.
God's further example: a hind with a narrow womb is bitten by a snake at the right moment, again showing precise timing that prevents confusing Iyov with oyev.
Job 34:35 cited: Job speaks without knowledge and his words lack wisdom.
Job 42:7 cited: God says the friends did not speak rightly about Him like His servant Job.
Rava: a person is not held accountable for what he says while in distress.
Job 2:11 quoted: the three friends heard of the evil and came together to mourn and comfort him.
What does the phrase 'they made an appointment together' mean?
Rav Yehuda says in Rav's name: they all entered through one gate together.
A baraita adds that each friend lived three hundred parasangs from the others.
How did they all know at once what had happened to Job?
Some say they each had a crown that showed signs, and others say they each had trees that withered when sorrow came.
Rava: this explains the saying that one needs either a friend like Job's friends or death.
Genesis 6:1 quoted: when men began to multiply on the earth and daughters were born to them.
Rabbi Yochanan: larov means that propagation came into the world through these daughters.
Reish Lakish: larov means that strife came into the world through these daughters.
Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan why Job's daughters were not doubled, given that his other losses were doubled.
Rabbi Yochanan replies that they were not doubled in number but were doubled in beauty.
Job 42:13 cited as the source for the account of Job's children.
Job 42:14 quoted, naming Job's three daughters Yemima, Keziah and Keren-happuch.
Explanation of the names: Yemima was like the day, Keziah's scent was like the cassia, and Keren-happuch was beautiful.
Report of the students of Rabbi Sheila on Keren-happuch's comparison to a horn, which was mocked in the West as a blemish.
Rav Chisda gives a better explanation: she was like garden saffron, the best of its kind.
Jeremiah 4:30 cited, where pukh means paint or ornament.
Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi was upset at having a daughter, and his father consoled him that propagation came into the world through daughters.
Bar Kappara calls that meaningless consolation, citing a baraita on the need for both sexes.
A baraita: the world cannot endure without males and females, and without spice sellers and tanners, and it is good to have a sweet-smelling occupation.
As a parallel dispute, Genesis 24:1 is cited: God blessed Abraham with everything.
What is meant by the word 'everything' in the verse?
Rabbi Meir: the blessing was that Abraham did not have a daughter.
Rabbi Yehuda: on the contrary, the blessing was that Abraham had a daughter.
Others say Abraham had a daughter and her name was Bakkol.
Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i: Abraham was so knowledgeable in astrology that kings of East and West came to his door.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: a precious stone hung on Abraham's neck healed the sick; after his death God hung it on the sun.
Abaye: this explains the saying that the day has its own time and the harvest has its own time.
An alternative reading of bakkol: Esau did not rebel in Abraham's lifetime, and Ishmael repented in his lifetime.
From where do we derive that Esau did not rebel in Abraham's lifetime?
Genesis 25:29 quoted: Esau came in from the field and was faint.
A baraita: on the day Abraham died, Jacob prepared a lentil stew to comfort Isaac, as it was customary to serve mourners lentils.
And what is the reason for lentils in particular?
Attributed to Rabba bar Mari: just as a lentil has no mouth, a mourner has no mouth; and just as it is round, mourning rolls around to people.
What is the practical difference between these two explanations?
The difference is whether it is appropriate to console a mourner with eggs.
Rabbi Yochanan: Esau committed five transgressions on the day Abraham died, including despising the birthright.
Proof for the charge of adultery with a betrothed maiden: the word 'came in from the field' compared with Deuteronomy 22:27.
Proof for the charge of murder: the word 'faint' compared with Jeremiah 4:31.
Proof for denying the principle of God: the phrase 'what profit is this' compared with Exodus 15:2.
Proof for denying resurrection: Genesis 25:32, where Esau says he is at the point of death.
Proof for despising the birthright: Genesis 25:34, where Esau despised the birthright.
And Ishmael repented in Abraham's lifetime.
From where do we derive that Ishmael repented in Abraham's lifetime?
Illustration: Ravina and Rav Chama bar Buzi were speaking before Rava while he dozed.
Ravina asks whether it is true that any death described with gevia is the death of the righteous.
Rav Chama says yes.
Ravina objects: what about the generation of the flood, which also died with gevia?
Rav Chama replies that gevia alone is not enough; the expression must include both gevia and asifa.
Ravina objects: Ishmael is described with both gevia and asifa.
Rava, who had heard the discussion while dozing, fully woke up.
Rava says that Rabbi Yochanan holds Ishmael repented in his father's lifetime.
Genesis 25:9 quoted: Isaac and Ishmael, his sons, buried Abraham.
Objection: perhaps the verse lists the sons by their wisdom and not by age.
Counter-objection: then the verse about Esau and Jacob burying Isaac would also be listed by wisdom, which it is not.
What is the reason the verse did not list them by wisdom?
Since Ishmael let Isaac precede him in speech and action, we learn that he repented in Abraham's lifetime.
A baraita: there were three people whom the Holy One, Blessed be He, gave a taste of the World-to-Come in this world.

17a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Introduces the three people who tasted the World-to-Come in this life.
Names the three: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
Genesis 24:1 cited for Abraham, who was blessed with everything.
Genesis 27:33 cited for Isaac, from whom Esau ate everything.
Genesis 33:11 cited for Jacob, who says he has everything.
The evil inclination had no sway over these three.
Restates the three names and their verse phrases: with everything, from everything, everything.
Some say King David is also included in this group.
Psalms 109:22 cited for David, whose heart died within him.
The other authority reads that verse as David describing his suffering, not his evil inclination.
A baraita: six people over whom the Angel of Death had no sway.
Lists the six: the three patriarchs, Moses, Aaron and Miriam.
Restates the patriarchs' verse phrases to show their full blessing.
Moses, Aaron and Miriam died by the mouth of God, as written in Numbers 33:38.
The objection: but Miriam's verse does not say 'by the mouth of the Lord'.
Rabbi Elazar: Miriam also died by a kiss, by verbal analogy; the phrase is omitted for a woman out of decorum.
A baraita: seven people over whom worm and maggot had no sway, adding Benjamin to the list.
Verses for the patriarchs and for Moses, Aaron and Miriam, with the bracketed words.
Deuteronomy 33:12 cited for Benjamin: the beloved of the Lord dwells in safety.
Some say David is also included in the list of those unaffected by worms.
Psalms 16:9 cited: my flesh also dwells secure.
The other authority explains that David was asking for mercy, and his request was not granted.
A baraita: four people died only because of the snake's counsel, not for personal sin.
Lists the four, noting they are known by tradition except Yishai, who needs a proof.
Introduces II Samuel 17:25 as the verse that proves Yishai's status.
The verse quoted about Amasa, son of Ithra, who had relations with Abigail, daughter of Nahash.
Was Abigail really the daughter of Nahash?
Objection: was she not the daughter of Yishai, as Chronicles states?
I Chronicles 2:16 cited: their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail.
She is called daughter of Nahash because her father died owing to the snake's counsel.
Closing formula marking the end of the chapter, Partners.
Mishna: one may not dig a pit beside a neighbor's pit, nor a ditch, cave, water channel or laundry pond.
Exception: unless he distances the laundry pond three handbreadths from the neighbor's wall.
He must distance pressed residue, manure, salt, lime and rocks three handbreadths from the neighbor's wall.
Alternatively, he may plaster the wall with lime and then distance these items.
Seeds, a plow and urine must be kept three handbreadths from the wall.
Mill and oven distances: three handbreadths from the wall, measured to the base or rim of each.

17b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why does the mishna open by speaking of a pit but end by referring to a wall?
Proposes that the tanna should simply teach distance from the other's pit, as the opening suggests.
Abaye, or some say Rav Yehuda: the mishna means distance from the wall of the other's pit.
Objects that the tanna could have stated the distance from the other's pit directly.
The wording teaches that the wall of a pit must be three handbreadths thick, with consequences for sales.
A baraita on a sale of a pit with its walls: the wall must be three handbreadths thick.
Introduces the dispute about one who wants to dig next to his neighbor's boundary.
Abaye holds that he may dig there.
Rava holds that he may not dig there.
All agree he may not dig near a field designated for pits; the dispute concerns a field not so designated.
Abaye's reasoning: the neighbor's field is not designated for pits, so there is no harm.
Rava's objection: the neighbor could say that just as you dug, I too might dig and then be blocked.
An alternative version: all agree a field not designated for pits is fine; the dispute concerns a designated field.
Abaye holds that even the Rabbis who require a tree to be twenty-five cubits from a cistern would permit this case.
The tree case differs because the cistern exists when the tree is planted, but not when the neighbor digs.
Rava holds that even Rabbi Yosei would prohibit digging in this case.
Rabbi Yosei: this one digs within his own field and that one plants within his own field.
Rava explains that the tree case applies only where the roots are not yet present, unlike digging here.
Rava's rebuttal: each strike of your hoe loosens my earth, so you already cause damage while digging.
The mishna is cited: one may not dig beside another's pit; the reason is the existence of a pit, so without one digging is allowed.
Analyzes the first version: it works for the mishna if it refers to a field not designated for pits.
Difficulty: on that version Rava's position conflicts with the mishna.
Rava could have answered: the mishna means distance from the wall of his pit, so the neighbor must also leave three handbreadths.
An alternative attribution of the same teaching, framed as a challenge to Abaye.
Analyzes the second version: it works for Abaye's view only if the case concerns a field designated for pits.
Difficulty: on the second version, Abaye's reading conflicts with the mishna.
Abaye could have answered: the mishna refers to two neighbors who dig at the same time, so both must distance.
A baraita is brought as a proof: soft rock crumbles in the hand, and each one distances his pit three handbreadths and plasters with lime.
Rock that crumbles in the hand is different, because the soil is soft and requires distance.
Why did the questioner raise this objection at all?
The baraita is specific, and it teaches that three handbreadths suffices even for soft soil.
A mishna is brought to test the principle: one must distance pressed residue and manure, and the list continues.

18a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna continued: salt, lime and rocks must be three handbreadths from the neighbor's wall, or the wall is plastered with lime.
The Gemara infers from the wall in the mishna that without a wall one could place these items at the boundary.
Rejects the inference: even without a wall these items may not be placed at the boundary.
Then what does the mention of a wall teach us?
It teaches that all these substances are damaging to a wall.
A second mishna is brought: seeds, the plow and urine must be kept three handbreadths from the wall, with the same inference.
Again rejects the inference: even without a wall these may not be placed at the boundary.
Then what does this ruling teach us?
It teaches that dampness is damaging to a wall.
A third mishna: a mill must be kept a distance from the wall, with the same inference that a wall is needed for the rule.
Rejects the inference: even without a wall the mill may not be placed at the boundary.
Then what does this ruling teach us?
It teaches that vibrations are damaging to a wall.
A fourth mishna: an oven must be distanced from the wall, with the same inference.
Rejects the inference: even without a wall an oven may not be placed at the boundary.
Then what does this ruling teach us?
It teaches that heat is damaging to a wall.
A mishna on bakeries, dye shops and cattle barns beneath another's storeroom, inferring that without a storeroom it is permitted, and applying this to pits.
A residence is different, and the mishna's language is precise, since a baraita explicitly permits the barn if built before the storeroom.
A mishna on planting a tree next to another's field: four cubits, and a baraita explains this is for the work of the vineyard.
The Gemara infers that the distance is due only to vineyard work, implying that roots alone would not forbid planting at the boundary.
Objects that, even though roots do damage here, apparently it is permitted.
We are dealing with a case where a hard rock divides the two fields so that roots cannot cross.
The mishna is cited about a fence between neighbors, where each plants close to it from his side.
If so, the last clause of the mishna should be read as describing roots that extend into the neighbor's field and may be cut to three handbreadths.
A mishna on distancing a tree twenty-five cubits from a cistern, inferring that without a cistern planting at the boundary would be permitted.
Rejects the inference: even without a cistern one may not plant close to the neighbor's field.
The mention of the cistern teaches that roots extend and damage the cistern up to twenty-five cubits.
If so, the last clause should be explained, since a tree that preceded the cistern could not be found if planting at the boundary is always forbidden.
Rav Pappa's explanation applies: the case concerns a buyer who purchased part of a field, so the tree preceded the cistern for the purchaser.
A mishna on distancing soaking flax from vegetables, leeks from onions, and mustard from bees, with the inference that vegetables are needed for the rule.
Rejects the inference: even without vegetables the water may not be placed close to the neighbor's field.
The tanna teaches that these items are harmful to each other.
If so, the last clause of the mishna should be explained instead.
Rabbi Yosei permits planting mustard near bees, since the bee owner can be told that his bees eat the mustard plants too, so both cause damage.

18b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If one may not place a damaging item near the boundary, how can each neighbor be damaging the other's property?
Rav Pappa: this refers to a buyer who purchased part of a field, so the damage is not the seller's fault.
What is the reasoning of the Rabbis, and of Rabbi Yosei, if the buyer did nothing improper, and why does Rabbi Yosei distinguish mustard and bees from water and vegetables?
Ravina: the Rabbis hold that the one who causes potential damage must distance himself, even if he acted properly.
Does Rabbi Yosei's view imply the injured party must distance himself, in which case why distinguish the cases?
Rabbi Yosei holds that the one causing damage must distance himself, and the distinction is that mustard and bees damage each other.
The Rabbis respond that bees do not damage mustard: a seed is not found by bees, and a leaf grows back.
Does Rabbi Yosei hold that the one causing damage must distance himself?
A mishna teaches Rabbi Yosei's view that the tree need not be cut, since each digs or plants in his own property.
Rabbi Yosei actually holds that the injured party must distance himself, and he spoke according to the Rabbis' view.
Rabbi Yosei explains to the Rabbis: in my view the injured party distances himself, and in your view the mustard and bees damage one another.
The Rabbis respond that bees do not damage mustard, and the discussion concerns a seed.

19a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbis' reply continued: if the item refers to a leaf, it grows back, so bees will not find it and no damage occurs.
Mishna: a launderer's pond may not be set up near a neighbor's wall unless three handbreadths away.
Rav Naḥman, citing Rabba bar Avuh: the three handbreadths applies to a soaking pond, while a washing pond needs four cubits.
A baraita states a four-cubit distance for a launderer's pond, supporting Rav Naḥman.
If the mishna says three handbreadths, must we conclude from the baraita that Rav Naḥman is right?
Some raise the mishna and the baraita as contradictory sources.
Rav Naḥman: there is no difficulty, since the mishna refers to a soaking pond and the baraita to a washing pond.
Rav Ḥiyya bar Avya explicitly teaches the mishna as distancing from the rim of the soaking pond and the wall.
The mishna's wording, per that version, requires three handbreadths from the neighbor's property and plastering with lime.
Is the mishna's wording plastering with lime in addition to distance, or plastering instead of distance?
Clearly the wording is 'and plasters': otherwise the tanna would have combined all the cases together.
Not necessarily: the cases are separate because moisture damage differs from heat damage.
Rabbi Yehuda's baraita on soft rock that crumbles in the hand is cited, with the inference that other rock needs no lime.
The same applies to other rock, but the tanna mentions crumbling rock to rule out a greater distance.
Mishna: one must distance pressed residue, manure, salt, lime and rocks three handbreadths from the neighbor's wall.
The mishna on insulating a pot on Shabbat eve is cited: one may not use pressed residue, manure, salt, lime or sand.
Why does one mishna mention rocks and not sand, while the other mentions sand and not rocks?
Rav Yosef: people do not customarily insulate food with rocks.
Abaye objects: people do insulate with wool fleece and purple wool, so customary use is not the reason.
Abaye: the tanna follows the verse that its neighbor tells about him, so one example stands for the other.
Rava objects: then the tanna should have taught all examples together, or one example in the other case.
Rava: rocks scratch the pot so no one uses them, and sand heats hot items and cools cold ones, so it does not damage the wall.
Objection from Rabbi Oshaya's baraita on sand: the tanna of our mishna should also teach sand, read as damp sand.
Rejects the answer: the mishna teaches a water channel and a launderer's pond, so it could have included sand too.
Both examples are needed: a water channel is fixed while a launderer's pond is not, and each needs a separate ruling.
Mishna: one must distance seeds, the plow and urine three handbreadths from the neighbor's wall.
Why mention seeds at all, since plowing already implies planting, and why mention the plow separately?
The tanna is speaking about Eretz Yisrael.
Deuteronomy 11:11 cited: a land that drinks water from the rain of heaven, so no irrigation channels are needed there.
Is this to say that seeds are indeed to be distanced in Eretz Yisrael?

19b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Do the growing roots of a plant spread sideways and damage a neighbor's wall?
Objection from the Kilayim mishna: a bent grapevine must have three handbreadths of earth over it before a seed may be planted above it.
The continuation of that mishna permits planting on either side, which implies roots are not a concern.
Rabbi Ḥagga in the name of Rabbi Yosei: seeds loosen the soil and raise loose earth, which damages the wall's foundation.
Mishna: urine must be kept three handbreadths from the neighbor's wall.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana: urinating beside another's wall is permitted, citing the verse about those who urinate against the wall.
Objection: the mishna itself requires three handbreadths for urine from the wall.
There the mishna refers to urine poured from a chamber pot.
A baraita: one may not pour water beside another's wall unless he distances it three handbreadths, so urination is all the more prohibited.
A baraita: one may not urinate beside another's wall unless he distances himself three handbreadths.
The baraita's details: three handbreadths for a brick wall, one handbreadth for a stone wall, and none needed for hard rock.
The baraita refutes Rabba bar bar Ḥana's opinion, and his ruling is rejected.
But Rabba bar bar Ḥana cited a verse; how can a baraita rule against a verse?
The verse means that the king's line will not even have a dog urinating against a wall, so people are not in view.
Shmuel: a thin wafer does not reduce the size of a window for the purpose of spread of impurity.
Why discuss a wafer specifically, when even thick bread would not reduce a window's size either?
Thick bread is fit for eating so it is not nullified, but a wafer becomes disgusting and might be nullified, so Shmuel teaches it is not nullified because it feeds animals.
Objection: the wafer should be excluded because it is susceptible to impurity, and such items do not serve as barriers.
Objection from the Oholot mishna: a basket of straw or a barrel of figs in a window counts as a barrier only if it can stand on its own.
Objection: straw that can stand is still fit for animal feed and would be removed, so it should not count as part of the window.
Shmuel: this refers to figs that became worm infested, as Rabba bar Avuh also teaches.
What are the exact circumstances of this barrel: is its opening facing outward or inward?

20a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects to treating the barrel itself as the barrier, since an earthenware vessel is impure only through its opening.
Alternatively, the opening faces outward, so the impurity enters from outside.
Asks what case is being discussed.
The case is a barrel made of metal.
Objects from a baraita that grass placed in windows or growing there reduces the window, contrary to Shmuel.
The baraita lists scraps that do not measure three by three fingerbreadths as reducing the window.
The baraita lists a limb or flesh dangling from an animal or beast as reducing the window.
The baraita lists a bird resting in the window as reducing it.
The baraita lists a gentile sitting in the window as reducing it.
The baraita lists a child born after eight months placed in the window as reducing it.
The baraita lists salt and earthenware vessels as reducing the window.
The baraita lists a Torah scroll and concludes that all these reduce the window.
The baraita states that snow, hail, frost, ice and water do not reduce the window.
Grass is fit for animal food, so by Shmuel's view it should not reduce the window.
Refers to poisonous grass that is unfit for animals.
The baraita adds that grass growing on its own also reduces the window.
Grass damages the wall, so the owner would remove it and it could not serve as a barrier.
Rabba: refers to a ruined wall whose owner does not bother to remove the grass.
Rav Pappa: even a wall of a settled house, with grass rooted three handbreadths away that the owner ignores.
Why do scraps reduce the window, since they can serve to patch a tear in a garment?
Refers to thick scraps, which are unsuitable for patching.
Thick scraps still suit a bloodletter for wiping blood at the incision.
If sackcloth is meant, why does the baraita give three by three rather than four by four handbreadths?
It is not real sackcloth but resembles it: stiff, so a bloodletter would not use it.
The baraita says a limb or flesh dangling from an animal or beast reduces the window.
By Shmuel's view the animal could get up and escape, so why should it count?
Refers to an animal tied in place.
The owner will take the animal and slaughter it.
Refers to a non-kosher animal that will not be slaughtered.
Even so, the owner will sell the animal to a gentile.
Refers to a lean animal that no one would buy.
Even if immobile, the owner could cut off the dangling part and throw it to dogs.
Cutting it off would cause the animal suffering, so the owner will not do it.
The baraita says a bird resting in the window reduces its dimensions.
The bird would fly away, so it should not count as part of the window.
Refers to a bird tied in place.
The owner will take the bird and slaughter it.
Refers to a non-kosher bird that he will not slaughter.
Even a non-kosher bird the owner will sell to a gentile.
Refers to a kelanita, a bird too bony for anyone to buy.
Even so, he could give the bird to a child to play with, so why does it reduce the window?
A kelanita does not scratch, so the answer does not fit.
Refers to a bird like a kelanita in being bony but inclined to scratch.
The baraita says a gentile sitting in the window reduces its dimensions.
The gentile would get up and leave, so why does he reduce the window?
Refers to someone who is tied up.
Another person could come and release him.
Refers to a leper, whom people are afraid to touch.
Another leper could come and release him.
Refers to a prisoner of the monarchy, whom others are afraid to release.
The baraita says a child born after eight months placed in the window reduces its dimensions.
His mother could come and remove him from the window.
Refers to Shabbat, when moving the child is prohibited.
Baraita: such a child is like a stone for set-aside purposes, so it may not be moved on Shabbat.
His mother may bend over and nurse him, since failing to nurse endangers her health.
Salt is fit for use, so people would remove it from the window.
Refers to bitter salt, which is not used as seasoning.
Even bitter salt is fit for tanning hides.
Refers to salt mixed with thorns, so it is not used for tanning.
Since the salt damages the wall, the owner would remove it.
It sits on a shard of earthenware, so it does not damage the wall.
If it rests on earthenware, the shard itself should serve as the barrier; why is salt mentioned?

20b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Clarifies that the shard in question lacks the measure needed to be susceptible to impurity.
Cites a mishna in Shabbat about a shard placed between pillars as the measure for such a shard.
A baraita teaches that an earthenware vessel also reduces the dimensions of a window.
Objects that the earthenware is fit for use, so it would likely be removed from the window.
Refers to earthenware that is dirty.
Even dirty earthenware is fit for a bloodletter to collect blood, so it would be removed.
Refers to earthenware that is perforated and so unfit for that use.
A baraita teaches that a Torah scroll also reduces the dimensions of a window.
Objects that a Torah scroll is fit for reading, so it would be removed.
Refers to a worn-out Torah scroll that is unfit for reading.
Objects that a worn-out scroll requires genizah, so its owner would certainly remove it.
The scroll was placed there intending that its genizah happen in that window.
Rav rules that any material may form a barrier except salt and fat, which crumble or melt.
Shmuel says even salt can serve as a barrier, contradicting Rav.
Rav Pappa reconciles: Shmuel speaks of Sodomite salt, Rav of isterokanit salt taken from the sea.
Cites Rabba's ruling about two salt piles supporting a cross beam.
Rabba rules that two salt piles with a cross beam across them form a valid barrier.
If so, even isterokanit salt can serve as a barrier, contradicting Rav.
They do not disagree: one ruling concerns a case with a cross beam, the other a case without.
The mishna requires a mill to be set three handbreadths from a neighbor's wall, four from the upper stone.
What is the reason for this required distance from the neighbor's property?
The distance is due to the vibrations the mill causes.
A baraita gives mill distances, and asks what vibrations exist there, objecting to the vibration explanation.
Rather, the reason for the distance is the noise the mill generates.
The mishna requires three handbreadths between an oven's base and the wall, four from its narrow rim.
Abaye infers the oven base is a handbreadth wider than its rim, which matters for buying and selling.
Mishna: an oven inside a house needs four cubits of clearance above, and a plaster floor beneath it of stated thickness.
Mishna: one who causes damage through these installations must pay compensation for it.
Rabbi Shimon says these measurements only mean he is exempt from paying if he took all precautions.
Mishna: no bakery, dye shop, or cattle barn beneath another's storeroom, though wine storerooms permit bakeries and dye shops.
A baraita gives different plaster-floor thicknesses for oven and stove, contradicting the mishna.
Abaye: the baraita refers to bakers' ovens, which run hot all day, like the mishna's oven.
Mishna repeats that one may not open a bakery or dye shop beneath another's storeroom, or a cattle barn.
A Sage taught that if the cattle barn preceded the storeroom, it is permitted to remain.
Abaye asks: if he cleaned and sprinkled the space but has not filled it, what is the halakha?
Abaye asks about added windows, an enclosed veranda below the storeroom, and an upper room built atop the house.
Teiku: the question stands unresolved.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua asks: if dates and pomegranates were placed there, what is the halakha?
Teiku: this question also stands unresolved.
The mishna restates that wine storerooms permit a bakery and dye shop beneath, but not a cattle barn.
A Sage taught that wine is permitted because heat and smoke improve it, while a barn is forbidden because it spoils wine.
Rav Yosef: our wine spoils quickly, so even a candle's smoke harms it.
Rav Sheshet: alfalfa is like a cattle barn, since it rots and creates a foul odor.
Mishna: a neighbor may protest opening a store in a courtyard because of the noise of customers coming and going.
Making crafts at home and selling in the market is allowed; the neighbor cannot protest hammering, milling, or children.
What distinguishes the first clause of the mishna from the latter clause?
Abaye: the latter clause refers to a different courtyard connected to the alley.
Rava objects: if so, the mishna should have specified a different courtyard, but it does not.
Rava begins an alternative explanation of the mishna's distinction.

21a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The latter clause refers to schoolchildren, and the ruling applies from Yehoshua ben Gamla's ordinance onward.
Cites a statement of Rav, transmitted by Rav Yehuda.
Yehoshua ben Gamla is to be remembered for good; his name is attached to this ordinance.
Without him the Torah would have been forgotten; earlier only those with a father were taught by him.
Those without a father did not learn Torah at all in earlier times.
What verse did they interpret homiletically to permit this arrangement?
They read the verse about teaching them to your sons as meaning fathers must teach their own children.
The Sages ordained that teachers of children be established in Jerusalem.
What verse did they interpret homiletically to enable this ordinance?
They interpreted the verse that Torah emerges from Zion.
Still, whoever had a father was taken up to Jerusalem to be taught by him.
Whoever had no father did not ascend to Jerusalem and so did not learn.
The Sages ordained teachers in every province, admitting students at ages sixteen and seventeen.
Older students were unruly; a student rebelled against an angry teacher and left.
Yehoshua ben Gamla ordained teachers in every town, admitting children at ages six and seven.
Rav instructed Rav Shmuel bar Sheilat not to accept a child before six, and then to take him in and teach him well.
Rav advised hitting a child for discipline only with a sandal strap, which causes little pain.
Those who can read should read on their own; those who cannot should keep company with friends to encourage them.
A baraita objects: neighbors can prevent a courtyard member from becoming a doctor, bloodletter, weaver, or teacher.
Answer: the baraita deals with gentile children, for whom there is no mitzva to teach.
Another baraita: one of two residents of a courtyard can prevent the other from becoming a teacher of children.
Here too the case is one of gentile children.
A third baraita: a courtyard owner may not rent to a doctor, bloodletter, weaver, or Jewish or gentile scribe.
The case is a town scribe who writes documents rather than teaching children, and neighbors can prevent him.
Rava: from Yehoshua ben Gamla's ordinance onward, each child is taught in the town where he lives.
Children may not be taken from one town to another, but may be moved from one synagogue to another.
A river separating two areas prevents transporting children unless a regular bridge spans it; a narrow bridge does not suffice.
Rava: a teacher may have at most twenty-five students.
With fifty children, two teachers are appointed; with forty, an assistant is appointed and the townspeople help pay him.
Rava: do not replace a teacher with a more learned one, lest the first grow negligent.
Rav Dimi objects: competition makes teachers better, since jealousy among teachers increases wisdom.
Rava: hire the teacher who covers much material but is imprecise, since his errors can be corrected.
Rav Dimi: hire the precise teacher, since once an error is taught it cannot be easily corrected.
Dimi's view is supported by the verse about Joab remaining in Edom until every male was cut off, followed by an anecdote with David.

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why Joab acted as he did in killing only the males.
Joab cites the verse about blotting out the males of Amalek.
David objects that the verse reads zekher, remembrance, not zakhar, males.
Joab upholds his reading, insisting he was taught zakhar.
Joab goes to his childhood teacher to check how he was taught.
Joab asks the teacher how he had read the word.
The teacher replies that he read it as zekher, never noticing the student had learned it wrongly.
Joab takes a sword in order to kill the teacher.
The teacher asks why Joab would do such a thing.
Joab cites Jeremiah's curse on whoever does God's work deceitfully, faulting the teacher's error.
The teacher replies that it is enough to leave him under the curse, with no need to kill him.
Joab rebuts with the verse that cursed is whoever withholds his sword from blood.
Some say Joab killed the teacher and others say he did not.
Rava: teachers of children, tree planters, butchers, bloodletters and town scribes are all considered forewarned.
The principle: whenever the loss is irreversible, the person is considered forewarned.
Rav Huna: a mill owner in an alleyway may prevent a newcomer from setting up a rival mill beside his.
A baraita says fish traps must be distanced from one another by the distance a fish travels.
How much is that distance?
Rabba bar Rav Huna: up to a parasang.
This is no proof, since fish differ: one fish explores ahead and the others avoid the second trap.
Ravina asks whether Rav Huna follows Rabbi Yehuda, who prohibits competitive handouts.
A mishna: Rabbi Yehuda forbids giving toasted grain and nuts to children to draw them away; the Rabbis permit it.
The Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Yehuda only about handouts; in the mill case even they concede the first owner may object.
A baraita objects: one may open a shop or bathhouse beside another's, and the neighbor cannot protest.
The matter is a dispute among tanna'im.
Baraita: alleyway residents may bar a tailor, tanner, teacher or craftsman, but cannot bar an existing neighbor; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says they may.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua: a town resident may bar an outside rival, but not one who pays that town's tax.
If the newcomer shares this town's tax obligations he cannot be stopped, and an alleyway resident may not stop a neighbor's business there.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua raises a dilemma about a resident of another alleyway setting up a rival mill.
Teiku: the dilemma stands unresolved.
Rav Yosef: Rav Huna concedes that teachers of children may not be prevented from working.
Cites Ezra's ordinance that a teacher must be established alongside another teacher.
Objects that competing teachers may become negligent; Rav Yosef responds to this objector.

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restates the principle that jealousy among teachers increases wisdom.
Rav Nahman: Rav Huna concedes that perfume salesmen may enter a town, reconciling his ruling with the ordinance.
Townspeople may bar peddlers from outside cities who come to their town to sell.
Cites Ezra's ordinance that peddlers travel from town to town so cosmetics reach Jewish women.
The purpose of the ordinance is to make adornments available to Jewish women, so peddlers cannot be barred.
The concession applies only to traveling peddlers, not to those who wish to establish a shop.
A Torah scholar may even set up a shop, as Rava permitted for certain rabbis, despite the halakha.
What is the reason for this ruling?
Since they are rabbis, travel would distract them from their studies.
Basket sellers from Babylonia were blocked by townspeople from selling, and the case went to Ravina.
Ravina rules that the sellers came from outside, so they may sell to outsiders rather than residents.
The ruling applies only on a market day, when outsiders come to shop; on other days they may not sell.
Even on market days the permission covers selling in the market, not circulating around the town.
Wool sellers brought wool to Pum Nahara, and townspeople prevented them from selling it.
Rav Kahana rules that the townspeople may prevent them from selling their wares.
The sellers object that they must sell to sustain themselves while collecting debts owed in the city.
Rav Kahana: sell only enough to sustain yourselves until you collect your debts, then leave.
Rav Dimi of Neharde'a brought dried figs on a ship to sell them.
The Exilarch asks Rava to check whether Dimi is a Torah scholar, and Rava sends Adda bar Abba to smell his jar.
Adda goes and asks Dimi a question.
Is a wicker basket swallowed by an elephant and excreted intact still susceptible to impurity?
Dimi had no answer.
Dimi retorts: are you Rava, that you ask such a difficult question?
Adda strikes Dimi's shoe disparagingly, saying there is a great difference between them; Adda is Dimi's teacher, Rava his teacher's teacher.
Because Adda did not reserve the market for him, Dimi's figs rotted.
Dimi complains to Rav Yosef about what was done to him.
Rav Yosef: as God did not delay retribution against Edom's king, He will not delay punishing those who humiliate you.
Cites Amos on Moab, which burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime and will be punished.
Rav Adda bar Abba died.
Rav Yosef: I am responsible for his death, since I cursed him.
Rav Dimi: I am responsible for his death, since he caused my loss of dried figs.
Abaye: he was punished on my account, for disrespecting me by preferring Rava's school to Abaye's.
Rava: he was punished because he claimed meat before Rava's servant at the butcher, boasting that he was greater.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak: he was punished on my account, since I led the kalla lectures.
Rav Nahman led the kalla lectures, and Adda reviewed the lesson with him before each session.
That day Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua seized Adda, who had missed the end of Rava's lecture.
They asked him to recite how Rava stated the halakhot of animal tithe.
Adda answered that Rava said this and Rava said that.
Meanwhile it grew late for Rav Nahman, and Adda had not yet arrived.
The Sages asked Rav Nahman to arise and teach them, since it was late.
Why does the master sit and wait?
He replied that he was waiting for the bier of Rav Adda bar Abba, who presumably had died.
A rumor spread that Rav Adda bar Abba had indeed died.
It is reasonable to conclude that Rav Nahman caused his death, since the news came just as he had announced it.
Mishna: a wall close to a neighbor's wall must be four cubits from it, and a wall opposite windows must be four cubits from them.
How did the first man place his wall close to the neighbor's wall in the first place?
Rav Yehuda: this is what the tanna is saying.

22b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: One who builds a wall near his neighbor's wall must place it four cubits away from the existing wall.
Rava objects: the mishna says one whose wall was near another's wall, implying a wall already stood there.
Rava offers a reinterpretation of how the mishna is worded.
If a wall stood four cubits away and fell, one may not build another wall close to the neighbor's wall.
Except if he distances the new wall four cubits from the neighbor's wall.
What is the reason for this distance requirement?
Walking here benefits the ground there, since people strengthen the land between the walls.
Rav: the rule applies only to a garden wall; for a courtyard wall one may build close by.
Rabbi Oshaya disagrees: for both garden and courtyard walls one may not build close by.
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina: they do not disagree; Rav refers to an old city, Oshaya to a new city.
Mishna: windows must be four cubits from a neighbor's windows above, below, or opposite.
A baraita explains: above, the wall must be high enough to prevent peering; opposite, it must not block the light.
The Gemara's analysis: the opposite distance is to avoid blocking light, not for walking on the land.
The case is a wall set to the side of the window, which blocks light but does not prevent walking.
Yeiva, citing Rav: a perpendicular wall must be as far from the window as the window's full width.
Why is that sufficient, if one can still peer into the window?
Rav Zevid: this refers to a wall sloped on its top so one cannot stand on it and look in.
Doesn't the mishna require four cubits from the window?
Not difficult: here the wall is on one side of the window, while the mishna has walls on two sides.
Come and hear a further difficulty: the mishna's gutter distance is for the ladder, not for walking.
Here the gutter slopes and protrudes, so one can walk beneath it, yet the distance is still required for repairs.
Mishna: a ladder must be four cubits from a neighbor's dovecote, and a wall four cubits from a roof gutter.
Suggests the mishna does not follow Rabbi Yosei, who would let each man act within his own land.
Baraita: one digs within his own land and the other plants within his own land.
The mishna may follow Rabbi Yosei after all, since he concedes one must avoid harming a neighbor.
Rav Ashi reports Rav Kahana taught that Rabbi Yosei concedes regarding arrows; a mongoose could jump up a ladder to the dovecote.
Objects that this is indirect damage, since he is not the immediate cause.
Rav Tovi bar Mattana: it is prohibited to cause even indirect damage.
Narrative begins: Rav Yosef had certain small palm trees.

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Bloodletters sit beneath the palm trees, crows come to eat the blood, and then fly up and damage the dates.
Rav Yosef tells the bloodletters to remove these crows from there to avoid further damage.
Abaye objects: this is indirect damage, since the bloodletters themselves do not damage the dates.
Rav Yosef: Rav Tovi bar Mattana said it is prohibited to cause even indirect damage.
Abaye objects: the bloodletters have an established acquired privilege to use that spot.
Rav Yosef: Rav Nahman taught that there is no acquired privilege where damage results.
Rav Mari says this applies to smoke, and Rav Zevid says it applies to a bathroom.
Rav Yosef: as I am sensitive, smoke and a bathroom are like the bloodletters' damage to me.
Mishna: a dovecote must be fifty cubits from the town, and fifty cubits in each direction from one's property line.
Rabbi Yehuda: the surrounding area must suffice for sowing four kor of seed, and a bought dovecote keeps its privilege even with less.
Must one distance a dovecote only fifty cubits from the city, and no more?
A contradiction: a mishna requires traps for doves to be at least thirty ris from settled areas.
Abaye: doves fly far, but their stomachs fill after fifty cubits, so they cause no more damage to seeds.
A baraita: in a settled area one may not set traps even if one's land extends a hundred mil.
Rav Yosef: this refers to a settled area of vineyards. Rava: it refers to a settled area of dovecotes, or to gentile or ownerless ones.
Rabbi Yehuda again: the surrounding area must suffice for sowing four kor of seed.
Rav Pappa, or some say Rav Zevid: a court issues claims on behalf of a buyer or heir, backed by the presumed agreement of the previous owner.
Why state this, since it is already taught with regard to an heir?
It was needed to cover a buyer.
But the same is taught with regard to a buyer in the mishna about a courtyard with projections and balconies.
The mishna is needed in both cases: one reading applies to public domain projections, while the other concerns damage to private individuals.
The conclusion: the dovecote remains in the owner's presumptive status.
Objects: Rav Nahman taught there is no privilege of use for damage, so why would the buyer keep it when his doves cause damage?
Rav Mari: Rav Nahman's statement refers to smoke; Rav Zevid: it refers to a bathroom.

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A chick found within fifty cubits of a dovecote belongs to its owner; beyond fifty cubits it belongs to the finder.
A chick found between two dovecotes belongs to the nearer owner; if equidistant, the two owners divide its value.
Rabbi Hanina: in a doubtful status, follow the majority, even when proximity points the other way.
Rabbi Zeira objects from the verse on the nearest city to a corpse, chosen even though a larger city exists.
The verse refers to a case where no other city is larger.
If the majority governs, why follow the closest city rather than the majority of the world?
The city sits isolated between mountains, so the murderer likely came from there.
The mishna gives the chick to the nearer owner even when another dovecote is larger, suggesting proximity governs.
The mishna refers to a case where there is no other larger dovecote.
If so, the latter clause gives a chick found beyond fifty cubits to the finder, though it surely fell from that dovecote.
Rav Ukva bar Hama: a hopping creature does not hop more than fifty cubits, so a chick within that range came from the dovecote.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks about a chick with one leg within fifty cubits of a dovecote and one leg beyond.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yirmeya was removed from the study hall for raising such a far-fetched question.
Comes to hear the mishna on a chick between two dovecotes, where proximity decides even if one dovecote is larger.
The case is one where the two dovecotes are equal in size.
Why not follow the majority of the world, since many other dovecotes exist with more doves?
The Gemara returns with another question about what case is meant, leaving the reply open.

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A chick found between vineyards must come from nearby dovecotes, since hopping birds that lose sight of their nest stop going farther.
Abaye cites a mishna on blood found in the corridor, presumed menstrual despite a nearer upper chamber, as support that majority outweighs proximity.
Rava objects that Abaye's proof involves both majority and frequency, and no one holds that proximity overrides majority when both apply.
Rava cites Rabbi Ḥiyya's baraita: corridor blood creates Temple-entry liability and burns teruma, so it is treated as definite menstrual blood.
Rava draws three lessons from Rabbi Ḥiyya's baraita: majority plus proximity favors majority, the rule is Torah law, and it supports Rabbi Zeira's principle.
Rabbi Zeira's meat ruling: one follows the majority even with locked city gates, since the woman resembles locked gates leaving a single majority.
The Gemara challenges Rava's inconsistency: he earlier said majority and frequency are required, so how can he derive a general rule from Rabbi Ḥiyya?
Rava retracted that claim, adopting the view that majority governs in all cases.
Rav's ruling on a barrel floating in a river: if found opposite a Jewish-majority town it is permitted, and opposite a gentile-majority town it is forbidden.
Shmuel rules the wine forbidden even when found opposite a Jewish-majority town, since it may have floated from a distant gentile town.
Shmuel explains the barrel may have come from distant Dekira, a gentile-majority place, since river currents can carry items far.
The Gemara asks whether Rav and Shmuel disagree about Rabbi Ḥanina's view that distant locales count in the majority.
The Gemara rejects that suggestion: all agree with Rabbi Ḥanina, and the dispute here concerns whether the barrel could have traveled by river.
Rav holds the barrel could not have come from Dekira, since weak river currents and bays would have sunk it, so it came from nearby.
Shmuel holds that the river's force may have carried the barrel from far away, as river flow can bring items great distances.
Ravina permitted a barrel of wine hidden in an orla vineyard, not worried it came from that vineyard's grapes.
The Gemara asks whether Ravina's leniency reflects Rabbi Ḥanina's view that the majority of non-orla vineyards governs over proximity.
It differs: thieves would not hide stolen wine in its own vineyard, but grapes could be hidden there, so grapes stay suspect.
Rava permitted jugs of wine found between a Jew's vines, unconcerned that they belonged to a gentile.
The Gemara asks whether Rava does not hold Rabbi Ḥanina's majority principle, since the majority here are gentiles.
The Gemara answers that the case there differs because of the majority involved, which governs the jugs' status.

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ruling on wine jugs: large jugs found among others are presumed Jewish-owned, while small jugs dropped by travelers may be gentile-owned.
Mishna sets tree distances from a city, with Abba Shaul's view, and rules on compensation depending on which came first.
What is the reason for distancing a tree from a city?
Ulla explains the reason is the beauty of the city, since branches obscuring its walls are unsightly.
Suggests deriving the rule from the Arakhin principle that fields and open areas cannot be converted into one another.
No, the beauty rationale is needed, since Rabbi Elazar permits such conversions, so tree planting is barred for beauty.
Rabbis' view: the conversion ban applies only to seeds, not trees, so the beauty reason alone bars planting trees here.
The Gemara asks what basis distinguishes seeds from trees in this regard.
A Shabbat baraita: an enclosure mostly planted with trees keeps the status of a courtyard, unlike seed planting, which makes it a garden.
Restates the mishna: if the city came first, the tree is cut down without compensation to its owner.
What distinguishes the cistern case, where the cistern owner pays, from the city case, where no compensation is given?
Rav Kahana's proverb: a pot shared by partners is neither hot nor cold, so no single party is responsible for a communal loss.
The Gemara challenges Rav Kahana's explanation: perhaps public damage is treated differently from individual damage.
Rav Kahana's comment applies to the latter clause, where the tree preceded the city and compensation is owed.
Restates the latter clause: if the tree came first, the owner cuts it down and the city pays him.
Asks why the tree owner should not first demand payment before cutting, which could delay cutting for a long time.
Rav Kahana replies that a community, like a pot of partners, need not pay immediately, unlike an individual.
Restates the mishna's uncertainty clause: if it is unclear which came first, the tree is cut down and no compensation is paid.
Asks how this uncertainty case differs from the cistern case, where the tree owner need not cut down the tree.
Answer: certainty would require cutting here but not at the cistern, so uncertainty still requires cutting; claiming payment requires proof of priority.
Mishna sets a fifty-cubit distance for permanent threshing floors from cities, and from others' plantings and fields, to prevent harm.
What distinguishes the first clause's fixed measurement from the latter clause's general standard of not causing damage?
Abaye: the latter clause concerns a non-permanent threshing floor, which must stay far enough from a neighbor not to cause damage.
Asks what defines a non-permanent threshing floor.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Ḥanina: a non-permanent floor processes small quantities without a winnowing shovel, so the chaff scatters less far.
Rav Ashi: the latter clause is not a distance but explains the first clause's rationale: the floor must be far enough not to cause damage.
Baraita objects to Abaye: distance from gourds and plantings is also required, which fits Rav Ashi but is difficult for Abaye's reading.
Asks why plowed-field distance is needed, since chaff clearly harms gourds and cucumbers by drying their flowers.
Rabbi Abba bar Zavda, or Rabbi Abba bar Zutra, begins an explanation for the plowed-field distance that continues on the next daf.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The chaff effectively acts as manure, and excessive manure harms the seeds.
Mishna requires distancing carcasses, graves, and tanneries fifty cubits from a city; tanneries go east, with Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei differing.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Akiva's exception for the west means a fifty-cubit distance there, or a complete ban.
A baraita states Rabbi Akiva bans tanneries on the west outright, because the western wind is frequent.
Rava asks Rav Naḥman what frequent means; if it means blowing constantly among winds, that seems problematic.
Rav teaches the northern wind blows with each of the other three, is most constant, and Ben Netz restrains the destructive south wind.
Upholds Rabbi Akiva: frequent means frequent with the Divine Presence, which dwells in the west, so tanneries are barred there.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: the celestial bodies, moving east to west, bow westward per Nehemiah 9:6, implying the Divine Presence is in the west.
Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov objects: perhaps the bodies are like a servant bowing while walking backward, so the Divine Presence is in the east.
Rabbi Oshaya holds that the Divine Presence is found in every place, opposing views that locate it in one direction.
Rabbi Oshaya reads Nehemiah 9:6 and Job 38:35: God's messengers report from where they are sent, showing the Divine Presence is everywhere.
Rabbi Yishmael also holds the Divine Presence is in every place.
A Yishmael school teaching cites Zechariah 2:7, which says to meet him, not after him, teaching presence everywhere.
Rav Sheshet also holds the Divine Presence is in every place.
Rav Sheshet told his servant to face any direction but east in prayer, because heretics face east, not because God is absent there.
Rabbi Abbahu holds the Divine Presence is in the west, reading oriyya as avir Yah, the air of God.
Rav Yehuda reads Deuteronomy 32:2 and Isaiah 46:6 to assign each of the four winds a role: west, north, east, and south.
A baraita begins a statement attributed to Rabbi Eliezer, which continues onto the next daf.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Eliezer compares the world to a partially enclosed veranda, open on the north, so the sun does not pass the north side.
Rabbi Yehoshua compares the world to a small tent with a northern partition, with the sun passing behind the dome to reach the east.
Ecclesiastes 1:5-6 describes the sun's movements; Rabbi Yehoshua reads ruaḥ as the eastern and western faces, where the sun turns.
The Gemara notes that this baraita reflects Rabbi Eliezer's view that the world is like a partially enclosed veranda.
Job 37:9-10 is cited to show the northern side is open: cold winds come from there, while the south forms the enclosed room.
Asks how the south wind can raise showers and grow herbs, given the baraita's association of the south with storms.
Not difficult: gentle rain waters plants, while a downpour causes damage, so each statement describes a different kind of rain.
Rav Ḥisda reads Job 37:22 as the north wind, supported by Isaiah 46:6, linking north wind to devalued gold.
Rafram bar Pappa, citing Rav Ḥisda: since the Temple's destruction, the south wind has never brought rain.
Isaiah 9:19 and Psalms 89:13 show that right means south, and the south wind brings famine as God decreed.
Rafram again, citing Rav Ḥisda: since the Temple's destruction, rain no longer descends from God's good storehouse.
Deuteronomy 28:12 is read to show rain comes from God's good storehouse only when Israel does God's will and dwells on its land.
Rabbi Yitzḥak: one who wants wisdom should face south, one who wants wealth north; the Temple table in north, candelabrum in south, as a mnemonic.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: always face south, because wisdom leads to wealth, so wisdom brings riches.
Proverbs 3:16 is cited: length of days in her right hand, riches and honor in her left, linking wisdom to wealth.
The Gemara asks: since Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the Divine Presence is in the west, how can one pray facing south?
One should turn slightly aside, so he faces southwest rather than directly south.
