Rabbi Ḥanina tells Rav Ashi that people living north of Eretz Yisrael, like you, should face south in prayer.
Jeremiah 1:14 shows Babylonia lies north of Eretz Yisrael, since evil breaks out from the north upon the land's inhabitants.
Recalls the mishna's rule that flax-steeping water must be distanced from vegetables.
Rabbi Yosei permits mustard near bees, since the beekeeper's bees damage the mustard as well, so neither can compel the other to move.
Mishna sets distances between trees and cisterns: twenty-five or fifty cubits, with cutting and payment rules depending on priority and Rabbi Yosei's view.
A tanna lists the cases: cistern below and tree above, or cistern above and tree below, both requiring the distance.
Asks why a tree below a cistern must be distanced, since its roots grow downward away from the cistern.
Rabbi Ḥagga, citing Rabbi Yosei: the roots form holes that loosen the soil and ruin the cistern's floor.
Rabbi Yosei: even if the cistern came first, the tree need not be cut down, since each person acts on his own property.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Ashi recalls that in Rav Kahana's study hall, Rabbi Yosei conceded when a neighbor's activity causes immediate damage.
Pappei Yona'a became wealthy, built a mansion, and complained to Rav Ashi that nearby sesame pressers shook it.
Rav Ashi rules that, following Rabbi Yosei's concession on arrows, the sesame pressers must move because their immediate damage is direct.
The Gemara asks how much the mansion must shake before the owner may compel the pressers to move.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The shaking must be enough to make a jug lid on a wall rattle, setting the threshold for the complaint.
Bar Maryon's household beat flax so chaff flew and harmed people, who complained to Ravina.
Ravina: Rabbi Yosei's concession covers only damage moved by one's direct force, not chaff carried by wind.
Mar bar Rav Ashi objects: winnowing with wind assistance counts as direct labor on Shabbat, so chaff should also count as direct force.
Asks how Ravina distinguishes flying chaff from a hammer's spark, which the wielder must pay for.
There he prefers the spark to fly far away; here he is indifferent whether chaff travels, so the cases differ.
Mishna: one may not plant a tree next to another's field within four cubits; fences, root and digging rules follow.
Four cubits serve vineyard work; Shmuel holds two cubits suffice in Babylonia, where plows are shorter, unlike Eretz Yisrael.
A baraita states the tree need only be two cubits from the field, supporting Shmuel's distinction for Babylonia.
But the mishna says four cubits, so the baraita seems to contradict it.
Rather, the Gemara concludes that the rule must follow Shmuel's Eretz Yisrael and Babylonia distinction.
Others raise the contradiction: the mishna's four cubits versus a baraita's two cubits.
Shmuel resolves it: the baraita refers to Babylonia, the mishna to Eretz Yisrael.
Rava bar Rav Ḥanan's palms let birds damage Rav Yosef's vineyard, so Rav Yosef orders them cut down.
Rava protests that he already distanced the palms as required.
Rav Yosef: the distance applies only to trees; vines require a greater distance.
Rava protests that the mishna's single distance covers both grapevines and any tree.
Rav Yosef: the single distance applies tree-to-tree or vine-to-vine, while tree-to-vine spacing needs more.
Rava refuses to cut his palms, citing Rav's ruling that a palm yielding a kav of fruit may not be cut down.
Rav's prohibition rests on Deuteronomy 20:19; Rabbi Ḥanina's son died after cutting a fig tree early, supporting caution.
Rav Pappa finds Rav Huna digging and cutting palm roots at a shared boundary and questions him.
Rav Pappa asks what Rav Huna is doing.
Rav Huna cites the mishna allowing digging three handbreadths to sever intruding roots so they do not impede the plow.
Rav Pappa objects that the mishna's allowance is up to three handbreadths, while Rav Huna digs deeper.
Rav Huna replies he digs cisterns, ditches, and caves, which the mishna lets him dig through, keeping the wood from roots.
Rav Pappa says he gave Rav Huna all the proofs he could find but failed to convince him.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Huna justifies his cutting, citing Rav Yehuda: land held in acquired use by many may not be damaged.
Rav Huna later reflects he should have answered that roots within sixteen cubits count as the tree, unlike roots beyond that distance.
The mishna: a person digging a cistern, ditch, or cave may cut downward, and the wood from roots is his.
Ya'akov of Hadeyyav asks Rav Ḥisda whose wood the roots' wood belongs to, the tree's owner or the land's owner.
Rav Ḥisda cites a Me'ila mishna: roots of an ordinary tree entering Temple land incur no misuse liability, resolving the dilemma.
If roots follow the tree, no misuse liability follows since the tree is not consecrated; if they follow the land, liability should arise.
The Gemara asks: if roots follow the tree, why is there no misuse liability in the mishna's second clause?
Not comparable: the mishna concerns later growths, and the tanna holds misuse applies only to the original consecrated plant, not its growths.
Ravina: no contradiction; within sixteen cubits roots belong to the tree, beyond that they belong to the ground.
Ulla holds that one who keeps a tree within sixteen cubits of a boundary is a robber and cannot bring first fruits from it.
The Gemara asks Ulla's source for that sixteen-cubit measurement.
Proposes a Shevi'it mishna as Ulla's source: ten saplings in a beit se'a permit plowing the whole area for their sake.
Calculation shows the ten saplings' share is 250 square cubits, far less than Ulla's 32-by-32 square, so that mishna does not support him.
The Gemara offers another Shevi'it mishna: three large trees of three owners in one beit se'a combine, so the whole area may be plowed.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Calculates the area for each tree: about 833 and a third square cubits, still above Ulla's amount.
Ulla was not precise in his measurement.
Asks whether an imprecise sage is excused only when the error is stringent, not when it is lenient.
The roots extend in a circle, not a square, so the area is smaller than the sixteen-cubit square.
Asks how much a square exceeds its circle, then whether the exact radius should be sixteen and a half cubits.
Ulla's error is in the stringent direction: first fruits are brought even from a tree sixteen cubits away.
Objects with a Bikkurim mishna on buying a tree and its land, then answers that it must mean sixteen cubits around the tree.
A Bikkurim mishna on two versus three trees is offered as proof, rejected as referring to sixteen cubits of land.
A Pe'a mishna: Rabbi Akiva holds any size of land is obligated in pe'a and first fruits, so prosbol may be written for it.

27b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects: the mishna says any amount of land acquires movables with it, implying any land bears first fruits, challenging Ulla's sixteen cubits.
Deals with wheat, needing little land; the mishna's any size is precise, since normal trees need more than a minimal amount.
A Tosefta on a tree partly in Eretz Yisrael and partly outside: tithed and untithed produce mix, per Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: each part of the tree takes the tithe status of the land where it grows.
The Gemara explains the dispute: Shimon accepts retroactive designation while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rejects it, so fruit is mixed; if fully outside, all exempt.
We deal with a rock dividing the roots up to the trunk, so the parts drawing from each land can be told apart.
Asks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's reasoning for treating the fruit as mixed if the parts are separable.
The roots are separable but mix within the trunk's body.
Asks what principle the two Sages dispute.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: air above ground mixes nutrients; Rabban Shimon: each part stands alone, like a tree cut along the border line.
Objects to Ulla: the mishna requires a tree twenty-five cubits from a cistern, implying roots reach beyond sixteen cubits.
Abaye: roots extend farther, but they weaken the soil only up to sixteen cubits, beyond which no harm occurs.
Rav Dimi reports Reish Lakish asked Rabbi Yoḥanan about a tree within sixteen cubits of a boundary.
Reish Lakish asks the halakha for a tree within sixteen cubits of a boundary.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: the owner is a robber, so one may not bring first fruits from that tree.
Ravin reports Rabbi Yoḥanan: trees near a boundary or leaning into a neighbor's yard yield first fruits, as Joshua's allotment assumed such tolerance.
Mishna: a tree leaning into a neighbor's field may be cut to ox-goad height; carob, sycamore, and irrigated-field rules; Abba Shaul adds barren trees.
Asks whether Abba Shaul's barren-tree ruling refers to the first clause or the irrigated-field latter clause.
A baraita on irrigated fields: Abba Shaul says all trees are cut along the plumb line, so he refers to the first clause.
Rav Ashi: the wording all barren trees is precise, showing Abba Shaul addresses the first clause.
Mishna: a tree extending into the public domain is cut so a camel and rider pass; Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon give other measures.
Asks which tanna holds that damage is assessed by current conditions, ignoring future growth.
Reish Lakish: the halakha is a dispute, following Rabbi Eliezer, who permits pits covered by a cover strong enough for a loaded wagon.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: even the Rabbis could hold the tree rule, since the branch damage is visible and cut as it grows, unlike a rotting cover.
Rabbi Yehuda: one cuts enough branches for a camel loaded with flax or branch bundles to pass beneath.
Asks whether Rabbi Yehuda's measure is greater than the Rabbis', or the reverse.
The Rabbis' measure is greater, since Rabbi Yehuda's would block a loaded camel; a rider can bend under branches.
Rabbi Shimon: cut all branches over the public domain along the plumb line because of ritual impurity.
A baraita specifies the concern is impurity imparted by a tent, implying branches over a corpse form one.
Expresses surprise: the mishna already says ritual impurity, so what else could transfer it besides a tent?
If the mishna alone, a crow might carry impurity to branches; a scarecrow would suffice, so the baraita teaches tent-based impurity. Chapter-closing formula follows.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah lists property types whose presumptive ownership requires three years of continuous profitable use.
Non-irrigated fields also establish presumptive ownership in three years, but not continuously day to day.
Rabbi Yishmael: three months in the first year, three in the last, and twelve in the middle, eighteen months total.
Rabbi Akiva: one month in the first year, one in the last, and twelve in the middle, fourteen months total.
Yishmael clarifies that the eighteen-month rule covers grain fields; for tree fields, three harvests count as three years.
Rabbi Yochanan reports what the scholars of Usha taught about the source for three-year presumptive ownership.
Where is the source that presumptive ownership is established by three years?
Derives the three-year rule from the forewarned ox: after three goring incidents it changes status, so the land passes to the buyer.
If so, just as the ox is not liable until the fourth goring, the land should not pass to the buyer until the fourth year.
Rejects the objection: the cases differ, since the ox becomes forewarned after three goring incidents, which is when its status changes.

28b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The fourth goring is needed only for the ox; for land, three years of use already establish ownership in the owner's hands.
If the forewarned-ox model is the basis, why does a possession without an accompanying claim not establish presumptive ownership?
Possession without a claim is insufficient because the other side may still prove a purchase, and the possessor cannot then claim one.
Rav Urria objects: a protest lodged outside the possessor's presence should not count, by analogy to the forewarned ox's warning.
The ox's warning verse requires presence, but a protest spreads through acquaintances, so presence is not required for land.
By Rabbi Meir, consuming three fruits on one day should suffice, since the ox's gorings may all occur together.
The ox analogy requires each goring to occur at a separate time, so the fruits must be consumed at separate times as well.
Would consuming three caper fruits over three days establish presumptive ownership, since they ripen one after another?
Caper fruit is still on the bush and is in the process of ripening, unlike the independent goring of the ox.
Consuming three alfalfa cuttings within thirty days should establish presumptive ownership, since the plant regrows quickly.
What scenario would be needed for alfalfa to be cut and eaten three times within thirty days?
That is a case where he seizes and cuts the alfalfa in an irregular way, which does not establish presumptive ownership.
Consuming three alfalfa harvests within three months, cut in the normal way, should establish presumptive ownership.
This follows Rabbi Yishmael's view, who holds that three harvests suffice, so the challenge applies only to his opinion.
Cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Yishmael says three harvests from a tree field count as three years.
According to the Rabbis, who require three years rather than three harvests, what is the source for this presumption?
Rav Yosef cites Jeremiah buying a field and having the deed sealed, since the prophet's warning shows three years was impossible.
Abaye objects that Jeremiah's verse may only offer good advice to keep documents, so it does not prove three years is required.

29a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If Jeremiah's instruction to build houses is not mere advice, what halakhic teaching does it actually convey?
It is only good advice, and the similar verse about dwelling in the land is also just advice.
Jeremiah's instruction to put documents in an earthen vessel shows the advice is about preservation, not law.
Rava's reason: a person waives a claim in the first or second year, but not in the third, so silence then concedes the land.
Abaye objects: if so, returned land should return with its produce, yet Rav Naḥman says the produce is returned too.
Rava's second reason: an owner does not object in years one or two, but does object by the third year.
Abaye objects: some owners object at any encroachment, so presumption would be immediate, making the law depend on each owner.
Rava's third reason: possessors keep their purchase documents for three years, after which they may discard them.
Abaye objects: an objection made outside the possessor's presence should count, since he would have kept his document.
The claimant can answer that word of any protest spreads to the possessor through acquaintances, so the protest reaches him.
Rav Huna: the three years required must be consecutive years of use.
What is Rav Huna teaching us with this, since the mishna already states three years from day to day?
The mishna's phrase: presumptive ownership is established by three years of use from day to day.
The phrase excludes broken years, so Rav Huna teaches that scattered years do not suffice, only consecutive ones.
Rav Ḥama: Rav Huna agrees that in places where fields are left fallow, alternate years combine into continuous use.
Is the point not obvious?
No, it is needed for places where some people leave fields fallow and some do not, and this man let his field lie fallow.
The claimant could say: if the land is yours, you should have sown it, rather than leaving it fallow.
The possessor replies he cannot guard one parcel within a large field, and so acted like others in that area.
Alternatively, fallow farming is better, since the land yields more later and the soil is not weakened by yearly planting.
The mishna speaks of presumptive ownership of houses, which is also established by three years of use.
How can houses be used continuously when witnesses only know who occupies them by day, not by night?
Abaye: neighbors can testify, since they know who is inside the house both by day and by night.
Rava: witnesses can be two tenants who rented the house and lived in it for three years, day and night.
Rav Yeimar objects: such tenant witnesses are biased, since admitting they rented would lose them the rent they paid.
Rav Ashi: only ignorant judges would accept that, but Rava's case stands, since tenants hold the rent and cannot choose the owner.
Mar Zutra: if the claimant contests, two witnesses may testify that the possessor lived in the house three years, day and night.

29b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mar Zutra: for peddlers who travel and whose houses others may use, the court presses the continuous-use requirement even unasked.
Rav Huna: for a shop used by day but not at night, continuous night use is not required to establish presumptive ownership.
Case: two partners buy a maidservant and use her in alternate years; a third party then contests ownership before Rava.
Rava rules the alternating use does not establish presumption against the partners or against the outside claimant.
Qualification: this holds only if no document records a partnership; a written document gives public notice of joint ownership.
Rava: after three years of use, a possessor acquires the whole field except a beit rova he did not work.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua limits this to a beit rova fit for sowing; an unsowable plot is acquired with the rest of the field.
Rav Beivai objects: rock cannot be planted, so presumption must come from animals or produce on it, applying the same test here.
What is the claimant doing with this house of mine?
The occupant replies that he bought it and used it for the three years needed to establish presumptive ownership.
The claimant explains he lived in distant settlements and did not know the occupant lived there, so he did not protest.
Rav Naḥman rules the occupant must prove by evidence that he actually used the house for the three years.
Rava objects: the burden of proof rests on the claimant, so the claimant must prove the occupant did not reside there.
The Gemara raises contradictions between Rava's rulings and between Rav Naḥman's rulings, which the text leaves incomplete.

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A seller sells all his bar Sisin property, but a parcel only named after bar Sisin is disputed; Rav Naḥman leaves it with the buyer.
Rava objects that the burden of proof is on the claimant, and Rava and Rav Naḥman each seem to contradict their own rulings.
The contradictions are resolved: the seller holds the land in one case and the buyer holds it in the other, so each ruling is consistent.
What is the claimant doing with this house of mine?
The occupant says he bought it from the claimant and used it for the years needed to establish presumptive ownership.
The claimant replies that he was in the outer marketplaces and did not know the occupant lived in his house, so he did not protest.
The occupant replies that the claimant came to the town thirty days each year, with witnesses, and could have protested then.
The claimant explains that during those thirty days he was occupied with business in the marketplace.
Rava: a person may well be busy in the marketplace for all thirty days, so the claimant's excuse is accepted.
What is the claimant doing with this land of mine?
The occupant says he bought it from a third party, who had bought it from the claimant.
The claimant challenges the occupant to concede a point that undermines his claimed purchase chain.

30b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The claimant says the land is his and was never sold to the possessor; Rava rules this is a legitimate claim and accepts it.
What is the claimant doing with this land of mine?
The possessor says he bought it from a named seller and used it for the years needed to establish presumptive ownership.
The claimant says the seller is a robber who took the field and had no authority to sell it.
The possessor replies with witnesses that the claimant advised him to buy the land, conceding the seller's authority.
The claimant explains he advised buying because the possessor is easier to deal with than the alleged robber.
Rava rules that the claimant's explanation is legitimate and accepts his claim.
Is Rava's ruling in accordance with Admon's opinion?
Cites the mishna: Admon says a claimant who signed as witness does not lose his right, while the Rabbis say he does.
The Rabbis may still be followed here, because there the claimant acted by signing, whereas here it was only speech, which does not forfeit a claim.
What is the claimant doing with this land of mine?
The possessor says he bought it from a named seller and used it for the years needed to establish presumptive ownership.
The claimant says the seller is a robber who took the field and had no authority to sell it.
The possessor says the claimant came to him at night and asked him to sell the land, as if it were his, to be repaid without paying.
The claimant explains he chose to pay to avoid litigation and recover his land.
Rava: a person may pay money to buy the benefit of avoiding litigation, so the claimant's explanation is accepted.
What is the claimant doing with this land of mine?
The possessor says he bought it from a named seller and used it for the years needed to establish presumptive ownership.
The claimant holds a document showing he bought the land four years ago, so the seller could not have sold it three years ago.
The possessor replies he meant many years of use, not exactly three, and his purchase predates the claimant's, so it was effective.
Rava: people commonly call many years the years needed to establish presumptive ownership, so the possessor's claim is accepted.
This applies only if the possessor used the land for seven years, so his presumptive ownership predates the claimant's document.

31a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the seller sold before the three years were complete, that sale alone shows he did not concede the possessor's ownership.
Two litigants each claim the land was their ancestors'; one brings witnesses of ancestral ownership, the other of three years of use.
Rabba: the possessor has credibility because he would not lie, since he could have claimed a purchase and won outright.
Abaye objects: a possessor's claim is not credible against witnesses who contradict it by showing ancestral ownership.
The possessor explains that his ancestral claim meant he relied on his ownership as if it were inherited, since he had bought it.
May a litigant state a claim, return, and state a modified version of it, or not?
Ulla holds a litigant may modify his claim; the Sages of Neharde'a hold he may not.
Ulla concedes a modified claim is barred if it contradicts the first claim or was learned outside the court.
The Neharde'a Sages concede a modification that only clarifies is allowed, and a claim first raised outside the court may be stated later.
Ameimar, though from Neharde'a, holds a litigant may modify his claim, and the halakha follows this view.
Two litigants claim ancestral ownership; the first has witnesses of ancestral ownership and of three years of use, the second only of use.
Rav Naḥman: the profiting testimonies cancel out, leaving the first litigant's ancestral testimony, so the land is his.
Rava objects that this testimony cannot be relied on, since it is contradicted by the other testimony.
Rav Naḥman replies that although the profiting testimony was contradicted, the ancestral testimony still stands.

31b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the testimony about ancestral ownership was contradicted.
Proposes that Rava and Rav Nachman disagree within the Rav Huna and Rav Chisda dispute.
Rav Huna rules that two contradicting groups of witnesses each may testify separately in other cases.
Rav Chisda holds that the lying witnesses are disqualified and asks why they would be needed at all.
Asks whether Rav Nachman follows Rav Huna while Rava follows Rav Chisda.
Explains that all agree under Rav Chisda, and Rav Nachman follows Rav Huna, limited to a different testimony.
Rav Nachman rules that the claimant is removed from the land, disregarding concern about appearing indecisive.
Objects with a baraita on contradictory witnesses about death or divorce, including Rabbi Menachem's stricter view.
Rabbi Menachem limits his view: she must leave only if witnesses came before the remarriage.
Rav Nachman replies that he will not act on his ruling, given the objections raised against him.
Narrates that Rav Nachman acted anyway, which onlookers took as error, because the matter is disputed among great authorities.
Cites a mishna in which Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Elazar and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dispute whether one witness suffices for priestly status.
Asks how Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel differs from Rabbi Elazar, and what practical difference a single challenger would make.

32a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that a challenge requires two witnesses.
Objects that Rabbi Yochanan said all agree a challenge needs two witnesses, which conflicts with this view.
Replies that the challenge in question involves two witnesses, defending Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view.
Asks what kind of case is being discussed here.
Explains the case: a man presumed a priest is downgraded after a rumor, then restored on one witness's testimony.
Continues the case: two witnesses downgrade him, one restores him, and all agree the single testimonies combine.
Explains that Rabbi Elazar does not restore a downgraded priest, out of concern about the court appearing indecisive.
Explains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel restores him, since the court's dignity is not a concern.
Objects to the explanation: why specify one witness, since the same would apply to two witnesses together.
Proposes that all agree the court's dignity is no concern, so the dispute concerns combining two single testimonies.
Cites a baraita: single witnesses' testimony combines only if both see the event together.
Cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: testimony combines even if seen separately, but must be given together in court.
Cites Rabbi Natan, who allows testimony heard on different days to combine.
Presents a land dispute: one man asks another what he wants with the first man's land.
The possessor replies that he bought the land and produces the bill of sale.

32b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The possessor replies that the bill of sale is forged.
Whispers to Rabba that it is forged, explaining that his proper bill was lost and he keeps this one anyway.
Rabba argues that a liar would simply claim a proper bill and would win the land.
Rav Yosef objects: a forged bill is a worthless shard and cannot ground awarding the land.
Introduces a parallel case: a man demands one hundred dinars based on a promissory note.
The debtor replies that the note is forged.
Whispers to Rava that the note is forged, explaining that his proper note was lost and he keeps this one anyway.
Rabba argues again that a liar would claim a proper note and win the money.
Rav Yosef objects that a forged note is a worthless shard and cannot support awarding the money.
Rav Idi bar Avin rules: land stays with the possessor under Rabba, money stays with the debtor under Rav Yosef.
A guarantor demands one hundred dinars for repaying the creditor on the debtor's behalf, showing the document.
The debtor asks whether he did not already repay the guarantor.
The guarantor replies that the debtor later took the money back from him.
Rav Idi bar Avin asks Abaye how to rule in such a case.
Abaye replies that Rav Idi's own ruling already settles it: the money stays where it is.
Clarifies the ruling: it applies only if the debtor borrowed back, but if the coins were defective the lien remains.
A rumor spreads that Rava bar Sharshom profits from the land of orphans.
Abaye asks Rava bar Sharshom how the incident itself arose.
Rava bar Sharshom explains he held the land as collateral from the orphans' father.

33a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava bar Sharshom explains that the father owed him other money and he profited from the collateral land.
Reasons that he may keep the land and collect his debt, since he could have claimed he bought it.
Abaye objects: a purchase claim fails because the land is publicly known as orphans' property; he must return it.
Introduces a case: a relative of Rav Idi bar Avin dies leaving a date tree, which another relative takes.
Rav Idi bar Avin claims he is the closer relative to the deceased.
The other claimant asserts he is closer, then admits Rav Idi is closer.
Rav Hisda awards the tree to Rav Idi bar Avin.
Rav Idi demands the value of the produce consumed since the tree was taken.
Rav Hisda challenges Rav Idi's claim, which rests on the other relative's earlier assertion, and limits ownership to the time of admission.
Notes that Abaye and Rava do not accept Rav Hisda's view on this point.

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Summarizes that the admitting relative must repay Rav Idi, since his admission removes any right to the produce.
Describes a dispute: each claimant says the land was his ancestors', one with ancestral witnesses, the other with usage witnesses.
Rav Chisda rules that the possessor is credible, since he could have claimed purchase and been believed.
Abaye and Rava reject that rule, because witnesses contradicting his claim defeat the credibility principle.
Describes a land case: the possessor claims purchase and brings witnesses for only two years of use.
Rav Nachman rules the land and the value of the produce revert to the prior owner, since the claim was unproven.
Rav Zevid says the possessor is credible if he claimed to enter only to consume purchased produce.
Brings proof: Rav Yehuda deems a man credible when he sets out to cull dates from a tree he claims he bought.
Concludes that people are not brazen enough to take produce that is not theirs, so the same applies here.
Asks: if so, the possessor should be credible about the land too.
Answers: for land, the possessor must show his bill of sale.
Asks: then for produce too, he should need a document to prove his claim.
Answers: people do not write documents for produce rights alone, so an oral agreement suffices.
Describes a case: a possessor claims purchase and brings one witness for three years of use.
The Rabbis propose that the case resembles the cast-metal case decided by Rabbi Abba.
Describes the cast-metal case: a man snatched metal from another, who brings one witness to the snatching.
The snatcher replies: yes, I snatched, but only what was mine.
Rabbi Ami begins his ruling on the case.

34a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks how judges should rule in this case: must the snatcher pay?
Weighs options: no exemption since one witness testifies against him, and no oath since he admitted snatching, like a robber.
Rabbi Abba rules that one who must swear but cannot swear must pay.
Abaye objects that the cases differ: the metal witness undermines the snatcher, while the land witness supports the possessor.
Offers a better comparison: one witness to two years of use, where the possessor cannot swear and must pay for produce.

34b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Describes a boat dispute: each claims ownership, and one asks the court to seize it until he brings witnesses.
Asks whether the court seizes the disputed boat or not.
Rav Huna holds that the court seizes it.
Rav Yehuda holds that the court does not seize it, since the court has no reason to intervene.
The claimant fails to find witnesses, asks for release, and proposes that the stronger party prevail.
Asks whether the court releases the boat in such a case.
Rav Yehuda holds that the court does not release it.
Rav Pappa holds that the court releases it.
Concludes the halakha: property with uncertain ownership is not seized, and once seized, is not released.
Describes a case of uncertain ownership: each claims the property belonged to his ancestors.
Rav Naḥman rules that the stronger party prevails in that situation.
Asks why this differs from two deeds of sale issued on the same day.

35a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Recalls Rav's view that the parties divide the property, and Shmuel's view that the judges decide at their discretion.
Answers: in the two-deeds case the court cannot clarify later, but in Rav Nachman's case it might.
Asks how this differs from the mishna on exchanged animals and sold maidservants, where the parties divide the newborn's value.
Begins to answer that the exchange case differs with regard to the buyer's position.

35b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Each litigant has a claim to the property, so dividing it is reasonable; contrast with a case where only one can own it.
The Neharde'a sages hold that an outsider who seized disputed property cannot be dispossessed by the court.
Rabbi Chiyya's baraita: a robber whose victims are unknown is not called a robber, supporting the Neharde'a view.
Rav Ashi rejects that reading and insists that such a person is in fact called a robber.
Asks what the baraita's phrase 'not called a robber' means.
It means the stolen goods cannot be returned, so the robber cannot fully atone since he does not know whom to repay.
The Mishnah's rule that presumptive ownership is established by three years of possession counted from day to day.
Rabbi Abba: for some property presumptive ownership arises immediately, if the prior owner himself lifted the produce.
Rav Zevid: a prior owner who claims he only let the field for produce is believed, but only within three years.
Rav Ashi asks Rav Kahana what the prior owner could have done in the sharecropping case to block the presumption.
Rav Kahana: he should have protested during the first three years and publicized that he granted only the produce.
Reductio: otherwise the Sura mortgage custom would let a creditor hide the document and claim purchase, which the Sages would never institute.
Rather, the debtor should have protested in the mortgage case; likewise the owner here should have protested.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: a Jew who obtains land from a gentile is treated like a gentile regarding presumptive ownership.
Analogy: as a gentile can establish presumption only by document, so a Jew claiming through a gentile needs a document.
Rava raises a counter-case about a Jew who speaks to the prior owner while claiming the land, challenging the analogy.

36a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A gentile's claim that he bought the land from the claimant is believed.
Asks whether any case exists where a gentile's claim is disbelieved but a Jew relaying it is believed.
Rava: a Jew relaying the gentile's sale is believed, since the buyer could have claimed the purchase directly.
Rav Yehuda: a man holding a sickle and rope who says he will harvest a palm he bought is believed.
Reason: no one would be so brazen as to harvest dates from a tree that is not his.
Rav Yehuda: holding a fence built against wild donkeys does not establish presumptive ownership.
Asks the reason for this ruling.
The owner reasons that wild donkeys would eat whatever he sows, so this is not owner-like use of the land.
Rav Yehuda: consuming orla produce does not establish presumptive ownership.
A baraita teaches the same for orla, Sabbatical, and diverse-kinds produce.
Rav Yosef: consuming unripe fodder-grain does not establish presumptive ownership.
Rava: in the Mehoza valley, where unripe harvesting is common, it does establish presumption.
Rav Nachman: produce from cracked land, or land yielding little, does not establish presumption because owners do not bother protesting.
Rav Nachman: exilarchic household members cannot establish presumption in our land, and we cannot establish it in theirs.
Mishnah: slaves are presumed owned after three years of use counted from day to day.
Objection from Reish Lakish: livestock cannot establish presumption, so slaves should not either.
Rava's reply: slaves cannot be presumed owned immediately, but do establish presumption after three years.
Rava: a small infant lying in a cradle establishes presumption of ownership immediately, like other movables.
Asks whether this is not obvious, since an infant cannot move himself.
The case is needed for a child with a mother, lest one think she moved him there; a mother does not forget her son.
Narrative: goats ate peeled barley in Neharde'a, and the barley owner seized them, claiming a large sum.
Shmuel's father: the claimant may claim up to the goats' value, since the holder can say he bought them.
Objection: Reish Lakish's rule that livestock lack presumption seems to apply to these goats too.
These goats are different, since they are handed to shepherds and do not wander alone.
Objection: goats are unsupervised morning and evening during transit, so the livestock rule should apply.
This occurred in Neharde'a, where animal thieves are common, so goats are always handed over supervised.
Mishnah: Rabbi Yishmael requires eighteen months of possession; the Gemara proposes the dispute is whether plowing counts.
Challenges the proposed explanation: on that view, why would Rabbi Akiva require a full month specifically?

36b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects: would even one day of plowing suffice? Rejected, since all agree plowing alone does not establish presumption.
Everyone agrees plowing does not establish presumption; the dispute is whether major or minor produce must grow.
A baraita: plowing does not establish presumption, but some say it does.
Asks which authorities are the 'some say' of the baraita.
Rav Chisda: it is the view of Rabbi Acha.
Rabbi Acha's baraita: plowing one year and sowing two, or the reverse, suffices, showing he holds plowing establishes presumption.
Rav Ashi reports that all the great men of the generation say plowing suffices.
Rav Beivai asks Rav Nachman the reason for the view that plowing establishes presumption.
No one would let another plow his land and stay silent.
Asks the reason for the view that plowing does not establish presumption.
The owner is willing for others to plow every clod, so he will sow and harvest later.
The residents of Pum Nahara ask Rav Nachman whether plowing establishes presumption.
Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda replies that Rabbi Acha and the great men say plowing suffices.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects: Rav, Shmuel, R' Yishmael and R' Akiva hold that plowing does not establish presumption.
The Gemara identifies the mishnah as the source for Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva's view.
Asks the source for ascribing the view that plowing does not count to Rav.
Rav Yehuda cites Rav: the month or three-month ruling is the view of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva.
The Sages' view as quoted: presumption requires three years, counted day to day.
Asks what 'from day to day' excludes, suggesting it excludes plowing.
Asks the source for ascribing the plowing view to Shmuel.
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel: R' Yishmael and R' Akiva accept a month or three months; the Sages require three harvests of date, grape, or olive crops.
Asks what the difference is between the views of Rav and Shmuel.
Abaye: the difference is whether three harvests of a young date palm, which bears three times a year, establish presumption.
R' Yishmael: the eighteen-month rule applies only to a white grain field, not to an orchard.
Abaye infers the Sages' view from R' Yishmael: an orchard requires three years of harvesting one crop.
Example: thirty trees, ten harvested each year for three years, establishes presumption of ownership.

37a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites R' Yishmael: harvesting one fruit type establishes presumption for all fruits in the field, so the trees establish presumption for each other.
Two limits: the rule applies only where the other trees bore no fruit, and only if the trees are scattered throughout the field.
Rav Zevid: whoever took possession of the trees acquires them, and the one who took the land acquires the land.
Rav Pappa objects: then the tree owner gets no land at all, and the landowner could tell him to uproot the trees and leave.
Rav Pappa's revised ruling: the tree holder acquires the trees plus half the land, and the other acquires half the land.
Obviously, a seller who keeps trees on sold land retains the land around them.
Even Rabbi Akiva's generous-sale rule applies to a retained pit or cistern, where the seller keeps no land around it.
A pit or cistern does not harm the land around it, but trees do, so the seller keeps the land with them.

37b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Since trees harm the land, the seller keeps the surrounding land; otherwise the buyer may tell him to uproot the trees and leave.
Reverse case, selling trees but keeping the land: R' Akiva says the buyer gets the land, the Rabbis say he does not.
Rav Zevid's rule covers only two separate buyers, so it does not conflict with R' Akiva's view of a single seller.
Here the generous-sale principle applies according to R' Akiva, but the Rabbis deny the buyer the surrounding land.
Rav Pappa's ruling likewise applies only to two buyers, so it does not conflict with the Rabbis' view of a single seller.
Here, by contrast, the seller sells sparingly according to the Rabbis, so the buyer gets no land around the trees.
The Neharde'a sages: consuming the produce of an overcrowded orchard does not establish presumptive ownership of it.
Rava objects: then how is an alfalfa field, planted without spacing, ever acquired?
Rava's answer: if an overcrowded orchard is sold, the buyer gets no surrounding land, since such trees will soon be uprooted.
Rabbi Zeira: this is a dispute between tanna'im about vineyards planted with less than four cubits between vines.
The Kilayim mishnah: R' Shimon says an overcrowded vineyard is not a vineyard; the Rabbis say the middle vines are ignored, so it counts.
The Neharde'a sages: one who sells a date palm to another conveys the land beneath it, down to the depths.

38a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava objects: the seller could say he sold only the saffron crocus, which the buyer normally uproots, so he should uproot it and leave.
Rava's reply: the ruling applies only when the buyer comes with a specific claim that the land was stipulated to him.
Mar Kashisha asks Rav Ashi: if the seller sold only the crocus, what could he have done to block a stipulation claim?
Rav Ashi: he should have protested during the first three years and publicized that the land was excluded.
Mortgage analogy: otherwise a Sura creditor could hide the document and claim purchase, and the Sages would not institute such a loss-causing rule.
Rather, the debtor should have protested in the mortgage case; likewise the owner here should have protested.
Mishnah: three independent lands for presumption are Judea, Transjordan, and the Galilee; owner and possessor must be in one province.
R' Yehuda: three years are required only so that an owner abroad can learn of the possession and return the next year.
Asks what the first tanna holds about a protest lodged outside the possessor's presence.
Analysis: if such a protest counts, Judea and Galilee should count; if not, even within Judea it should not count.
Rav Abba bar Memel, citing Rav: the tanna holds such protests valid, and the mishna addresses a time of emergency when news cannot travel.
Asks what distinguishes Judea and Galilee, since emergency conditions would apply within a single land too.
The tanna's choice of two different lands is meant to teach a specific lesson about the mishna.

38b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ordinary travel between Judea and the Galilee is treated the same as a period of crisis.
Rav: one cannot establish presumption over the property of one who is fleeing, since he cannot lodge a protest.
Shmuel objects: the owner need not protest in the possessor's presence, so he can protest anywhere and presumption may be established.
Asks what Rav is teaching if a protest outside the possessor's presence is invalid, since Rav elsewhere says it is valid.
Objection: but Rav himself says a protest made outside the possessor's presence is valid.
Rav was explaining the reasoning of our mishna's tanna but does not hold that way himself; he follows R' Yehuda.
Alternative version: Rav Yehuda cites Rav that presumption can be established over a fleeing person's property; Shmuel says this is obvious.
Asks why Rav repeats that a protest outside the possessor's presence is valid, if he already stated it.
Objection: Rav already said this once, so he would not need to repeat it.
Rather, Rav teaches that a protest made before two witnesses who cannot themselves tell the possessor is still valid.
Rav Anan, citing Shmuel: a protest before two who can tell the possessor is valid; Rav's view rests on word spreading through a chain of friends.
Rava: one cannot establish presumption over a fleeing person's property, and a protest outside the possessor's presence is valid.
No contradiction: one fleeing money matters can publicize the protest, while one fleeing a capital charge cannot.
Asks what constitutes a valid protest in the first place.
Rav Zevid: calling someone a robber in general is no protest; saying he holds my land by robbery is valid.

39a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A protest is valid if the owner says he will sue the possessor in court tomorrow.
Asks the halakha if the protester also says: do not tell the possessor.
Rav Zevid: not a valid protest, since the protester said not to tell him, so word will not reach him.
Rav Pappa: he meant only not to tell him personally; others should be told, so the protest stands.
Chain of friends: your friend tells a friend, who tells another, so word of the protest reaches the possessor.
Asks the halakha when witnesses tell the protester they will not tell the possessor.
Rav Zevid: invalid, since the witnesses themselves say they will not tell him.
Rav Pappa: they meant only not to tell him personally, so others should be told and the protest stands.
The same chain-of-friends reasoning shows word of the protest reaches the possessor.
Asks the halakha when the protester says: let no word emerge from you about this.
Rav Zevid: not a valid protest, since the protester tells them no word should emerge from them.
Rav Pappa agrees: invalid, since the witnesses are saying they will not let a word emerge.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua: valid, since people often let slip what is not strictly secret, so word reaches the possessor.
Rava reports Rav Nachman: a protest lodged outside the possessor's presence is valid.
Rava objects from R' Yehuda's mishna: if such protests count, why would the owner need to come back to court?
R' Yehuda teaches good advice: the owner should come and collect the land and its produce.
Asks: Rava's objection implies he rejects such protests, yet he himself says they are valid?
Rava held that conclusion only after hearing this halakha from Rav Nachman.
R' Yossei son of R' Chanina asks the students of R' Yochanan how many people must witness a protest.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, citing Rabbi Yochanan: a protest must be made before two people.
Rabbi Abbahu, citing Rabbi Yochanan: a protest must be made before three people.
Proposal: perhaps they disagree about Rabba bar Rav Huna's principle that anything said before three people is publicized.

39b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Proposed resolution: the dispute over two versus three witnesses turns on whether Rabba bar Rav Huna's ruling is accepted.
Rejects that resolution: all agree with Rabba bar Rav Huna, so the disagreement lies elsewhere.
One view holds that a protest lodged absent the owner is not a valid protest.
The opposing view holds that an absent protest is valid, so three witnesses are needed to convey it.
Alternative resolution: everyone accepts absent protest, and the sages disagree about the purpose of the witnesses.
The two-witness view: testimony is what is required, and two witnesses suffice for testimony.
The three-witness view: the matter of the protest must be made known, requiring three people.
Narrative: Giddel bar Minyumi protested before sages, returned a year later, and was told not to repeat it.
Rav's ruling: once the owner protested in the first year, he no longer needs to protest.
A variant report that Ḥiyya bar Rav gave the same ruling on his own authority, not in Rav's name.
Reish Lakish, in the name of bar Kappara, rules that protest is needed at the end of every three years.
Rabbi Yoḥanan is puzzled: a robber cannot gain a presumption of ownership once protested.
The Gemara reframes the objection as one about someone akin to a robber, keeping Reish Lakish's ruling.
Rava rules that the halakha follows Reish Lakish: protest at the end of each three-year period.
A baraita supports this: repeated protests on the same claim defeat presumption, while new claims do not.
Rava, citing Rav Naḥman, teaches that a protest may be lodged in the presence of two witnesses.

40a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A protest and a preemptive declaration require two witnesses, and no directive to write a document is needed.
An admission of obligation needs two witnesses, and the party must direct them to write it down.
An acquisition by a symbolic cloth act needs two witnesses, and no directive to write is needed.
Ratification of documents requires three people; a mnemonic lists the four cases discussed.
Rava's difficulty: if this acquisition resembles a court act, it would need three witnesses.
If it does not resemble a court act, why would the parties not need to direct a written record?
Rava asks why no directive to write is needed for this acquisition.
Rava resolves it: the acquisition is not like a court act, despite appearances.
The Gemara asks what the reason is that no directive to write is needed here.
A symbolic acquisition is designed to be finalized, so a record is presumed desired and written without instruction.
Rabba and Rav Yosef: a preemptive declaration is written only against a party who would not obey the court.
Abaye and Rava: a preemptive declaration may be written even for law-abiding parties, since courts cannot settle everything.
The sages of Neharde'a extend the rule: any protest may be written as such a declaration.

40b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A preemptive declaration lacking the duress formula is invalid, since it does not state the nature of the coercion.
For what kind of transaction is a preemptive declaration written, and what does it accomplish for divorce or gifts?
Objection: Rava says a preemptive declaration is never written for a sale, so this cannot be the case.
Reply: the case is a sale, and Rava concedes that declarations apply when a sale was made under compulsion.
Illustration: a man mortgaged his orchard for three years and then pressured the buyer, showing compelled sale.
The mortgagee's position: sell it to me as agreed, or I will hide the mortgage and claim outright purchase.
Hiding the mortgage document and claiming purchase is a case where a declaration is written.
Rav Yehuda rules that one cannot collect on a concealed gift document.
What exactly does a concealed gift look like in practice?
Rav Yosef: witnesses are told to hide and write the document for the recipient of the gift.
An alternative version of Rav Yosef: witnesses are not told to hide, so the gift is written openly.
Continuing the alternative version: witnesses sit publicly in the marketplace and write the document.
What is the difference between the two versions, given that no specific instruction was given?
Rava: a concealed gift can serve as a preemptive declaration against a later public gift to another.
Rav Pappa: Rava's ruling was not stated explicitly but by inference, and he did not really hold it.
A case of a man who wished to betroth a woman, illustrating how property transfers were arranged.
The woman's condition: she will marry him only if he signs all his property over to her.
The man writes a document signing all his property over to the woman.
His eldest son asks what will become of him if all the property goes to the woman.
The father tells witnesses to hide and write a gift document of the property for the son.
The witnesses bring the case to Rava, who rules that neither the son nor the wife acquired the property.
The observer's mistaken inference: he thought Rava invalidated the wife's acquisition because of the concealed gift.
Correction: in the woman's case the document was clearly written under duress, unlike the son's concealed gift.
Here the matter differs: one party wants the transfer and the other does not, which leaves the question open.
A dilemma is raised before the Sages.

41a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What is the status of an unspecified gift document regarding whether it was meant to be publicized?
Ravina: we are not concerned that the gift was secret.
Rav Ashi: we are concerned that the gift was secret.
The halakha follows the view that we are concerned.
Mishna: possession without an accompanying claim does not establish the presumption of ownership.
Example: a possessor who says nobody ever told him anything about his presence cannot establish ownership.
Valid claims include a sale or gift from the owner or his father, which suffice to establish presumptive ownership.
A claim of inheritance needs no further explanation of how the ancestors acquired the land.
Why does the mishna need to say this, since no claim obviously means no presumption?
Hypothetical: the possessor did buy the land, but his bill of sale was lost.
He avoided claiming a sale because the court would demand the bill of sale he lacked.
So the court need not supply the claim; he must make it himself or lose the presumption.
The court may speak for the mute, citing Proverbs 31:8, but here it does not advance the claim.
A mnemonic for the discussion that follows: ayin, nun, bet.
Rav Anan's wall was swept away by a torrent and rebuilt on the neighbor's land; he consulted Rav Naḥman.
Rav Naḥman tells him to return the boundary to its original position.
Rav Anan objects that he already established presumptive ownership of the land.
Rav Naḥman replies that his claim follows Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yishmael, whose view is not the halakha.
Rav Anan objects that the neighbor waived his claim by helping build the wall.
Rav Naḥman: the waiver was a mistake, since Rav Anan himself did not know the wall was misplaced.
A similar case: Rav Kahana's wall was swept away and rebuilt on land that was not his.

41b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Kahana's neighbor brings two witnesses whose testimony conflicts: one says two rows encroached, another says three.
Rav Yehuda rules that Rav Kahana pays two of the three rows claimed, relying on the overlapping testimony.
Rav Kahana asks whose opinion Rav Yehuda follows, namely that of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
A baraita quotes Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that the larger sum includes the smaller.
The schools disagree only when one witness says one hundred and another two hundred, and their testimony is combined or not.
Rav Kahana objects with a letter from Eretz Yisrael rejecting Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view as halakha.
Rav Yehuda answers that he will accept the letter only once it actually arrives.
A man lived in a loft in Kashta for four years, and the prior owner found him there and challenged his possession.
Rabbi Ḥiyya rules that the possessor needs witnesses that the seller lived there, even for a single day.
Rav reports sitting before Rabbi Ḥiyya and recalling his teaching on this matter.
Rav asks whether it is common to buy and sell a house within a single night, so no witnesses saw residence.
Rabbi Ḥiyya's view: the possessor's claim is credible, since he could have simply claimed to have bought it directly.
Rava rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Ḥiyya, as the mishna teaches.
The mishna on inherited land: no claim is needed, but proof of ancestral possession is required.
The Gemara rejects the inference: perhaps the mishna requires neither proof nor claim in this case.
Alternatively the inference stands, but a buyer would not pay money for nothing, so he must have verified the seller's right.
If the seller was seen in the house, does this prove that he purchased it?
Abaye: seeing him reside there is identical to testimony that he resided there.
Rava: this is no proof, since a person may survey land and then decide not to buy it.
Rav rules that three successive buyers combine to establish the presumption of ownership over three years.
Does Rav hold that a document has public reputation while witnesses do not, and so needs a separate reason?
Rav's own ruling that a seller of a field with witnesses collects from encumbered property seems to conflict with this.

42a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Buyers who fail to check for liens on property bring their loss on themselves.
Did Rav really hold that a creditor can collect from sold property on the strength of witnesses alone?
A mishna distinguishes a creditor with a promissory note, who collects from sold property, from one with only witnesses.
Rav himself, with Shmuel, held that an oral loan cannot collect from sold property, so Rav cannot hold otherwise.
A loan is taken discreetly, so buyers are presumed unaware of it, whereas a sale is public, so the cases differ.
The sages teach that successive possession by father, son, and buyer, totaling three years, establishes presumptive ownership.
Does this imply that a purchase by a buyer generates public notice of the transaction?
A baraita contradicts this: a sale by the son is a clear protest, so the buyer does not gain presumption.
If a buyer's purchase gave public notice, the son's sale would be the strongest protest, so the baraita conflicts.
Rav Pappa: the baraita concerns a sale of fields without specification, so there is no conflict.
Mishna: craftsmen, partners, sharecroppers, and stewards cannot establish presumption, and neither can spouses over each other's property.
Exceptions: this applies to a possessor, but not to a donee, to brothers who divided property, or to one who fences a convert's land.

42b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita taught by Shmuel's father and Levi: a partner cannot establish presumptive ownership, so a craftsman certainly cannot.
Shmuel's variant: a craftsman cannot establish presumption, but a partner can.
Gemara explains Shmuel's reasoning: partners hold each other's share, testify for each other, and act as paid bailees.
Rabbi Abba objects to Rav Yehuda, citing Rav Zakkai's cave: is Shmuel really saying a partner establishes presumption?
Shmuel also says a partner is like one who enters with permission, which seems to deny presumption for partners.
Resolution: the case of entering the whole field differs from entering only half of it.

Rabba reports three of Shmuel's rules: the law of the kingdom binds, Persian sharecropping lapses after forty years, and tax-seized land sales are valid.

The Gemara infers that even Ravin would not apply the boundary rule to Shabbat.
Rava holds that boundaries do divide fields for Shabbat as well.
A baraita on carrying half a fig out in one or two lapses of awareness supports Rava's position on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yosei holds the opposite on the one-lapse case, which the baraita goes on to state.

ranges.en: Rabbi Yosei rules that carrying within one public domain makes one liable, but carrying across two domains makes one exempt.

The lands of the Kenite, Kenizzite, and Kadmonite, which are not tithable.
Baraita: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon each identify the three excluded lands differently.
Mishna: witnesses found to be conspiring against a landholder who had three years of use must pay him the full value.

Abba Ḥalafta explains that Rabbi Akiva's verse requires full testimony, and the mishna follows the Rabbis, who accept testimony by year.

Ulla's principle: an act that acquires ownerless property by its nature establishes presumptive ownership, if done over three years with a claim of purchase.

Rav Naḥman reports Rabba bar Avuh's view on the same point.

ranges.en: The mishna concerns partners in a courtyard, who tolerate placed items but not partitions, so silence there signals concession.

Rav Naḥman, citing Rabba bar Avuh: the case is a back yard of houses used for storage, where partitions still matter.
Rav Pappa: both mishnayot concern shared courtyards; monetary rulings are lenient, vow rulings stringent.
Ravina: partners are not particular, and the Nedarim mishna follows Rabbi Eliezer, who forbids even negligible benefits.

Even with no other path, one must compel himself to avoid looking at the women.
Rabbi Bena'a taught Rabbi Yoḥanan the garment, cloak, and table rules for a Torah scholar, including where the table ring sits.
Doesn't a baraita say the table ring should be on the inside, contradicting this?
Three reconciliations: a child, an attendant, or daytime versus night service explain the two baraitot's different rulings.

Rabbi Bena'a sees an inscription that a summoned judge is not a judge, and raises an objection about outsiders.

ranges.en: The judge inscription is amended: a judge ordered to return money taken from someone is disqualified, as the elders say.

Glossary of measures, then the mishna on acquiring privileges: gutter spouts, ladders, and windows, with Rabbi Yehuda's view on windows.
What does the mishna mean by a spout having no privilege for its use but having one for its place?
Three readings of the spout rule: Rav Yehuda and Shmuel on sides, Rabbi Ḥanina on length, and Rav Yirmeya bar Abba on building beneath.

ranges.en: The mishna says a gutter pipe does establish privilege for its use, because it is fixed in place, unlike a spout.
Under Rav Yirmeya bar Abba's reading, what does it matter to the gutter owner if the field owner builds beneath it?
The case is a stone gutter built into the walls, where the owner says building beneath it would weaken his walls.
Shmuel rules that the courtyard owner may prevent the roof owner from sealing a drain, since he acquired its water.
Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Ḥama disagree on that rule; Rabbi Bisa rules for Oshaya, and a verse is applied to their family of scholars.
Mishna: an Egyptian ladder, small and portable, establishes no privilege for its use.
What is an Egyptian ladder?
The school of Rabbi Yannai: any ladder lacking four fastenings.
Mishna: an Egyptian window establishes no privilege for its use.
Why does the mishna define the window but not the ladder?
The mishna defines the window in order to cite Rabbi Yehuda's dissent in the later clause.
Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Ile'a dispute whether a window above four cubits can be protested by a neighbor.
Do they dispute whether coercion applies to conduct resembling Sodom's?
Everyone accepts coercion here; Rabbi Ile'a's view applies since the window lets the owner look into the neighbor's home.
Shmuel rules that a window for light has privilege whatever its size, and cannot later be forced closed if unprotested.
Mishna: a projection overhanging a courtyard acquires privilege if it protrudes at least a handbreadth.

59b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Opening ruling: less than a handbreadth projection gives no acquired privilege and no protest right.
Rabbi Mani's principle: a handbreadth projection establishes privilege for four handbreadths.
Asks what Rabbi Mani's principle actually means.
Abaye explains it as a one-handbreadth-wide projection extended to four handbreadths in length.
Restates the mishna: sub-handbreadth projection gives no privilege and no protest right.
Rav Huna: only the roof owner is barred from protesting; the courtyard owner may protest.
Rav Yehuda: even the courtyard owner cannot protest against the roof owner.
Proposes that the amoraim disagree over whether damage by sight counts as damage.
Rejects that proposal: everyone agrees damage by sight is damage.

Mishna: one may not open windows onto a courtyard shared with partners.
Mishna: a loft or a purchased house may not open onto the shared courtyard; build inside instead.
Asks why the mishna singles out partners' courtyards if opening onto another's courtyard is also forbidden.
Explains the mishna's wording as 'it is not necessary': the partner's window argument is raised as a point.
Baraita case: Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei rules the windows stay, through acquired privilege.
Rabbi Hiyya rules the windows must be sealed, since partners may prevent their use.
Rav Naḥman begins a further teaching that follows in the text.

60a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Sealing a window in one's presence without protest establishes an acquired privilege to keep it sealed.
Quotes the mishna: one who buys a house in another courtyard may not open it onto the partners' courtyard.

The reason: opening there would increase the burden of the shared path.
Asks whether the mishna's latter clause should be read instead to fit this reason.
Objects: a loft built on the house also increases the path, so the stated reason does not fit.
Rav Huna replies: the mishna means a room split between two owners, or a loft built suddenly.
Mishna: no opening may face an opening or window facing a window; a small one may not be enlarged.
Mishna: one may open onto the public domain, and a small facing opening may be enlarged or split.
Asks from where these rules about openings are derived.
Rabbi Yoḥanan derives the rule from Balaam seeing Israel's tents not facing each other, as a sign of worthiness.
Concludes the derived rule: a small opening may not be enlarged.
Rami bar Ḥama's view: a four-cubit opening may not be made into eight, but two can be made into four.
Rava objects: one can conceal from a small opening but not from a large one, so the view fails.
Restates the mishna's ruling that one opening may not be made into two.
Rami bar Ḥama's second version: a four-opening arrangement may not be made into eight, as the numbers are fitted.
Rava objects that one can conceal from a single opening but not from two.
Restates the mishna: one may open onto the public domain, facing an opening.
Rava's continued point: opening toward the public domain also requires concealment from passersby.
Mishna: one may not dig pits, cisterns or caves under the public domain; Rabbi Eliezer permits a wagon's passage.
Mishna: one may not project balconies or beams into the public domain; a buyer of a courtyard with them keeps them.
Explains the Sages' view: a projection may be reduced sometimes unintentionally, so no privilege is granted.
Restates the mishna's ruling that projections and balconies may not be extended into the public domain.
Narrative: Rabbi Ami and another man each have a projection that obstructs passage into the public domain.
The man comes before Rabbi Ami, who tells him to remove the projection.
The man objects that Rabbi Ami's own drains and projections also extend, so who is exempt?
Case of Rabbi Yannai: he has a tree leaning over the public domain.
Another man with a leaning tree is obstructed by passersby and comes before Rabbi Yannai, who answers.

ranges.en: Narrative setup: Yannai orders his tree cut at night, and the man returns to him the next day.

Yannai replies: go and see; if mine is cut, cut yours, and if not, you need not cut yours.

Reish Lakish's homily from Zephaniah: correct yourself before correcting others.
Mishnah: one may draw back into his own property and then extend the projection.

Reish Lakish holds that one who drew back may not extend the projection later.

The reversed version: Rabbi Yochanan says the walls may not be returned to their place.
Reish Lakish says the walls may be returned to their place.
Rabbi Yochanan's own position: the walls may not be restored.
He cites Rav Yehuda: once the public uses a path, it is forbidden to ruin it.

His limit: Rav Yehuda's rule applies only without room for passage; here there is room.
Mishnah: a purchased courtyard with projections and balconies keeps its presumptive status.
Rav Huna: if the courtyard wall fell, the owner may rebuild it as it was.
A baraita bars rebuilding a fallen courtyard that was plastered, tiled or painted in prohibited ways.
Reply: a prohibited matter is different, whereas here the issue is encroachment, so the privilege stands.
Baraita: plastering a house with lime is forbidden, but mixing in sand or straw makes it permitted.
Rabbi Yehuda: adding sand makes it prohibited white cement, but straw is permitted.
Baraita: after the Temple's destruction, ascetics abstained from eating meat and drinking wine.
Rabbi Yehoshua asks the ascetics why they avoid meat and wine.
They reply that meat and wine were used on the altar, which no longer stands.
Yehoshua argues that then they should abstain from bread too, since meal-offerings have ceased.
They reply that bread can be replaced by produce.
Yehoshua argues that then produce should be abstained from too, since first-fruit offerings have ceased.
They reply that other produce can substitute.
Yehoshua argues that water too must be abstained from, since the water libation ceased; they fall silent.
Yehoshua: full abstention is impossible now that the decree stands, and excess mourning is impossible since decrees need majority ability.
He cites Malachi 3:9 to show that rebuke for neglect applies only when the whole nation accepted the observance.
Sages' ruling: one may plaster his house but must leave a small part unplastered.

Rav Yosef: one cubit by one cubit.
Rav Hisda: the unplastered part should be opposite the entrance, where it is visible.
Sages: one may prepare all meal needs but must leave out a small item as a reminder.
The Gemara asks what that small item is.
Rav Pappa: a small fried fish.
Sages: a woman may do all her cosmetic preparations but must leave out a small matter.
The Gemara asks what that small matter is.
Rav: she leaves unremoved the hair on the temple area where women usually depilate.
Psalm 137 is cited as the scriptural source for these mourning practices.
The Gemara asks what 'above my highest joy' (rosh) means.
Rav Yitzhak: it refers to the burnt ashes placed on grooms' heads at weddings.
Rav Pappa asks Abaye where the ashes are placed.
Abaye: on the place where phylacteries are placed.
He cites Isaiah 61:3 about a garland in place of ashes, inferring the ashes go where phylacteries sit.
Baraita: whoever mourns Jerusalem merits seeing its joy.
He cites Isaiah 66:10 to support that those who mourn Jerusalem will rejoice.
Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha: we should abstain from meat and wine after the Temple's fall, but public decrees need majority ability.
From Rome's harsh decrees onward, which block Torah, mitzvot and circumcision; the text notes a variant wording.

Chapter-closing formula naming the chapter.

ranges.en: Mishnah: selling a house does not include the gallery, the room behind it, or a roof with a ten-handbreadth parapet.
Rabbi Yehuda: a roof whose parapet has a doorway shape is excluded even if the parapet is short.
The Gemara asks what a gallery (yatzia) is.
Babylonian translation: an attic; Rav Yosef says a windowed structure, and the two readings yield different sale outcomes.
Rav Yosef's teaching: a small attached structure has three biblical names: gallery, side chamber and cell.
Verses from Kings and Ezekiel, plus a Middot mishna, illustrate those three names and their measurements.
Mar Zutra: a gallery is excluded from a sale only if it measures at least four by four cubits.
Ravina objects: by that logic a pit or cistern would never be excluded, since it is narrower than four cubits.
Ravina cites the mishna that a pit and cistern are excluded even when depth and height are written in the deed.
Ravina presses that the pit rule would then exclude only pits of four by four cubits, which is not the case.
Mar Zutra replies: the pit and the house have separate uses, but gallery and house share one use, so size matters.
Mishnah: selling a house also excludes the room behind it, even if reachable only from inside.
The Gemara asks: since the gallery is excluded, is it necessary to teach that the room is excluded too?

61b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Reply: the rule is needed, following Rav Nachman's view, and the room is excluded even when outer boundaries are drawn.
Rav Nachman reports Rabba bar Avuh: selling a residence within a large building, drawn by outer bounds, does not transfer the whole building.
The Gemara asks in which circumstances this holds, and why the whole building should not pass when outer bounds are drawn.
Answer: the case is a place where some call a building a residence; without a clause reserving nothing, the seller kept something back.
Rav Nachman reports the parallel ruling for fields: selling one field in a large expanse does not transfer the whole expanse.
The Gemara again asks the circumstances, and why the whole expanse should not pass given the drawn outer boundaries.
Answer: some locals call an expanse a field; without the reservation clause, the seller is presumed to have kept something back.
Both cases must be stated: a residence has its own use, while an expanse has one shared use, so each needs its own ruling.
The Gemara asks whose view supports the rule that the seller must write a clause reserving nothing.
Rav Mari, citing Abaye: a seller must write that he reserves nothing, to prevent later disputes.
It accords with Rav Nachman's view, which holds that drawn boundaries alone do not show intent to sell everything.
A man sold land of the house of Hiyya, though two plots bore that name; the Sages debated whether both passed.
Rav Ashi: the singular term sold only one plot, since he did not say two.
Selling fields in the plural without a number means at least two of the seller's fields.
Selling all his fields excludes orchards and vineyards.
Selling his landed property includes orchards and vineyards, but excludes houses and Canaanite slaves.

ranges.en: If the seller says his property, the sale includes even his houses and Canaanite slaves.
Setup: the seller marks one boundary of the field as long and the opposite boundary as short.

Rav Kahana and Rav Asi object: the buyer should also get the triangle cut off by the diagonal.
Rav stays silent and concedes the objection.
Where neighbors are named on only one side, the omission implies the triangle is included, since he would have written more.
If the field is bounded east-west and north-south, the bill must name the neighbors on both sides of each pair.
Two dilemmas: whether marking only the corners sells the corners or the whole field, and whether a gamma or L-shaped marking sells the whole field.

ranges.en: Dilemma on boundaries given in alternation; the question is left unresolved.
Case: the seller marks the first three boundaries of the field and omits the fourth.
Rav: the buyer gets everything except the furrow along the unmarked fourth boundary.
Shmuel: the buyer gets even the furrow along the unmarked fourth boundary.
Rav Asi: the buyer gets only one furrow running along the full perimeter of the three marked boundaries.
Explains Rav Asi: since Rav holds the seller kept a furrow at the fourth boundary, he kept some of the whole field too.
Rava, following Rav: the furrow passes only if the fourth boundary juts out beyond the adjacent boundaries, not if it lies within them.
Rava's further limit: trees or room for nine kav withhold a jutting furrow; otherwise it passes, and the reverse follows by inference.
Another version: Rava follows Shmuel, so the furrow passes only when the fourth boundary lies within the adjacent boundaries.
The second version continues: trees or nine-kav space withhold the furrow, and the reverse follows by inference.
Conclusion: both versions agree on the cases, but where the ruling is unclear, judges decide by the seller's apparent intent.
Rabba: selling half of one's share in a jointly held field means half the field; selling half of my land means a quarter.
Abaye objects: why rule differently for the two wordings?
Abaye clarifies: he had assumed Rabba's silence meant retraction, but that is not so.
Abaye cites bills of sale issued from Rabba's house using these two wordings, showing the distinction in practice.
Rabba: a fourth boundary marked as the land that halves the field sells half; one marked as land set apart sells only nine kav.
Abaye repeats the objection about the two wordings, and Rabba again says nothing.
The Sages read Rabba's silence as conceding that half is acquired in both cases.

ranges.en: Rejects the Sages' conclusion, citing Abaye's ruling via Rav Yeimar: half if the bounds are declared, otherwise nine kav.

If he says give so-and-so a portion of my property, what portion must be given?
Ravina cites a baraita on giving a portion of a cistern: Sumakhos's minimum for an unqualified portion is one quarter.
Baraita: a Levite selling a field reserves its first tithe; the reservation passes to his sons, but lapses after resale and repurchase.
Why would the seller have a claim on tithe from produce that does not yet exist? No one can transfer what has not come into being.

Reish Lakish: selling a house while reserving the upper story keeps the upper story with the seller.

ranges.en: Asks which halakha Reish Lakish's statement is teaching.
Rav Zevid: the upper story is the seller's, so he may extend projections over the courtyard.

Asks how Rav Pappa's reading fits Reish Lakish's wording, since it is not derived from the baraita.
Rav Dimi: a house sale must also say from the earth's depth to the sky's height to convey pits and tunnels.

ranges.en: If depth and height pass by default, why would a roof with a ten-handbreadth parapet not pass as well?
