Ravina cites Reish Lakish's upper-story case as proof for the Gemara's line of questioning.
Recalls two readings of Reish Lakish: Rav Zevid on extending projections, Rav Pappa on rebuilding a collapsed upper story.
If depth and height are not sold by default, why must the upper-story condition be stated?
The stipulation lets the seller rebuild the upper story if it collapses, which he could not otherwise do.
Mishnah: selling a house excludes the pit and cistern, even if depth and height are written.
Rabbi Akiva: the seller must secure a path through the buyer's property to reach the excluded pit.
The Rabbis: the seller need not secure such a path, since it is part of what he kept back.
Rabbi Akiva concedes that if the seller explicitly excludes them, no path is needed.
If the seller kept the house and sold the pit, Rabbi Akiva says no path is needed; the Rabbis require one.
Ravina asks why both pit and cistern are mentioned if they are the same thing.
Rava Tosfa'a cites a baraita: a pit is only dug, while a cistern is also finished with masonry, answering the question.
Rav Ashi raises the same difficulty about pit and cistern.
Mar Kashisha cites the same baraita to answer Rav Ashi.

ranges.en: Explains the dispute: Rabbi Akiva holds a seller sells generously, the Rabbis sparingly, and Rabbi Akiva applies this consistently.

Cites the field mishna on an excluded cistern and winepress, showing the same dispute on sales of fields.

Rav Huna: it follows Rav Nachman, who sits near the Exilarch's gate where judges gather and knows monetary law.

Rav Hamnuna is answered that shrubs are not significant like trees, so the ground does not pass with them.
Mishna on sales of animal parts: a large animal's head, forelegs, windpipe, lungs and liver are separate, but small animals differ.
Mishna on the four cases of sellers and buyers with wheat: who may renege depends on whether the quality was as represented.
Mishna: a sale of a different item than delivered, such as wheat colour, wood type or wine for vinegar, can be cancelled by either party.
Rav Ḥisda's case: a buyer paid six dinars for an item worth five, and the buyer alone may cancel the sale when the price rises.

84a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A buyer who was exploited may renege, while the seller cannot; the mishna's tanna teaches the same for wheat represented as good but found bad.
Rav Ḥisda's case: when the price falls, the seller was exploited and alone may renege, as the buyer had already exploited him.
Asks what Rav Ḥisda teaches, since the mishna already seems to cover it.
Without the mishna one might think both parties may renege in exploitation cases, so the mishna is needed to show the buyer may renege.
The teaching is needed because one might think sellers' praise and buyers' disparagement means no exploitation, citing Proverbs 20:14.
Mishna: if wheat said to be reddish-brown is found white, either party may renege.
Rav Pappa infers from the mishna's contrast with white that the sun is red, reddening at morning and evening.
Objects that Leviticus compares leprosy to the sun while leprosy is white, so the sun cannot be red; the reply is that the likeness is partial.
Asks: if the sun is white, why does it redden in the morning and evening?
The sun reddens passing the roses of Eden in the morning and the entrance to Gehenna in the evening, though some reverse this.
Mishna: if wine is sold and found to be vinegar, or vice versa, both parties may renege.
Asks whether the mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rather than the Rabbis, as a baraita is then cited.

84b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Wine and vinegar are one type of food according to the Rabbis, while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds they are two types.
Replies that the Rabbis disagree only about tithes and teruma for redeeming wine with vinegar, following Rabbi Ela.
Rabbi Ela derives from a verse about bearing no sin for setting aside the best that setting aside poor produce for better is valid teruma.
In buying and selling, all agree wine and vinegar are different, since people prefer one or the other.
Mishna on acquiring movables: pulling without measuring, measuring without pulling, renting the place, and flax lifted from its place.
Rabbi Asi cites Rabbi Yoḥanan: measuring and placing produce in an alleyway acquires it for the buyer even without pulling.
Rabbi Zeira suggests Rabbi Yoḥanan meant only measuring into the buyer's own basket, not produce left on the alleyway floor.
Rabbi Asi replies that basket placement obviously acquires, so Rabbi Yoḥanan's alleyway statement must mean produce placed on the floor.
Asks whether Rabbi Zeira accepted Rabbi Asi's explanation or rejected it.
Cites Rabbi Yannai's report of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi on partners' courtyards, which supports Rabbi Asi's reading as a parallel.
Resolves the apparent contradiction in Rabbi Yoḥanan's two statements: basket placement acquires, ground placement in an alleyway does not.
Brings the mishna that measuring without pulling does not acquire, read as an alleyway case supporting Rabbi Zeira.
Objects that if the mishna refers to the public domain, pulling there should not acquire, yet the first clause says it does.
Abaye and Rava hold that passing acquires in the public domain, pulling does not, so the mishna cannot allow acquisition by pulling there.
Explains that the mishna's pulling means pulling from the public domain into an alleyway.
Asks how the latter clause about renting the place can apply if the produce lies in the public domain.
The latter clause is a separate ruling: if the produce is on property with an owner, the buyer rents the place from that owner.
Rav and Shmuel both hold that acquisition takes place in a further manner, as the Gemara goes on to discuss.

85a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish hold that a person's vessels acquire items placed in them for him, even in the public domain.
Rav Pappa reconciles this with Rav and Shmuel: vessels in the public domain do not acquire, while the alleyway is called public only because it is not private.
Rabbi Abbahu cites Rabbi Yoḥanan that vessels acquire wherever one may keep them, which supports reading his public domain as an alleyway.
Raises a difficulty from a baraita on four methods of acquisition, where the buyer acquires as items fill a vessel belonging to one party.
Explains the baraita: the rule applies to a neutral vessel in the public domain or a jointly held courtyard, and the seller's or bailee's domain differs.
Concludes that the baraita's rule on vessels belonging to one party holds in the public domain or a jointly owned courtyard.

85b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that the baraita must mean the actual public domain, since it compares the case to a courtyard owned by neither party.
Explains that a courtyard belonging to neither party refers to jointly owned property, which makes the case like an alleyway.
Rav Sheshet asks Rav Huna whether a buyer's vessels acquire merchandise for him when they sit in the seller's domain.
Rav Huna answers from a mishna: a divorce thrown into a woman's lap or basket is valid even in her husband's domain.
Rav Nachman objects that the Sages have qualified that mishna so heavily it cannot serve as a straightforward proof.
Several amoraim explain the mishna's conditions, such as a hanging basket, a tied basket, or a basket seller, to uphold its use.
Rabbi Yochanan asserts that the spot of a woman's lap and the spot of her basket are acquired to her within the husband's property.
Rava asks what the reasoning behind Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is.
Explains that people are not particular about the small spots of a lap or basket, so they are granted without a sale.
Rather, the Gemara resolves the dilemma from a baraita: a buyer does not acquire goods in the seller's domain until he lifts or removes them.
Objects that the baraita may refer to goods in the buyer's vessels, so the latter clause would have to refer to the seller's vessels too.
Proposes that the latter clause refers to goods in the buyer's domain, where the buyer acquires once the seller accepted the sale.
Objects that if the latter clause refers to the seller's vessels, it is unclear why the buyer would acquire the goods.
Responds that the latter clause actually addresses a different case, the buyer's own vessels.
Asks why the baraita is stated without qualification if its clauses describe different situations.
Explains the baraita is unqualified because a seller's vessels are commonly found at his house and a buyer's at his.
Rava brings a baraita: if one pulled his drivers, laborers or donkeys with goods, both parties may renege before unloading.

86a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Quotes the baraita on unloading goods and infers that a buyer's vessels in the seller's domain do not acquire for him.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rejects the proof: the baraita speaks of goods emptied onto the ground, not left in vessels.
Rava rebuts that the baraita says unloaded, not emptied, so the goods stay in the seller's vessels as the proof requires.
Mar bar Rav Ashi offers another rejection: the baraita concerns bundles of garlic tied together, not full vessels.
Huna son of Mar Zutra argues that since unloading acquires, whether a price was fixed makes no difference.
Ravina replies that fixing a price shows intent to sell, so the transaction takes effect only in that case.
Ravina brings the ruling of Rav and Shmuel that a person's vessel acquires any item placed in it, in any place.
Asks what the phrase in any place adds, if it does not include the seller's domain.
Rav Ashi says that case is specific, where the seller told the buyer to go and acquire the goods.
Cites a Mishnah in Kiddushin: guaranteed property is acquired by money, document, or possession; unguaranteed property only by pulling.
Records variant traditions limiting pulling to items not usually lifted; items usually lifted are acquired only by lifting.
Abaye sits and states this halakha, that items usually lifted are not acquired by pulling.
Rav Adda bar Mattana raises an objection to Abaye from a baraita.
Baraita on stealing a purse on Shabbat: liable for theft when lifted first, exempt when dragged, since both violations coincide.
Rav Adda argues a purse is liftable, yet the baraita shows it is acquired by pulling, contradicting Abaye.
Abaye replies that the baraita concerns a thief who pulled the purse with a rope.
Rav Adda insists the objection stands even when the purse was pulled with a rope.
Abaye clarifies the purse must have been so large it needed a rope, so it is acquired by pulling.
Brings a baraita: goods in the seller's domain are not acquired until lifted or removed from his domain.
Objects that the baraita suggests liftable goods may be acquired either way, by lifting or by pulling.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that the baraita is disjunctive: liftable items by lifting, pullable items by pulling.

86b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites a mishnah: a buyer who pulls produce from a seller without measuring has acquired it by pulling.
Objects that produce is liftable, yet the mishnah teaches it is acquired by pulling.
Explains the mishnah deals with large bundles that are pulled from place to place rather than carried.
Argues that if so, the latter clause of the mishnah should be read the same way.
The latter clause says one who buys flax has not acquired it until he carries it from one place to another.
Asks whether flax is not also packed in large bundles that can be pulled.
Answers that flax differs: large bundles would slip apart, so it is packed in small bundles.
Ravina brings a mishnah: large animals are acquired by leash, small ones by lifting; the Rabbis hold small animals by pulling.
Ravina explains that small animals are liftable, yet the mishnah teaches they are acquired by pulling.
Rav Ashi replies that animals differ, since they cling to the ground and are hard to lift.
Rav and Shmuel rule that a whole kor sold at once can be reneged on until measured, but se'ah priced individually is acquired one by one.
Cites a baraita: if the measure belonged to one party, the buyer acquires each item as measured, even before the measure is full.
Explains the baraita concerns a hin priced per log, and the measure's markings show each log was filled, as Rav Kahana taught.
Introduces a baraita on one who hires a laborer for a dinar a day to work at the threshing floor.

87a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continues the baraita on hiring a laborer: a harvest-day hire is prohibited, but a hire starting now at the set daily wage is permitted.
If Rav and Shmuel's kor ruling holds, the permitted case should be prohibited as interest, so the baraita seems to conflict with it.
Asks why the permitted case is not forbidden, since the employer's advance payment looks like payment for the laborer's waiting.
Rava rejects the premise: lowering a wage to secure employment is not interest, so it violates no prohibition.
Asks what distinguishes the prohibited first clause from the permitted latter clause if neither is interest.
Explains that when the laborer does not start working now, the arrangement looks like advance payment, but not when he works from now.
Quotes the mishnah: if flax was attached to the ground and the buyer detached any amount, he has acquired it.
Asks how the buyer can acquire all the flax merely by detaching some of it.
Rav Sheshet explains the seller told him to clear any amount of land, so detaching flax counts as renting the land and acquiring all of it.
Mishnah on selling wine or oil: the sale is final once the measure fills, a middleman's broken barrel is his loss, and three drops are owed.
Asks whose measure is meant: if the buyer's, why is the goods still the seller's; if the seller's, why does it pass when filled?
Rabbi Ela says the mishnah refers to a measure belonging to a middleman, lent first to the seller and then to the buyer.
Objects that the latter clause's middleman case implies the first clause is not about a middleman at all.
The first clause is a measure without a middleman present; the latter clause concerns a middleman who is present at the sale.
Restates the mishnah: liquid left when a barrel is tipped and drained belongs to the seller.
Rabbi Elazar comes up to Eretz Yisrael and asks who the tanna is that Rav taught on measures; he is directed to Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi.
Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi asks what difficulty the halakha poses for Rabbi Elazar.
Rabbi Elazar states the difficulty: the mishnah says the drained liquid belongs to the seller, which conflicts with the ruling.

87b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that a mishnah in Terumot treats drained remnants differently, so the seller's entitlement here looks inconsistent.
Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi replies that the seller's claim rests on the owner's despair over tiny amounts, which does not apply to teruma.
Quotes the mishnah: a storekeeper is not obligated to drip three drops.
Raises a dilemma: does Rabbi Yehuda's Shabbat-eve ruling refer to the first clause, which is lenient, or the latter clause, which is stringent?
Resolves the dilemma with a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda exempts a storekeeper on Shabbat eve because he is busy, so he refers to the latter clause.
Mishnah: a storekeeper sent a child with a coin and a jug is liable if the jug breaks, but Rabbi Yehuda exempts him on the father's intent.
Explains the disagreement: the Rabbis think the father sent the child only to inform the storekeeper, while Rabbi Yehuda thinks he sent him to return the goods.
Asks why the Rabbis hold the storekeeper liable if the child broke the jug, since the father deliberately entrusted it to him.
Rav Hoshaya says the case is a storekeeper who examines a jug on terms like Shmuel's ruling, which makes him liable like a borrower.
Asks whether Shmuel's view is itself a tannaitic dispute, since Rabbi Yehuda's ruling seems to contradict it.
Rabba and Rav Yosef explain the case as a storekeeper selling jugs, where each side follows its own view of the father's intent.
Objects that the last clause's concession would contradict this explanation, since the father sent the child only to inform the storekeeper.
Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin offer another explanation of which case the disagreement addresses.

88a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the mishnah's case: the storekeeper took the jug to measure, so he is liable for accidents, as Rabba holds for lost animals taken in hand.
Objects that Rabba spoke of animals driven farther from their owner, and that taking the jug here does not make breakage more likely.
Rava says Rabbi Zeira explained the case: the storekeeper took the jug without the father's knowledge, and the Sages disagree whether such a borrower is a robber.
Restates Shmuel's ruling: one who takes a craftsman's vessel to examine and it breaks owes restitution, but only when its value is fixed.
Two stories illustrate the rule: a buyer who lifted meat and buyers who lifted pumpkins, both cases where lifting finalized a fixed-price purchase.
Rav Kahana rules that the consecration is void, since a person cannot consecrate what is not his, and lifting finalized the sale.
A baraita: a buyer who selects vegetables from an unreliable seller acquires them and owes tithes only if he decided to buy, then tithes and pays the seller.
Asks whether merely deciding to buy effects acquisition and tithe liability, even without any act or words.
Rav Hoshaya explains this concerns a God-fearing buyer like Rav Safra, who is bound by his thoughts during negotiations.
Mishnah and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: measures must be cleaned at set intervals; storekeepers clean more often, and dry goods need no cleaning.

88b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah on weighing: the seller lets the scale tilt a handbreadth or adds extra amounts, and local custom governs measuring vessels.
Asks the source of the requirement that the seller let the scale tilt an extra handbreadth.
Reish Lakish derives it from the verse 'a perfect and just weight', read as telling the seller to be righteous with his own goods.
Objects: if so, the latter clause's exact-weight case conflicts with a Torah obligation to let the scale tilt.
Rather, the first clause concerns local custom, and Reish Lakish's principle was stated about the latter clause.
Restates the latter clause: if the seller weighed exactly, he must give the buyer added amounts.
Reish Lakish cites the verse 'and just' as the source of the obligation to add the extra amounts.
Asks how much the added amounts should be.
Reports Rav's ruling on the amounts: one-tenth extra for liquids, measured per ten litra, and a corresponding amount for dry goods.
Raises a dilemma about whether the mishnah's fractions apply per unit or per whole measure; the dilemma is left unresolved.
Rabbi Levi says the punishment for false measures is more severe than the punishment for forbidden sexual relations.
Supports this from verses: 'elleh' is used for false measures, 'el' for forbidden relations, and 'eilei' in Ezekiel shows the short form signals severity.
Asks why false measures are considered harsher, since forbidden relations are also described with 'elleh'.
Replies that 'elleh' in the forbidden relations verse excludes users of false measures from excision in the World-to-Come.
Asks what the greater severity of false measures is, if their penalty is in fact lighter.
Relations offenders can repent, but false-measure users cannot, since they cannot know whom they cheated to repay.
Rabbi Levi says robbing an ordinary person is more severe than robbing the Most High, meaning consecrated property.
Supports this from verses: ordinary robbery places sin before me'ila, while misuse of consecrated items places me'ila before sin.
Rabbi Levi says God's conduct differs from human conduct: God blessed Israel with twenty-two and cursed them with eight.
Lists the verse-opening letters: blessings run alef to tav and curses vav to mem, while Moses reversed the pattern.

89a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continues the verses on blessings and curses: the curses run from vav to heh, together covering all twenty-two letters.
Quotes the mishnah on local measuring custom and gives a mnemonic listing its rulings, from balancing and heaping to weights.
Baraitot derive from 'a perfect weight' and 'a perfect and just weight' that measures and scales must follow local custom.
Rav Yehuda of Sura reads the verses on diverse weights and measures homiletically, linking them to becoming a pauper.
Baraita: the court appoints inspectors for measures but not prices; Shmuel sends Karna to teach this, and Karna, teaching otherwise, is cursed with a growth.
Asks whose opinion Karna followed when he disregarded his teacher's statement.
Rami bar Chama reports Rabbi Yitzchak: inspectors are appointed for both measures and prices because of swindlers.
Baraita: a buyer who asks for a litra, half a litra, or a quarter is weighed with the matching weight.
Asks what the baraita teaches, since that seems obvious.
It teaches that weights are set up down to a quarter-litra, and a smaller requested amount is not granted.
Baraita: a buyer may not demand three-quarters of a litra be weighed in quarter units; it must be weighed all at once.
Baraita: for ten litra, the buyer may not demand each litra be weighed separately with a tilt; it is weighed all at once.
Baraita on scale dimensions: fulcrum heights and pan and lever lengths for scales of different trades, and for gold scales.
Asks what purpose the large balance scale, mentioned first in the baraita, serves.

89b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Pappa identifies a scale for blacksmiths; Rabbi Mani bar Pattish says its ritual impurity follows the same criteria as the prohibitions on scales.
Asks what Rabbi Mani's statement teaches, since a mishnah in Kelim already covers the rope length.
Answers that the mishnah covers only the suspension rope, so Rabbi Mani needed to add the lever and cord.
Baraita: weights may not be made of tin, lead, alloy, or other metals, which deteriorate, but may be made of hard rock or glass.
Baraita: a leveler may not be made of gourd or metal, but may be made of olive, nut, sycamore, or boxwood.
Baraita: a leveler must not be thick on one side, and may neither level all at once nor little by little, since each favors one party.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai laments: teaching these rules may instruct swindlers, but not teaching them lets swindlers mock scholars' ignorance.
Raises a dilemma whether Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai actually said these halakhot in public.
Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak says he did, citing Hosea: the ways of the Lord are right, and transgressors stumble in them.
Baraita on Leviticus 19:35 defines the terms: land measured fairly across seasons, weights not salted, and liquids not poured so as to foam.
An a fortiori argument: if the Torah is strict about the smallest mesura, it is strict about larger measures, down to the ukla.
Rav says it is forbidden to keep a wrong-sized measure at home, even one used as a chamber pot.
Rav Pappa limits this to places without government stamps, where buyers would not accept unstamped measures and inspections exist.
Rejects the limitation: a wrong measure kept at home may still be used at twilight, when buyers may take goods without checking.
Cites a baraita: one may not keep a wrong measure at home, but may prepare standard measures such as the se'ah, tarkav, and kav.

90a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Lists the permitted liquid measures, from the ukla and its fractions of the hin down to the kortov, the smallest unit.
Asks why one may not also prepare a two-kav measure.
Answers that a two-kav measure could be confused with the tarkav, and reasons from that error margin about which measures are barred.
Argues by the same logic that the half-tomen and ukla should be barred, since they differ by only a fifth.
Rav Pappa replies that people are skilled at telling small measures apart.
Argues that since people err by a quarter, the three-log measure should also be barred.
Explains that the Sages did not forbid measures already used in the Temple.
Asks whether the Sages should then have decreed against those measures in the Temple too.
The priests serving in the Temple are vigilant and would not make that mistake.
Shmuel rules that a community may raise measures or coin value by at most one-sixth, and a merchant may not profit more than that.
Asks the reason for Shmuel's rule: if it is due to higher prices, a one-sixth rise should also be barred.
Explains the rule is due to exploitation: a change of up to one-sixth keeps the transaction from being nullified.
Objects citing Rava: for items sold by measure, weight, or number, any deviation nullifies the sale, not just beyond one-sixth.
Rather, the rule protects merchants from loss if they sell by the old standard unaware of the new one.
Objects that merchants need profit, so the decree should ensure they earn it, which makes this explanation difficult.
Rav Hisda says the rule has no logical basis: Shmuel derived it homiletically from a verse.
Cites Ezekiel 45:12 on the shekel, gera, and maneh, whose numbers add up to sixty shekels, equal to a maneh.

90b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that a maneh cannot equal sixty shekels, since that would be 240 dinars rather than the standard amount.
Learns three points from the verse: the sacred maneh was doubled, communities may raise measures by at most one-sixth, and it is computed on the final sum.
Objects that Rav Pappa bar Shmuel's new three-kefiza measure adds a third, exceeding Shmuel's one-sixth limit.
Rav Pappa replies that he introduced a new measure, which Paphunya accepted and named after him, though Pumbedita did not.
Gives a mnemonic for the rulings that follow on hoarding, exporting, profiting, and sounding alarms.
Baraita: hoarders, usurers, and manipulators of measures and prices are condemned, citing Amos 8:4-7.
Asks who the hoarders named in the baraita actually were.
Rabbi Yochanan names Shabtai, who bought and hoarded large amounts of produce to sell later at a high price.
Shmuel's father sold early at the early price while Shmuel held produce to sell late; a message from Eretz Yisrael prefers the father's practice.
The reason: a price that starts low stays low through the year, so early sales help people all year long.
Rav says a person may hoard produce from his own field, turning his kav into a storeroom.
Baraita: hoarding applies to staples bought from the market, while spices and produce from one's own field are permitted.
Baraita: hoarding in Eretz Yisrael is permitted for three years, but in drought even a kav of carobs may not be hoarded.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina tells his servant to hoard for the three years, an example of the permitted practice.
Baraita: staples may not be exported from Eretz Yisrael; Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira allows wine, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi allows exports.

91a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Clarifies the boundary: from the northernmost province of Eretz Yisrael to the southernmost province of Syria.
Baraita: one may not profit in Eretz Yisrael by reselling staples such as wine, oil, and flour, since that raises their price; growers should sell directly.
Explains that Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya profited on wine following Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, and on oil where oil was locally common.
Baraita: one may not profit twice from the sale of eggs.
Mari bar Mari reports that Rav and Shmuel disagree whether this means doubling the price or forbidding merchants from selling to other merchants.
Baraita: a community sounds the alarm and holds public prayer when goods drop in price, even on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yochanan limits this to staples of the local economy; Rav Yosef says only when prices fell sharply, from ten to six.
Baraita: one may leave Eretz Yisrael only when two se'ah of grain cost a sela; Rabbi Shimon limits leaving to those who cannot buy food.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai names Elimelech, Mahlon and Chilion, leaders of their generation, who were punished for leaving Eretz Yisrael.
Asks why they were punished.
They were punished because they left Eretz Yisrael for the outside.
Cites Ruth 1:19: the whole city was astir over them, and the women asked whether this was Naomi.
Rabbi Yitzchak explains the women were saying: see what befell Naomi, who left Eretz Yisrael and lost her status.
Rabbi Yitzchak says Ruth's arrival in Eretz Yisrael coincided with Boaz's wife's death, opening the way for their marriage.
Rabba bar Rav Huna reports Rav's view that the judge Ibzan of Bethlehem is Boaz.
Asks what this identification teaches us.
Explains the identification fits Rav's statement that Boaz made 120 feasts for his children's weddings.
Cites Judges 12:9: Ibzan had thirty sons and thirty daughters sent abroad and thirty brought in, indicating sixty children.
Boaz made two feasts for each wedding and omitted Manoah, deeming him a sterile mule unable to repay.
A Sage taught that all of Ibzan's children died in his lifetime, explaining the adage that one diligent child outweighs sixty.
Gives a mnemonic: Abraham's ten years, when he died, and the phrase 'he alone was exalted'.
Rav Hanan bar Rava says Rav lists Elimelech, Salmon, and other relatives as descendants of Nahshon.
Asks what this statement teaches us.
Even the merit of ancestors does not protect one who leaves Eretz Yisrael, as Elimelech's death shows.
Rav states Abraham's mother was Amatlai bat Karnevo and Haman's mother Amatlai bat Orevati, and gives a mnemonic to tell them apart.
Gives the names of David's mother, Samson's mother, and Samson's sister.
Asks what practical difference the names make.
The names matter for answering heretics, who may be answered by a tradition that transmitted them.
Rav says Abraham was imprisoned ten years, split between Khuta and Karddu; Rav Dimi reverses the split, and Rav Hisda identifies Khuta with Ur.
Rav says that on the day Abraham died, the leaders of the nations lined up in mourning and lamented the loss of the world.

91b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Completes the proverb: a ship that has lost its captain is doomed.
Cites Chronicles 29:11 for God's exaltation as head above all, applied to those who rise to leadership.
Rav says even the smallest position of authority, such as an irrigation overseer, is appointed by Heaven.
Rav Hiyya bar Avin reports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's view that Elimelech did not leave the land even for bran, so they were not punished for material gain.
Asks for what reason they were then punished.
They were punished because they should have prayed for their generation and did not.
Cites Isaiah 57:13: when you cry out, let your gathered ones deliver you.
Rabba bar bar Chana reports Rabbi Yochanan: leaving the land is forbidden only when money is cheap, while leaving is allowed when money is scarce even if four se'ah cost a sela.
Gives a mnemonic for Rabbi Yochanan's memories: sela, laborer, carob, boy, and they would say.
Rabbi Yochanan recalls four se'ah to a sela, yet people in Tiberias swelled from hunger, lacking even one issar.
Rabbi Yochanan recalls laborers refusing to work on the east side, since bread smells from the west side would overwhelm them.
Rabbi Yochanan recalls a child breaking a carob with honey running over his two arms.
Rabbi Elazar recalls a raven carrying meat, with fat dripping from the wall all the way to the ground.
Rabbi Yochanan recalls boys and girls of sixteen and seventeen walking together in the market without sinning.
Rabbi Yochanan recalls study-hall teaching that one who relies on gentiles sees his property become theirs.
Notes the names Mahlon and Chilion from Ruth 1:2.
Cites Chronicles 4:22 with the names Joash and Saraph as a second source for the same men.
Rav and Shmuel offer opposing explanations of why these men were called Mahlon, Chilion, Joash, and Saraph.
Baraita reads Chronicles 4:22 as referring to Joshua, the Gibeonites, Mahlon and Chilion, and Ruth, and notes David descends from Moab.
Baraita reads Chronicles 4:23 as referring to the sons of Jonadab, Solomon, the Sanhedrin, and Ruth, citing I Kings 2:19.
Rabbi Elazar says the mother of the kingdom's dynasty refers to Ruth.
Cites Leviticus 25:22 on eating old produce from the sixth year.
Asks what 'without salmanton' means.
Rav Nachman says it means without worms; Rav Sheshet says without blight.
Notes that baraitot are cited in accordance with each of Rav Sheshet's and Rav Nachman's views.
Baraita for Rav Nachman: 'until its produce comes in' means they keep eating old produce until the new arrives on its own.
Baraita for Rav Sheshet: old produce must not be spoiled by blight, so they keep eating it until new produce arrives on its own.
Baraita on Leviticus 26:10: aged produce is better, and storehouses hold old produce while threshing floors hold new.
Rav Pappa says all aged things are superior to new, except dates, liquor, and small fish.
Chapter-closing formula: the chapter beginning 'one who sells a ship' is complete.

92a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: a seller of produce or flax seed is not liable if the planted seed fails to sprout, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel makes him liable for garden seeds.
Rav rules that if the ox sold turns out to be a gorer, the sale is a mistaken transaction.
Shmuel says the seller may reply that he sold the ox for slaughter, so the sale stands.
Asks how to test the case by examining whether the buyer bought the ox for one purpose or several.
Explains the case is needed when the price of meat rose and the buyer stood by the original price.
Asks what practical difference this makes.
The difference concerns the trouble involved for the buyer.
Asks how exactly these cases should be understood.

92b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what the practical difference between Rav and Shmuel is if the seller cannot repay, since the buyer could simply keep the ox.
Answers the case is where the seller can repay; Rav follows the majority in monetary matters, while Shmuel does not.
Gives a mnemonic listing the cases to be cited: woman, slave, ox, oxen, and produce.
Objects to Rav from a mishnah on a widow's marriage-contract dispute, where her claim succeeds only with witnesses, not by the majority of women.
Asks why the majority of women who marry as virgins should not decide the case.
Ravina replies that, unlike most women, this woman's marriage lacked public notice, so the majority presumption is undermined.
Objects: if virgin marriages are publicized, the witnesses for this woman would be false, so Ravina's argument proves nothing.
Refines the argument: most virgin marriages generate publicity, and this woman's lack of it undermines the majority presumption.
Challenges Shmuel with a baraita: a slave found to be a thief or gambler cannot be returned, but one found to be an armed bandit or condemned can be.

93a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the sale is valid because most slaves are thieves or gamblers, which would show that majority rules in money matters.
No: all slaves are like this, so the case proves nothing about majority in monetary matters.
Cites a Bava Kamma mishnah: an ox gored a cow whose fetus died with uncertain timing, so the owner pays half for the cow and a quarter for the fetus.
Objects that by the majority of cows conceiving live young, the fetus should be presumed lost to the goring, which Rav does not apply.
Replies that here the uncertainty is real, since the ox may have frightened the cow from the front, so the damage is disputed property split equally.
Suggests the Rav-Shmuel dispute mirrors a tannaitic dispute, citing a baraita and Rabbi Aha on a rutting camel that killed another camel.
Explains the suggested parallel: majority and presumption are treated as equivalent, aligning Rav with Rabbi Aha and Shmuel with the first tanna.
Rav could hold his view even with the first tanna, who concedes that majority rules in monetary matters.
Shmuel could hold his view even with Rabbi Aha, who concedes that majority does not decide monetary matters.
Cites the mishnah on the seller of produce whose planted seed fails to sprout: not liable, even for flaxseed that is mostly bought for planting.
Explains the proof: the sale stands even for flaxseed mostly bought for planting, showing majority is not followed in monetary matters.
Gives a baraita: garden seeds make the seller liable, flaxseed does not; the Gemara suggests a tannaitic dispute, with Rabbi Yosei's view following.

93b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Seller refunds only seed value; most buyers buy seed for other uses, so the sale stands.
Asks who the tanna'im are who dispute like Rav and Shmuel.
Rejects identifying the disputants as Yosei and the anonymous view, since both follow the majority.
Proposes the real dispute is between the first tanna and Yosei, or the first tanna and the anonymous view.
Baraita: seller returns only seed value; some say he also returns the buyer's planting expenses.
Asks who holds the view attributed to some.
Rav Hisda identifies that view as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's.
Asks which statement of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel shows this; proposes the mishna's flax clause.
Objects that the first clause already makes the first tanna say the same, leaving no dispute.
Proposes the dispute is whether the seller is liable for the buyer's expenses.
Asks how we know Rabban Shimon holds the expenses view rather than the reverse.
Not difficult: the later tanna always adds to the first tanna's ruling, not detracts.
Suggests the whole mishna is Rabban Shimon's view with an omitted clause, so no proof of expenses.
Brings a baraita where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds a worker liable as a paid bailee.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the worker pays compensation for the owner's and guests' humiliation.
Cites the Jerusalem custom under Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel as evidence for that liability.
Another Jerusalem custom: a cloth at the hall entrance signals guests may still enter.
Mishna: acceptable proportions of impurities, figs, wine barrels and jugs a buyer tolerates.
Rav Ketina taught the buyer accepts legumes in the grain but not dirt.
Objects with Rabba's ruling that a buyer also accepts some dirt, contradicting Rav Ketina.

94a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes the pebble-taker must repay the wheat value, so buyers accept some dirt in produce.
Answer: buyers accept a quarter-kav of dirt per se'a in legumes, but less than that in dirt generally.
Objects: but a baraita is taught that buyers accept a quarter-kav of dirt in purchases.
Brings the baraita listing the acceptable quarter-kav admixtures for wheat, barley and lentils.
Asks whether wheat and barley should be treated the same as lentils.
No: lentils are uprooted, so they naturally carry more dirt than harvested grains.
Proposes resolving the dilemma: buyers of wheat and barley accept no quarter-kav of dirt.
Rejects this: lentils were stated specifically, lest one think buyers accept even more dirt in them.
Rav Huna rules the buyer may sift all produce and return all impurities, a strict law or a penalty.
Strict-law reading: a buyer paying for clean produce expects none, so sifting one quarter-kav leads to sifting all.
Penalty reading: the seller is suspected of deceitfully adding impurities, so he pays for all of them.
Gemara gives a mnemonic labeling the cases it will cite, involving two documents of Ravin bar Rav Naḥman.
Objects from a mishna in Kilayim: a quarter-kav of diverse seeds only requires reduction, not full removal.
Deflects: diverse-kinds admixture and dirt admixture in sales may both be acceptable quarter-kav levels.
Asks: if a quarter-kav of diverse seeds is acceptable, why must the mishna require reducing it?
The requirement is due to the severity of the prohibition against diverse kinds.
Challenges this answer: if so, why is the diverse-kinds rule treated as a stringency here?

94b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites the latter clause, where Rabbi Yosei permits sifting the produce to remove the dirt.
Asks: granted the dispute concerns dirt above a quarter-kav, what exactly are the tanna'im disputing?
The first tanna holds we do not penalize the permitted as if forbidden; Rabbi Yosei holds we do penalize.
Explains Rabbi Yosei's reason for permitting sifting: otherwise it would look like keeping diverse kinds.
Brings a baraita of two claimants to a deposit, where one gets a mina and the other a mina.
Compares: there the deposit is certain, but here we cannot know the whole mixture was deliberate.
Brings the latter clause: Rabbi Yosei asks what the cheater loses if all is held until Elijah.
Rejects the parallel: there a cheater is certain, but here we cannot know the mixing was deliberate.
Brings a baraita on a note with interest: the lender is penalized and collects neither principal nor interest.
Rejects this parallel as well: there the amount is certain from the writing, but here it is not.
Brings the latter clause: the Sages say the lender collects the principal but not the interest.
Rejects the parallel: there the principal is certainly permitted, but here the whole may not be mixed.
Brings a baraita from Ravin bar Rav Naḥman: the seller returns all the quarter-kavs, not only the excess.
Concludes that where the buyer wishes to return it all, he returns the whole amount.

95a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Discusses whether a quarter-kav surplus or shortfall counts, under the earlier principle.
A quarter-kav is not significant, but a surplus can combine to nine kavs, so the excess counts as a field.
Brings a baraita: overreaching by less than a sixth stands, while more than a sixth voids the sale.
Asks why the buyer may return the overcharge only down to less than a sixth.
Concludes that where one wants to return all the overcharge, he returns all of it.
Distinguishes: where the price was originally equal, a sixth shortfall is no known error, but a surplus voids the sale.
Brings a baraita on one who receives a field to plant: ten per hundred is accepted, but more voids all.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua rules that any excess beyond the stated proportion is counted from the original price.
Cites the mishna's case of a cellar of wine and the rest of its ruling.
Asks how the cellar case is understood, whether stated generally or as this particular cellar.
Brings a baraita: selling a cellar of wine means he delivers all good wine.
Continues the baraita: wine sold from a shop cellar binds the seller even if all of it turned to vinegar.
Explains the case: the first clause of the baraita concerns a cellar of wine stated generally.
Asks whether one who sells generally accepts ten inferior jugs per hundred as well.
Objects: a Tanna taught that selling a barrel of wine means all of it is good; a barrel differs as one wine.
Objects further: a teaching of Rav Zavid's school says the cellar sale delivers all good wine.
Continues that teaching: the seller accepts ten inferior jugs per hundred, supporting the cellar rule.

95b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Introduces the mishna's cellar-of-wine ruling as a storehouse of questions to be examined.
Presents an apparent contradiction between two rulings, one of which seems difficult against the other.
Reconciles: the cases differ depending on whether the seller said to assess the cellar or not.
Accordingly, where he says of a cellar of wine that he sells it, he gives all good wine if told to assess.
Parallel case: where the cellar is said to be assessed, the seller gives all good wine and accepts ten jugs per hundred.
Where the cellar is not said to be assessed, the seller gives all good wine, as with wine sold in a shop.
Poses an open dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina on whether the buyer accepts the cellar's defects when not told to assess.
The one who holds the buyer accepts infers this from Rav Zavid's teaching about the cellar of wine.
Establishes Rav Zavid's teaching as concerning the case where the seller said to assess the cellar.
The opposing view infers from a baraita: selling a cellar of wine means delivering all good wine.
Restates the baraita on the cellar sale, establishing it as the case where the seller was not told to assess.
Objects that the inference from Rav Zavid is difficult against the baraita.
The baraita is missing words; the full text says he accepts the defects only if told to assess.
Where the cellar of wine is sold without being told to assess, he gives all good wine, as for shop wine.
Raises a difficulty for the one who infers from the baraita, against Rav Zavid's teaching.
Explains Rav Zavid's teaching as applying where the seller said to assess the cellar.
Where he was told to assess he accepts; by parity, where not told he does not accept.
Explains why this case is established as one where he was told to assess, since otherwise it is difficult.
Rav Yehuda and Rav Chisda dispute the blessing over wine sold in a shop and the case of sour wine.
Objects with a baraita on the blessing over moldy bread and sour wine, which all came into being by His word.
Rav Zavid says Rav Yehuda concedes in the case of a wine barrel sold in the market.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef which of Rav Yehuda and Rav Chisda's positions he follows.
Rav Yosef replies that he knows the mishna's ruling, which settles the question.

96a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Brings a baraita: one who checks a barrel and separates terumah from it, then finds it turned to vinegar.
Asks what the baraita means by saying the first three days are certain and afterward doubtful.
Rabbi Yoḥanan explains: the first three days it is certainly wine, and afterward it is doubtful.
Asks the reason for this ruling.
Reason: wine from the top of the barrel is removed by tasting; the taste, not smell, decides it is still wine.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds the last three days are certainly vinegar, and the earlier period is doubtful.
Asks the reason: wine from the bottom of the barrel may be the one removed, not the top.
Objects that the taster may have removed wine after tasting, so the smell and taste may mislead.
Quotes Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's teaching: first days certain wine, last days certain vinegar, middle doubtful.
Notes the very baraita is difficult: its first and last rulings both seem to rest on smell and taste.
Gives a case: vinegar found in a sealed jug, which could only appear if the first three days were removed.
Asks whose view the baraita follows, Rabbi Yoḥanan or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.
Rav Mari and Rav Zavid split: one says it follows Rabbi Yoḥanan, the other Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.
Stated rule: a seller of a barrel of wine that turned sour is responsible for the first three days, then the buyer.

96b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel rules that wine is treated as wine in a case involving Rav Yosef; the halakha follows Shmuel on wine, not Rav on beer.
Brings a baraita: one who sells dates, barley or wine lees blesses all came into being by His word; others say lees with wine taste bless the vine.
Rabba and Rav Yosef both hold the halakha is not like the other opinion.
Rava holds all agree that if one put in three measures and got four, the result is wine.
Following his own reasoning, Rava holds any wine not diluted with a one-to-three water ratio is not wine.
Where they dispute, if three went in and three and a half came out, the Rabbis hold it is still wine.
The Rabbis hold three measures in and three out, with half the water drawn off, is nothing at all.
Others hold two and a half come out after three go in, so the wine is good and more than its measure.
Asks why they dispute, since a mishna has already taught the matter.

97a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: One who soaks produce and adds water is exempt if the result is within the measure, though Rabbi Yehuda holds him liable.
Clarifies: the two views dispute only amounts within the measure; beyond it they agree.
Even beyond the measure they dispute, and the dispute is raised here to show the strength of Rabbi Yehuda's view.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak asks Rav Ḥiyya bar Abin whether lees that have a wine taste count as wine.
Rav Ḥiyya replies that the lees are not wine at all, merely a drink of sediment.
Brings a baraita on terumah lees: the first and second batches are forbidden, the third permitted.
Rabbi Meir adds that the third batch is forbidden if it imparts taste, and tithe lees follow the same pattern.
Rabbi Meir extends this: the second batch is forbidden if it imparts taste; for consecrated lees the third is forbidden.
Rabbi Meir adds that the fourth batch is also forbidden if it imparts taste.
Objects with a baraita: consecrated lees are always forbidden and tithe lees are always permitted.
Notes a further contradiction between consecrated lees and consecrated lees, and tithe with tithe.
Resolves: one ruling concerns the sanctity of the body, the other the sanctity of money.
Resolves the tithe case: one refers to certain tithe, the other to demai produce.
Quotes Rabbi Yoḥanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak: as the law is for prohibition, so for permission.
Asks: if the lees act like water, do they make the produce fit; if like wine, do they?
Explains the case: the lees were soaked in rain water, and the grain absorbed the wine-taste into its volume.
Rav Pappa's case concerns a cow that drinks first and the first batch.
Rav Zutra bar Tuvia quotes Rav: the sanctification of the day is said only over wine fit for the altar.
Objects: if this excludes wine from the press, a teaching of Rabbi Ḥiyya says wine from the press may not be brought.
Answers: if it was brought, it is fit, so the rule applies even ab initio.

97b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava: one who squeezes a cluster of grapes and says sanctification of the day over it has sanctified the day with that wine.
Objects: if it excludes wine from the mouth and the drippings, Rabbi Ḥiyya taught it may not be brought, and if brought it is fit.
Objects that the exclusion would be for Kushi wine, yet a teaching says all of these may not be brought.
Asks what the exclusion is meant to cover: mixed wine, uncovered wine, or wine with lees.
Suggests the exclusion of mixed wine is the dispute between Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.
Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Ḥanina says the Sages agree with Rabbi Eliezer that a blessing cup needs water added before blessing.
Asks whether the exclusion is for uncovered wine, which is a danger.
Asks how the lees case is understood: whether wine of three in and four out is fine, or a dispute of the Rabbanan.
Rather, it excludes wine whose smell is bad.
Alternatively, it always excludes uncovered wine, even though it was strained, as Rabbi Neḥemya holds.
Cites a verse from Malachi: offer it to your governor, to show the prohibited offering is refused.
Rav Kahana asks Rava what the red-hued wine of Rav's source is.
Rava answers with a verse in Proverbs: do not look at wine when it reddens.
Taught: jars of Sharon wine, good pitsot and those sealed with sulphur.
Mishna: one who sells wine that turns sour is not liable, unless it is known that wine turns sour, making the sale a mistake.

98a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A seller of perfumed wine must keep it for the buyer until the festival; old wine is kept three years.
Rabbi Yossi bar Ḥanina says the ruling applies only to jars belonging to the buyer, not the seller.
Asks what the seller's jars mean; the seller could simply say there is no need to wait.
Explains: the case is one where he said to set it aside, and asks why Rabbi Yossi must read the mishna as buyer's jars.
Rava says the mishna's wording is difficult: why does it not say he has no need to wait, unless he was told to set aside.
Rav Ḥiyya bar Yosef holds wine makes its owner's luck, supported by Habakkuk on the treacherous proud man.
Rav Marei holds the proud man is not accepted even in his own household, as in Habakkuk.
Rav's teaching: one who takes pride in a scholar's garment without being a scholar is not admitted to God's presence.
Compares Habakkuk's wording 'shall not dwell' with Exodus's 'holy dwelling' to support the teaching.
Rava: one who buys a jar of wine from a shopkeeper intending to drink it acquires it, if the seller can still bring it.
Limits the ruling: it applies only when the wine was not opened by a tap, and before market day.
Rava adds: one who takes wine intending to bring it to the market and it is not sold, and it turns, the buyer receives it.
Doubt arises: if the wine turned to vinegar, what is the law?
Rav Hillel asks Rav Ashi; Rav Kahana taught us that vinegar is not accepted, contrary to Rabbi Yossi bar Ḥanina.
Some say even vinegar is accepted by the buyer.
Asks according to whom that view is held: Rabbi Yossi bar Ḥanina.
The mishna continues: old wine from last year and aged wine are kept for the buyer as mentioned.

98b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A tanna teaches that the wine keeps aging until the festival.
Mishna: one who sells a place, or receives a place to build a wedding house for a son and a widow's house for a daughter, builds four cubits by six.
Rabbi Akiva's view; Rabbi Yishmael says this is a cattle stall, where one builds four by six.
Lists the house dimensions: a small house six by eight, a large one eight by ten, a salon ten by ten, height half its length.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds the height should be like the building of the Temple.
Asks why the mishna separates the son and daughter cases instead of stating them together.
Answers: the point is incidental, teaching that the son-in-law does not dwell in his father-in-law's house.
Quotes Ben Sira: a son-in-law living in his father-in-law's house, and answering before hearing is folly.
Rabbi Yishmael says the cattle stall case is one who wants to build a cattle stall, building four by six.
Asks which tanna holds the cattle stall ruling, Rabbi Yishmael or Rabbi Akiva, and how each reads it.
Explains: even though it is a cattle stall, a person sometimes makes his dwelling like a cattle stall.
Rabbi Yishmael's teaching: one who wants to make a cattle stall builds four cubits by six.
Asks what a salon, the tarkelin, is.
Answers that a salon is a bedchamber, and a kantir is a twelve-by-twelve measure with a stone floor.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view: the height is measured like the building of the Temple.
Asks for the proof of this view, and whose teaching it reflects.
Rabban Shimon says everything is like the building of the Temple.
Some hold the first tanna teaches this, and Rabban Shimon is astonished at it.
Rabban Shimon asks for the proof from the Temple, since everyone builds according to the Temple.
Brings a baraita: others say the height is like its beams, which is compared to its breadth.
Answers: the upper space is open, or the Temple had side chambers; Rabbi Ḥanina found verses that conflict.
Cites 1 Kings: the Temple was sixty cubits long, twenty wide and thirty high, while the inner sanctuary was twenty cubits.
Asks what is taught by measuring from the cherubim upward.

99a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The space below the cherubs is teaching-wise like the space above them: both were empty and unused.
Supports Rabbi Levi's tradition view, and a baraita adds that the Ark had ten cubits of free space on each side.
Shmuel holds that the cherubs stood miraculously and occupied no physical space.
A verse about the cherubs' wings, measured at five cubits each, is cited to support Shmuel.
If the cherubs' wings filled the width, where were their bodies standing?
The conclusion drawn from the verse is that the cherubs stood miraculously.
Abaye objects that the cherubs may have stood with bodies beneath their wings, like chickens.
Rava objects that the cherubs may have stood side by side with overlapping wings.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov objects that the cherubs may have stood diagonally across the room.
Rav Huna objects that the room may have widened at the top, giving space for bodies and wings.
Rav Pappa objects that the wings may have been partly folded, leaving room for the bodies.
Rav Ashi objects that the wings may have crossed over one another, taking up less space.
How exactly were the cherubs standing?
Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Elazar disagree: one says the faces were toward each other, one says toward the House.
Against the view that faces were toward each other, a verse says their faces were toward the House.
The contradiction is resolved: the cherubs' direction depended on whether Israel did God's will.
Against the view that faces were toward the House, a verse says their faces were toward each other.
They were angled sideways, so faces turned partly toward each other and partly toward the Sanctuary.
A baraita of Onkelos describes the cherubs as child-like figures whose faces were angled toward the Ark.
Mishna: a cistern owner beyond another's house may enter only at usual times, and each side builds a lock.
The Gemara asks: a lock to where, what does the lock guard?
Rabbi Yohanan says both parties build a lock on the cistern opening to block unilateral access.
Why does the homeowner need a lock, since only the cistern owner needs to protect his water?
Rabbi Elazar begins his answer to why the homeowner also needs a lock.

99b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The reason the owner of the inner garden may not enter freely: suspicion about his neighbor's wife.
Mishna: rules on when a landlocked garden owner may enter, bring merchants, or use the outer garden as a path.
Shmuel's rule on how much land a seller must give for the channel itself and for its banks.
Who may sow the banks of the water channel?
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, says the field owner may sow the banks.
Rav Naḥman, citing Shmuel, says the field owner may plant trees on the banks.
Explains how the two views fit: planting is allowed under both, and sowing is barred because roots weaken the ground.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, permits repairing collapsed banks with earth from the same field.
Rav Pappa objects: the field owner could say the channel's own water removed the earth.
Rav Pappa's reply: the channel owner accepted that condition when he bought the rights.
Mishna on public thoroughfares: alternative routes, standard path widths, and the widths of royal, burial and mourning paths.
Why can't the landowner simply take a stick and block the path, if the original path now belongs to him?
Rav Zevid, in Rava's name: the Sages decreed against self-help here, lest the owner create a longer circuitous route.
Rav Mesharshiyya, in Rava's name: the ruling applies only when a circuitous route is given instead of a straight one.

100a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ashi holds any alternative path beside the original is a circuitous route, so a public path may never be exchanged.
Objection: the owner could ask the public to return his original path and take back the path he gave them.
Whose opinion does the mishna follow?
It follows Rabbi Eliezer's opinion.
A baraita quotes Rabbi Eliezer: public travelers who chose a path through private land acquired the right to use it.
Rav Giddel, citing Rav, limits Rabbi Eliezer's view to cases where the public lost the original path.
If so, why does Rabba bar Rav Huna say the halakha is not like Rabbi Eliezer?
Rabba bar Rav Huna explains that whoever teaches the limited case does not teach that Rav rules against Rabbi Eliezer.
What is the reason the owner may not reclaim the alternative path?
Rav Yehuda's ruling that a border strip used by the public may not be destroyed supports this reason.
By what means did the public acquire the path, according to Rabbi Eliezer?
By walking along it.
A baraita: Rabbi Eliezer says walking acquires land, while the Rabbis require an act of taking possession.
Rabbi Elazar derives Rabbi Eliezer's view from God's command to Abraham to walk the land.
The Rabbis explain the verse differently: Abraham walked out of love, to make conquest easier for his descendants, not to acquire.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina says the Rabbis agree with Rabbi Eliezer about a path through vineyards.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Ami's ruling on the width of a vineyard path, and why a fenced path must be widened differently.
The mishna's rule: a private path is four cubits wide.
A baraita: others say a private path must allow a donkey to pass with its load.
Rav Huna rules the halakha follows the others.
A different baraita: the judges of the exile say the standard width is two and a half cubits.
Rav Huna rules the halakha follows the judges of the exile.
Objection: Rav Huna also said the halakha follows the others, so the rulings seem to conflict.
Resolution: the two definitions describe one and the same measure.
The mishna's rule: a public thoroughfare is sixteen cubits wide.
A baraita: private path four cubits, and a road from city to city eight cubits.

100b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A public thoroughfare is sixteen cubits, and a road to a city of refuge must be twice that width.
What is the verse from which the double width of the refuge road is derived?
The verse says prepare the way, not just a way, implying a road of double width.
A king's road has no maximum width, since a king may breach a private fence to make his own road.
A burial path has no maximum width, out of honor for the deceased.
The judges of Tzippori set the standing area for mourners at the size needed to sow four kav of seed.
A baraita: relatives may bury a family member in his plot even against a buyer's will, to avoid a family flaw.
A baraita: mourners perform at least seven standings and sittings, matching the seven references to vanity in Ecclesiastes.
How exactly do they perform this ceremony?
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda describes the earlier Judean practice of standings and sittings, with a set formula at each stop.
The Rabbis object: if that is all the ceremony entails, it should be permitted even on Shabbat.
Rav Avya performed the standing and sitting ceremony for his wife, the sister of Rami bar Pappa.
Rav Yosef says Rav Avya erred twice: he used distant relatives and performed the rite on the second day.
Abaye adds that the rite must be performed only in the cemetery, not in the city.
Rava adds that the rite applies only where the custom exists, and that was not the custom there.
Objection to Rav Yosef and Abaye: the Shabbat case makes sense only if the rite happened in a city near a cemetery at twilight.
Mishna: rules for a catacomb plot, with dimensions for each burial chamber and the eight niches cut into its walls.

101a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The width of each burial niche is six handbreadths.

ranges.en: Asks why the verse needs the firstborn prohibition, if the father's permission to bequeath is already stated earlier.

ranges.en: Rava says a judge rules only on what he sees with his own eyes, so a later reader should not take over a ruling the author cannot explain.
