Offers an alternative: the mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who prefers daughters.
Asks which of Rabbi Yehuda's statements the mishnah follows.
Cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda reads the blessing with everything as Abraham having a daughter named Bakkol.
Objects that the Merciful One deprived Abraham of nothing, so Rabbi Yehuda need not prefer daughters to sons.
Cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says it is a mitzva to sustain daughters, showing preference for daughters.
Asks, from the baraita on a male and female birth payment, what situation it describes.
Rav Ashi explains the baraita as a case of inverted gift stipulations with uncertain birth order, to be split equally.
Asks how the other baraita, giving a male only one hundred dinars, can be realized.
Ravina says it refers to someone who promised a sum to whoever informs him.

141b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: a man pays one hundred dinars to whoever correctly names his wife's child's sex, with stated conditions.
Challenges why the informant is paid on a male and female birth when his stipulation does not cover that case.
Asks what the stipulations serve to exclude if all possibilities were stated.
They exclude a non-viable newborn, for which the informant receives nothing.
Rav Huna rules that one who transfers property to a fetus does not make the fetus acquire it.
Rav Nachman objects from the mishnah, which implies the fetus did acquire the money.
Rav Huna replies that he does not know who taught the mishnah, so it cannot be a known view.
Asks why Rav Huna did not attribute the mishnah to Rabbi Meir, who allows transfer to a not-yet-existing entity.
Rejects that reading: Rabbi Meir speaks only of transfer to existing entities, not to a fetus.
Asks whether the mishnah follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds that a fetus acquires ownership.
Cites a mishnah in Yevamot where Rabbi Yosei treats a fetus as inheriting its father's property.
Rejects this: inheritance comes by itself, unlike a gift, so the fetus can inherit but not acquire gifts.
Asks whether the mishnah follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who treats gifts and inheritance alike.
Cites a mishnah where Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka says a statement about a fit heir stands.
Rejects this: Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka may speak only of gifts to existing entities, not a fetus.
Proposes that Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka compares gifts to inheritance and so follows Rabbi Yosei.
Asks who says Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka holds like Rabbi Yosei.
Proposes that the mishnah concerns a payment to an informant who already exists, not a gift to a fetus.
Rejects this: then the mishnah's heir clause would be pointless, since no gift is made to the heir.
Proposes that the gift was made after birth but before the sex was known.
Rejects this: then the phrase whatever offspring my wife gives birth to would be incorrect wording.

142a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Proposes that Rav Chuna's ruling concerns a transfer taking effect only when the child is born.
Rejects this: Rav Huna holds that even a transfer effective at birth gives nothing to a fetus.
States the positions of Rav Nachman, Rav Huna and Rav Sheshet on whether a fetus acquires transferred property.
Rav Sheshet cites a baraita about a convert's property plundered and then returned after a possible heir's death or miscarriage.
Rav Sheshet argues that the second taking of possession shows the miscarried fetus had acquired ownership.
Abaye and Rava refute the proof: inheritance differs from acquisition, and the plunderers' hold was loose.
Asks what practical difference lies between Abaye's refutation and Rava's refutation.
Objects from a mishnah: a one-day-old child inherits and bequeaths, implying a fetus does not.
Replies that Rav Sheshet's mishnah teaches a different rule: a one-day-old child inherits from his mother.
Asks what the reason is that a fetus whose mother died does not inherit from her.

142b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the reason: the fetus is presumed to have died first, so it cannot pass the mother's estate to paternal brothers.
Asks whether it is certain that the fetus died first.
Objects that there was an incident where the fetus made spasmodic motions after the mother died.
Mar bar Rav Ashi says those motions are like a severed lizard tail, not signs of life.
Mar son of Rav Yosef, in Rava's name, says a one-day-old child reduces the firstborn's double portion, but a fetus does not.
Similarly, a son born after his father's death does not reduce the firstborn's portion, since children excludes a fetus.
Sura and Pumbedita versions differ; the halakha follows all of them, with a posthumous firstborn denied a double portion.
Rabbi Yitzchak in Rabbi Yochanan's name: a fetus does not acquire a transfer, while parents' gifts to their own unborn child are an exception.
Shmuel has Rav Chana gather ten men to publicize his ruling that a fetus does not acquire a transfer.
Relates the case of a man who promised property to future sons, and the older son is given a share.
Asks whether a young son receives an extra share where other sons exist.
Lists the amoraim on each side of whether the young son receives an extra share.
Rabbi Abbahu asks whether the halakha follows his opinion or Rabbi Yirmeya's.
Rabbi Yirmeya says it follows his side by age; Rabbi Abbahu replies the matter depends on the reasoning.
Yirmeya asks Abbahu's reasoning; Abbahu refers him to Rabbi Avin, to whom he explained it.

143a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Avin explains Abbahu's reasoning: a father's donkey-like acquisition language gives the son nothing, like unborn children.
States the three views on whether a person and a donkey named together acquire property: half, nothing, or all.
Rav Sheshet cites Rabbi Yosei's baraita on separating the inner bitter part of a cucumber as teruma.
Asks why the teruma separation takes effect if it resembles the donkey-and-person acquisition.
Replies that the bitter inner part is properly teruma by Torah law, so the designation is not mixed.
Rabbi Ile'a derives from a verse that separating inferior teruma is valid though improper.
Rav Avya objects to Rav Chamnuna from a mishnah about betrothing five women, two of them sisters, with a basket of figs.
Infers from the mishnah that only the sisters are not betrothed, while the unrelated women are.
Asks why that is so, given the donkey-like analogy.
Rav Ashi replies the mishnah refers to a case of those eligible for him, so the analogy fails.
Rav Yosef rules that a wife and her sons named together take half of the property.
Rav Yosef cites a baraita on the shewbread, which is divided half for Aaron and half for his sons.
Abaye distinguishes Aaron, a priest, from a woman who inherits only as one of the sons.
Objects from incidents in Neharde'a, Tiberias and the coronation tax, where a group and individual split half and half.
Distinguishes the coronation tax case, since the royal writ named only the councilmen and the notables helped pay.
Rabbi Zeira objects to Rav Yosef from a baraita on a meal-offering split across two vessels.

143b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita: bringing fifty-tenths in each of two vessels fulfills the obligation after the fact, though not ab initio.
Objects that if every such case splits half and half, dividing ab initio should be permitted too.
Replies the cases differ: the meal-offering was meant to be large, so only sixty-tenths fit one vessel.
Concludes the halakha follows Rav Yosef in three disputed matters, including equal halves of an unspecified division.
Rabbi Ami rules that silk swaths go to sons or daughters by suitability, depending on daughters-in-law and unmarried daughters.
Asks whether a single son can be called sons, so a will excludes the daughter from her dowry tenth.
Abaye cites the verse naming Dan's sons, Hushim, as proof that a single son may be called sons.
Rava objects that Hushim may be a name for numerous reed-like groups, so the proof fails.
Rava and Rav Yosef cite verses naming Eliab and Azariah as single sons, proving the usage.
Asks whether a grandson is called a son in a will leaving property to sons.
Rav Chaviva says a grandson is called a son; Mar bar Rav Ashi says he is not.
A baraita follows Mar bar Rav Ashi: one vowed from benefit from sons may benefit from grandsons.
Mishnah: adult sons who enhance the estate share the gain with all heirs unless they declared they act for themselves.
Rav Chaviva, in Rava's name, limits the mishnah to gains from the property itself, not from the heirs' efforts.
Objects that Rabbi Chanina says even if the father left them nothing, the sons' enhancement would count for them.

144a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that rent from a mortar is profit from the son's own effort, so it should not be shared with the estate.
Dismisses the objection: a mortar needs only supervision, which minors can do, so adults gain no extra share.
Recites the mishnah: adult sons who declared at the outset that they work for themselves keep the profit.
Relates that Rav Safra invested his inheritance, and Rava ruled the profit was his own since he was a scholar.
Recites the mishnah on a wife who enhanced her late husband's property, so profit goes to the middle.
Asks what right a widow has to manage orphans' property.
Rabbi Yirmeya says the mishnah refers to a wife who is herself an heiress.
Asks whether this is obvious, since she is just like any other heir.
Teaches it is needed lest one think a woman's unexpected toil alone shows she works for herself, so it requires an explicit statement.
Recites the mishnah: if a wife declares she works for herself with her own share, the profit is hers.
Asks whether the wife's explicit statement point is obvious.
Explains it is needed lest one think her praiseworthy toil for orphans means she forgoes profit to be split.
Rabbi Chanina rules that a father's house designated for a son's wedding is acquired by the son, under stated conditions.
Concludes that the son acquires the house but not an upper story, with the portico's status a further question.
Raises unresolved questions on a portico and on a house within a house, which remain undecided.
Raises a baraita objection that a son acquires furniture but not the house his father designated for his wedding.
Rabbi Yirmeya explains the baraita as a case where the father's storeroom was placed there, so no house was intended.
Sages of Neharde'a, Rav Yehuda, Rav Pappi, and Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi give examples of signs showing no intent to gift the house.
Mar Zutra says three rulings were instituted as halakha without stated reasons, including the wedding house and a deed to a wife.

144b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: a brother's forced public service or illness costs are shared from the common estate, or borne by himself if negligent.
Baraita: profit from a brother's appointment as tax collector or commander goes to all brothers if he was appointed for them.
Asks whether it is not obvious that profit goes to all brothers when the appointment was on their account.
Explains it is needed for a brother sharper than the others, lest his talent alone earn him the profit.
Baraita: a brother who took two hundred dinars to study Torah or a trade gets sustenance only if he is present with the family.
Asks why they should not provide his sustenance wherever he is.
Supports Rav Huna's view that a household's blessing is in its abundance, so per-capita costs fall with more people.
Asks whether they should provide according to the household blessing, the expenses he would incur at home.
Yes, they must cover the expenses he would have incurred anyway.
Restates the mishnah: a brother who falls ill and is treated pays from his own resources.
Ravin, in Rabbi Ela's name, limits this to illness by negligence; otherwise the cost comes from the middle.
Asks what counts as negligence.
Rabbi Chanina: all is in heaven's hands except colds and snares one can guard against, so negligence is avoidable exposure.
Mishnah: gifts of groomsmen given in the father's lifetime are reciprocated to the middle, since they are a collectible debt.
Raises a contradiction with a baraita where a father's groomsman gifts are reciprocated to the son.
Rabbi Asi, in Rabbi Yochanan's name, says the mishnah concerns gifts sent to the father for a son's wedding.
Rabbi Asi says no emendation is needed: the mishnah and baraita concern unspecified versus specified credit to a son.
Shmuel: the mishnah concerns a childless deceased brother's yavam, who inherits only what was not yet due at death.
Asks whether a friend who received groomsman gifts from the deceased must repay them, since the giver is dead.
Cites a baraita on betrothal money returned by local custom, to show repayment depends on custom.
Rav Yosef bar Abba, in Mar Ukva's name, says Shmuel limits return of betrothal money to when the woman dies, not the man.
Asks the reason: since the woman can say she does not want the money back, so it is not returned.

145a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the same logic applies to a groomsman: let him say give me my groomsman and I will rejoice.
Rav Yosef explains Shmuel's case: the groomsman rejoiced for seven days but died before being repaid.
Asks whether Shmuel's claim give me my husband is a dispute between tanna'im.
Baraita: a virgin collects two hundred and a widow one hundred; return of betrothal money depends on local custom, per Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Asks whether the tanna'im really differ on whether the claim give me my husband is valid.
Explains the baraita is incomplete and supplies the missing words, separating death of the husband from death of the wife.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says the custom governs whichever party dies, and the woman cannot claim give me my husband.
Rejects this: everyone agrees she may make the claim, and the dispute is whether betrothal money is a sunk cost.
Asks why Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's baraita says custom governs return if he does not hold it is a sunk cost.
Replies the baraita refers to gifts sent during the betrothal, which are returned by local custom, not the betrothal money.
Baraita on a talent-value betrothal: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei each give different sums to the woman.
Asks which case the talent baraita describes: a death, an adulterous betrothed wife, or a rape.
Explains the case is a priest's betrothed wife who was raped, and the tanna'im dispute whether betrothal money is a sunk cost.
Explains Rabbi Yosei's view: since it is uncertain, the woman returns or receives half-sums to reach her marriage contract amount.
Rav Yosef bar Minyumi, in Rav Nachman's name, says betrothal money is returned wherever that is the custom.
Asks what the halakha is for the rest of Babylonia outside Neharde'a.
Rabba, Rav Yosef and Rav Pappa rule the presents are returned but betrothal money is not, except on a divorce by the woman.
Ameimar holds betrothal money is never returned, as a decree lest people think the betrothal can be undone with her sister; Rav Ashi uses the bill of divorce.
Objects that Rav Ashi's reasoning is a mistake, since some heard of the return but not of the divorce bill.
Tosefta: five statements on gifts of groomsmen, including that they are collectible in court and not subject to the prohibition of interest.

145b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita continues: gifts of groomsmen are not abrogated by the Sabbatical Year, and the firstborn takes no double portion from them.
Explains that gifts are collectible like a loan and not interest, and that the Sabbatical release verse does not apply to them.
Baraita: the firstborn takes no double portion of the gifts.
Explains the reason: gifts are potential inheritance, and the firstborn takes only what the deceased already possessed.
Rav Kahana states the principle: the recipient must repay even if absent, and a grievance lies against a betrothed man who did not inform him.
Asks how far the recipient may deduct from the reciprocal gift for missing the wedding feast.
Abaye: gifts up to one dinar are fully deducted, up to four dinars half, and beyond that each deducts by prominence.
Tosefta: a groomsman may refuse a reciprocal service that differs in public or private, virgin or widow, or number of wives.
Baraita on types of Torah scholars: homiletics, dialectics, halakhic traditions, and Talmud as the source of all.
Rabbi Zeira cites Rav and Proverbs to say the Talmud master is weary while the Mishnah master feasts.
Rava says the opposite, citing Ecclesiastes: Mishnah masters labor without benefit, while Talmud masters are warmed.
Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yannai offer further readings of the verse on the poor and the good-hearted, about wife and temperament.
Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi read the verse as about empathy, cruelty, and patience or impatience.

146a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether all days of the poor are terrible, since Shabbatot and festivals bring them rest and enjoyment.
Explains via Shmuel that a change of regimen causes illness, and cites Ben Sira's description of the poor man's hardships.
Recites the mishnah: presents to a father-in-law are not returned if the groom ate a feast there, but are if they were conditional.
Rava rules the feast-value exemption applies only at a full dinar's worth, not less.
Asks whether this is obvious, since the mishnah already speaks of a dinar.
Explains the mishnah states a dinar because that is the usual amount eaten, and Rava confirms its wording is precise.
Asks the halakha if the betrothed drank, if his agent ate, or if the father-in-law sent a feast to his home.
Brings an incident from Rav Yehuda in Shmuel's name: a man sent wagons of gifts and died after drinking hot drink at his father-in-law's door.
Rabbi Acha Sar HaBira's ruling at Usha: consumable presents are not returned, and others are returned.
Asks whether the incident shows presents are not returned even when only less than a dinar was consumed.
Rav Ashi replies that the drink may have been a pearl worth a thousand dinars, so the incident is not conclusive.
Rejects the feast-at-entrance question: the whole entrance may count as the father-in-law's house.
Raises dilemmas on proportional division of presents and on enhancement of their value, which remain unresolved.
Rava asks the halakha for presents typically consumed but not actually consumed.
Cites Rabbi Acha's ruling as a proof, and the Gemara rejects reading it as referring to unconsumed presents.
Cites the mishnah on minor presents for use at home, and Rava reads them as snoods or hairnets.
Rav Yehuda, in Rav's name, relates a man who sent new wine, oil and linen at Shavuot.
Asks what this incident teaches.
Says it teaches the greatness of Eretz Yisrael, or that the sender's claim of timing is plausible.
Rav Yehuda, in Rav's name, relates a man testing his betrothed's sense of smell in a ruin, with a radish scent in Galilee.

146b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Sages rule that since he entered only to test her sense of smell, a man does not inherit a betrothed woman who dies.
Recites the mishnah: a few presents for her use at her father's house are not collected.
Ravin the Elder, before Rav Pappa, rules on return of presents; Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua sets the appraisal for meat.
Recites the mishnah: a dying man who grants all his property and keeps no land has a gift that fails if he recovers.
Asks which tanna holds that we assess a person's intentions even when unstated.
Rav Nachman says it is Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya.
Cites a Tosefta where a father's gift made on a false report of his son's death is void under Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya.
Rav Sheshet says it is Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's view.
Cites a mishnah on bills of divorce for one led to execution or dangerously ill, supporting Rabbi Shimon Shezuri.
Asks why Rav Nachman does not follow Rabbi Shimon Shezuri on the mishnah.
Rav Nachman holds that there the husband partly stated his intention to divorce, which the mishnah lacks.
Asks why Rav Sheshet does not follow Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya.
Intentions proven clearly differ from less evident ones, which Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya may not apply.
Asks which tanna taught the Tosefta on a bedridden man asked to whom his property should go.
Cites the Tosefta's case of a bedridden man who is asked to whom his property shall be given and answers.

147a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Bedridden man who gives property to others believing he had no son or pregnant wife; the gift is void if the heir later appears.
Asks whether this follows Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya rather than the Rabbis.
Replies that even the Rabbis agree, since the case where he stated his reason differs.
Asks what the phrase he said and why he mentioned it signifies.
Lest one think the mention of a son only expresses sorrow, the baraita shows it was the reason for the gift.
Rav Zeira, in Rav's name, derives from the verse about passing an inheritance to a daughter that a deathbed gift is Torah law.
Rav Nachman, in Rabba bar Avuh's name, derives the same rule from the verse about giving inheritance to brothers.
Asks why Rav Nachman did not derive the rule from the verse's wording about passing inheritance.
Rav Nachman needs that verse for Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's point that only a daughter's inheritance can pass across tribes.
Asks why Rabbi Zeira did not derive the rule from the wording about giving.
Rabbi Zeira holds that this wording is the verse's usual manner, so nothing can be derived from it.
Rav Menashya bar Yirmeya derives from the Kings account of Hezekiah that a deathbed instruction transfers ownership.
Rami bar Yechezkel derives the same from Ahithophel instructing his household before he strangled himself.
Sages taught Ahithophel's three instructions to his sons, including the Shavuot signs of a clear or cloudy day for sowing wheat.
Rabbi Abba says the crop-sign teaching is attributed to Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi, whose Sukkot smoke signs predict rain and prices.
Smoke direction by wind: north or south winds, and east or west, signal plenty or drought and storage ability.
Raises a contradiction with a baraita giving different winds as beneficial or harmful for wheat and olives.
Rav Yosef offers a mnemonic: the table in the north favors wheat and the candelabrum in the south favors olives.
Resolves the contradiction: the east wind is beneficial in Babylonia and the west wind in Eretz Yisrael.
Baraita: Abba Shaul says a clear Shavuot signals a good year; Rav Zevid says the warmth or cold of Rosh HaShana sets the year.
Asks what practical difference there is whether one knows this or not.

147b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the disputed point concerns the High Priest's prayer, whose knowledge shaped what he requested.
Rava reports Rav Nahman's view that a deathbed gift is rabbinic, lest the dying man's grief unhinge his mind.
Asks whether Rav Nahman really said this, given his own stated view.
Quotes Rav Nahman's report of Shmuel's ruling that a deathbed promissory note cannot be forgiven by the heir, conflicting with the position.
Asks why, if the deathbed gift is rabbinic, the heir still cannot forgive the debt.
Replies that Rav Nahman holds the gift is not Torah law, yet the Sages made it binding as if it were.
Rava reports Rav Nahman's ruling: a deathbed donor's bare words about residence or fruit are void until he transfers the house or tree itself.
Asks whether Rav Nahman holds that deathbed gifts can only convey what a healthy person could give by acquisition.
Objects that Rava quotes Rav Nahman saying otherwise, which conflicts with that reading.

148a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A deathbed donor's instruction to give his loan to another takes effect, even though a healthy person cannot transfer a loan without a note.
Rav Pappa holds that since an heir inherits loans without a note, the deathbed gift is treated as an inheritance.
Rav Aha son of Rav Ika holds that a loan without a note can be conferred as a gift by a healthy person.
Supports Rav Aha by citing Rav Huna's report of Rav's ruling that a sum given in the presence of three parties is acquired by the third party.
Raises a dilemma: if a palm tree and its fruit are given to different people, does the donor reserve the fruit's place for himself?
Rava reports Rav Nahman's answer: reserving the fruit for oneself also reserves its place, since a person is generous toward himself.
Rabbi Abba cites a teaching of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish on selling a house with a retained upper story as a parallel supporting that principle.

148b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether selling a house to one buyer and its upper story to another reserves rights for the second buyer, and the same for a retained upper story.
Rav Naḥman's reply: a split sale of house and upper story is not a reservation, yet keeping the upper story alone is a reservation.
Supports this with Rav Zevid's view that a seller who keeps the upper story also keeps room for projections, so the palm tree case parallels it.
Rav Yosef bar Maniomi reports Rav Naḥman: a dying donor who divides his property is bound by the gift, while one who deliberates and then stands may revoke only the last gift.
Objects that the donor may have been deliberating before giving, so the unqualified dying person's words should be read as careful and final.
Rav Aha bar Maniomi reports Rav Naḥman: a dying donor who gave all his property and then stood cannot revoke, since he may have property elsewhere.
Asks how the mishna's rule, that a gift is void if no land is kept, can apply to a case where the donor keeps nothing at all.
Rav Hama and Mar bar Rav Ashi explain that the rule concerns a donor who is known to have no property, so the gift is valid.
Raises a dilemma: does partial revocation of a gift count as revoking the whole gift?
Brings a baraita on division between two recipients as a source, reasoning from its latter clause about partial gifts.
Challenges the inference: if the second recipient gets nothing when the donor stands, why would both acquire when the donor dies, as Rav Yimar pressed Rav Ashi.
Works through the consequences: if partial revocation counts as full revocation, then the second recipient cannot acquire, and the case reduces to a division.
Rules that partial revocation counts as full revocation; the first clause fits death or standing, while the latter clause applies only to standing.
Raises the dilemma of a dying person who dedicates all his property to the Temple and then stands: does he acquire the gift as a dedication?
Raises the dilemma of a dying person who declares all his property ownerless: does this count as a gift to the poor, like a rich person's gift?
Raises the dilemma of a dying person who divides all his property among the poor: is this charity or a gift, and the question is left undecided.
Restates the same dedication, abandonment and division dilemmas in a parenthetical alternative version, also left undecided.
Rav Sheshet rules that taking, acquiring and holding are all terms of gift language, so the ruling applies to each of these.
Cites a baraita on inheritance: a person may inherit only what is vested in him, and Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka's view is noted.
Opens a new dilemma on the same subject.

149a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Lists dilemmas on what a dying man means by saying someone shall benefit from, be seen in, stand in or rely on his property; all are left unresolved.
Raises the dilemma of a dying person who sold all his property: can he retract the sale if he recovers?
Rav Yehuda reports Rav's two rulings and reconciles them: retraction is allowed if the payment is still in hand, and not if he already repaid debts.
Raises the dilemma whether a dying person's admission of a debt counts as a deathbed gift.
Brings a case as proof: Issur the convert's twelve thousand zuz in Rava's house, and the status of his sons born before and after conversion.
Rava reasons that Rav Mari cannot acquire the money by inheritance or by gift, since a deathbed gift has inheritance status, and other acts of acquisition also fail.
Rav Ika son of Rav Ami objects: Issur could simply admit the money belongs to Rav Mari and transfer it by a document of admission.
The document emerges from Issur's house, which supports the admission as a valid transfer; Rava rebukes those who build claims that cause him loss.

149b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks how much land counts as any amount that a dying donor may reserve for himself while his gift stands.
Rav Yehuda says it means land sufficient for livelihood, and Rav Yirmeya bar Abba extends the rule to movable property sufficient for livelihood.
Rabbi Zeira praises these rulings as meticulous, explaining that the donor must reserve enough land or goods to rely on if he recovers.
Rav Yosef objects that both views conflict with the mishna, which requires reserving land and accepts any amount.
Abaye asks whether the term land in these statements means specifically land and nothing else.
Cites a mishna on a master who gives all his property to his slave: reserving any land means the slave is not freed, and Rabbi Shimon's view is noted.

150a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Dimi bar Yosef cites Rabbi Elazar: movable property counts as a reservation against a slave's emancipation but not against a wife's marriage contract.
Rav Yosef explains the mishna mentions land only because the preceding clause, Rabbi Akiva's ruling on land, was taught with land.
Abaye objects that a term like any amount must have a measure, since the mishna on wool sets one.
Cites Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas's mishna on the wool of five sheep, which uses a measure, as evidence that any amount can carry a minimum.
Rav states the measure: one hundred and fifty dinars of wool divided among five sheep.
Rav Yosef defends his reading: the mishna's any amount is only a small measure, while the deathbed gift case is taken literally.
States the obvious rules: a gift of movables excludes grain, while a gift of all movables includes it, and the lower millstone is included only when described as movable.
Raises the dilemma whether a Canaanite slave has the legal status of land or of movable property.
Rav Aha son of Avya cites a mishna on selling a city, which includes houses and fields but not movables, and notes that all the property is sold once it is stated.
Argues that if slaves are like movables they would not be sold first, but if they are like land there is no reason for that outcome either.
Offers the distinction that movables that can be moved differ from land that can be moved, so the slave follows neither rule fully.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi to hear a baraita on the case of a master who gives all his property to his slave, where reserving land means the slave is not freed.
Rav Dimi bar Yosef restates Rabbi Elazar's ruling as the basis for the distinction between a slave and a marriage contract.

ranges.en: The dispute concerns generic postdated notes; Rabbi Yehuda forbids a receipt, Rabbi Yosei permits it.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua: a receipt is written only for partial payment, not for full repayment.
The Gemara rejects that limit: a receipt is written even for full payment.
Illustrative case of Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef and Rabbi Abba, showing receipts are written for full repayment.
Rabbi Abba objects that Rav and Shmuel both forbid writing a receipt in that case.
Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi counters that Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish permit writing the receipt.
Ravin reports Rabbi Ilai's ruling from Eretz Yisrael that one writes a receipt.
It is reasonable to write receipts, since otherwise a lost note would let the creditor profit unjustly.
Abaye objects that a lost receipt would equally let the creditor collect twice, so injustice results either way.
Rava replies that the debtor bears the risk, since the borrower is a servant to the lender.
A mishna teaches that antedated notes are invalid while postdated notes are valid.
Rav Hamnuna limits this to loans; postdated bills of sale are invalid.
Explains the stringency: a seller could backdate a sale and then buy the field back unfairly.
If so, loans could be abused the same way via receipts, so why allow postdated loan notes?
Rav Hamnuna holds no receipt is written, so the abuse cannot occur, consistent with Rabbi Yehuda.
Why do we still write postdated notes and receipts today, risking double collection?
Rabbi Abba instructed scribes to state the note was postdated and written later, preventing abuse.
What about today, when scribes do not follow Rabbi Abba's practice?
Rav Safra instructed that receipts omit the date when the note's date is unknown, so the receipt can weaken the note.

ranges.en: If today scribes do not follow the precaution, how can double collection be avoided?
Rav Kahana: the Sages instituted the precaution, and whoever neglects it bears the loss himself.
Rava bar Rav Sheila instructs scribes to date an acquisition deed by the actual acquisition day, if known.
Rav and Rav Huna instruct scribes to write the place where the document is actually written.
Rava rules that a court does not split one hundred-dinar note into two fifty-dinar notes for the creditor.
Reason: the split benefits the creditor's leverage and the debtor's protection, so the Sages instituted it.
Rava rules that two fifty-dinar notes are not merged into one hundred-dinar note.
Reason: keeping smaller notes protects the debtor from quick coercion and the creditor from an oath.
Rav Ashi rules that a hundred-dinar note is not split into one fifty-dinar note after half is paid.
Reason: a new note could enable a fraudulent claim using an earlier receipt for a different loan.
Mishna: two brothers inherit a bathhouse or olive press; its use depends on whether it was built for profit.
Mishna: when two debtors share a name, neither can be sued on a note alone.
Mishna: if a receipt for one of two same-named debtors is found, both notes count as repaid.
Mishna: same-named people distinguish themselves by triple names, then indications, then priesthood.
Introduces a case: a note presented at Rav Huna's court names no creditor.

172b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Huna: the phrase from you in a document need not identify a specific person, even a king.
Rav Hisda tells Rabba to investigate, since Rav Huna will ask him about it that night.
Rabba finds a baraita: an undated bill of divorce with witnesses is valid if it says today.
Rabba infers that today refers to the day the document is produced, so from you means the bearer.
Abaye objects: Abba Shaul may follow Rabbi Eliezer, so the note could have fallen and been found.
Rabba replies that we are not concerned about a note falling and being found by another, and asks for proof.
The mishna on two Yosef ben Shimons shows we are not concerned about a note falling from one of them.
Why did Abaye not cite this mishna against his own concern about falling notes?

173a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita seems to contradict the mishna on whether two same-named men can collect from others.
The dispute is whether letters are acquired by transferring the document itself.
Our mishna holds letters are acquired by transfer; the baraita holds they are not.
Alternatively, both hold letters are acquired by transfer and dispute whether proof of transfer is needed.
Abaye requires the new holder to prove acquisition; Rava does not.
Abaye cites a baraita requiring a brother to prove a note was legally transferred to him.
Rava replies that brothers are different, since co-heirs often seize estate property from one another.
The other version: Rava cites the same baraita, limited to brothers, to show others need no proof.
Abaye counters that the brothers are mentioned only to teach that they too must prove the note.
What disagrees with the mishna on whether two same-named men may sue each other?
The disagreement is whether a scribe may write a note for a debtor without the creditor present.
The mishna's view: a scribe may write it, and fraud is prevented by the requirement for a sum to be repaid.
The baraita's view: a scribe may write a note only when the creditor is present and consenting.
Mishna: a note found repaid makes both same-named debts repaid; its implication is set out.
But didn't the mishna already say neither can sue on a note found among others' papers?
Rabbi Yirmeya: the later line concerns notes identified by tripled names.
Why is it uncertain which Yosef ben Shimon the receipt refers to?
Rav Hoshaya: names are tripled in the note but not in the receipt.
Abaye: the mishna concerns a debtor's receipt found among his papers, which voids both notes.
Mishna: same-named men triple their names, then mark them, then note priesthood, with a baraita on further ancestry.
Mishna: a man's notes are all repaid if he says one is repaid without specifying which.
Rava: the creditor's ambiguous statement about one of two notes favors the debtor; a debt of yours covers all.
Ravina asks whether the same ambiguity rule applies to sales of fields.
Rava: the holder of a deed is at a disadvantage, so the minimal meaning applies to notes too.
Mishna: a creditor who lent on a guarantor's assurance cannot collect from the guarantor.

173b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a guarantor is not sued first unless the creditor stipulated he may collect from whomever he chooses; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds a condition.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's parallel rule on a guarantor for a marriage contract, guarding against collusion in divorce.
Rabba and Rav Yosef explain the guarantor's exemption: the creditor was given the debtor back, so he bears the loss.
Rav Naḥman calls that Persian law; the Gemara replies the Persian courts pursue guarantors directly.
Rav Naḥman reinterprets the mishna: the creditor may not sue the guarantor first, only after the debtor defaults.
A baraita confirms that the creditor must first claim from the debtor, unless stipulated otherwise.
Rav Huna asks from where a guarantor becomes obligated to repay.
Rav Huna cites Judah's guarantee of Benjamin in Genesis 43:9.
Rav Ḥisda objects that Judah's case was an unconditional guarantee, not a standard one.
Rabbi Yitzchak cites Proverbs 20:16, and Proverbs 6:1-3 with its explanation, to show a guarantor must repay.
Ameimar: a guarantor is obligated per Rabbi Yosei, who accepts an asmakhta, but not per Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Ashi objects that Ameimar conflates the two issues, since both principles are taken for granted.
Rav Ashi explains the guarantor's obligation arises from satisfaction at the creditor's trust, so it is real.
The mishna's second case, and Rabba bar bar Ḥana's teaching of Rabbi Yoḥanan: only when the debtor lacks property.
The Gemara objects that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's clause implies the first tanna ignores the debtor's property.
The mishna is incomplete; the full halakha separates standard guarantors from unconditional ones.

174a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: when the debtor has property, the creditor cannot collect from either guarantor type.
Rabba bar Ḥana quotes Rabbi Yoḥanan: the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel except in three cases.
Rav Huna lists which wording makes a standard guarantor and which an unconditional one; give-wording means unconditional.
A dilemma: which status applies when the wording of lend and give conflicts with the guarantee phrase?
Rabbi Yitzchak resolves it: the explicit guarantee phrase decides, whatever verb is used.
Rav Ḥisda and Rava each offer rival classifications of the same wordings.
Mar bar Ameimar reports his father: give-and-I-will-repay leaves the creditor only the guarantor.
The Gemara rejects that: the debtor is freed only if the guarantor hands the money over himself.
A judge let a creditor seize the debtor's property before claiming from the debtor; Rav Ḥanin overruled him.
Rava backs Rav Ḥanin: property acts as a guarantee, so the creditor must first claim from the debtor.
Orphans' guarantor repaid the creditor before telling the orphans and now seeks reimbursement.
Rav Pappa: repaying a creditor is a mitzva orphans are exempt from, so they need not pay until adulthood.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua: a different reason, since the father may have paid in cash secretly, so wait until majority.

174b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What distinguishes Rav Pappa's view from Rav Huna son of Yehoshua, since both exempt orphans?
The difference: if the deceased admitted he had not repaid, or died under excommunication, Rav Huna requires payment.
Ruling: the halakha follows Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua, so orphans repay immediately in those cases.
Objection from a baraita: a guarantor holding a repaid note cannot collect from minor heirs, except if the note records receipt.
Resolution: the creditor wrote the receipt for the guarantor, so the note itself binds the heirs.
Story of a guarantor for a gentile creditor; Avimi, in the name of Rava, rules a gentile creditor is not suspected of double payment.
Rav Ashi counters that a gentile creditor's direct claim on guarantors means no bundles of money were given.
Mishna on a marriage-contract guarantor, and the incident of Moshe bar Atzari's son Rav Huna, with Abaye's advice to divorce.
Rava objects: the mishna requires a vow, so the divorce advice cannot avoid the prohibition.
Abaye replies that not every divorce is done in court, so an out-of-court divorce is possible.
Rav Huna was a priest who could not remarry his divorcee, so Abaye's advice was unavailable; poverty follows the poor.
Would Abaye really advise this, given he calls advice to sell property per Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel wicked?
Advising a father to pay his son, or a Torah scholar, is not wicked.
Was Moshe bar Atzari a guarantor, when a marriage-contract guarantor does not pay? Answer: he was unconditional.
If the husband had no property, an unconditional marriage guarantor would not be obligated, so why was the father held?
Rav Huna had property that was later lost, or the father sincerely bound himself for his son's marriage.
Agreed: a standard marriage guarantor is not obligated, and a loan guarantor is; the sages dispute the rest.
Halakha: the marriage guarantor is never obligated, since his intent is a mitzva and the wife bears no loss.
Rav Huna: a dying man who dedicated his property to the Temple and names a debt is believed, since no one defrauds the Temple.
Rav Naḥman objects: a dying man may falsely claim debts to avoid making his sons look wealthy.

175a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Apply the same logic to the Temple treasury: a dying man may falsely claim debts, so payment may be unwarranted.
Rav Huna's ruling applies only where the creditor holds a promissory note corroborating the admission.
By inference Rav and Shmuel cover the case without a note, yet heirs would then pay an oral loan, which they reject.
Rav Naḥman: the note was court-ratified in Rav Huna's case, and in Rav and Shmuel's case it was not ratified.
Rabba: orphans are believed about repayment when the father only admitted, but not when he ordered payment.
The Gemara objects that the opposite is more reasonable, since an explicit order makes repayment more plausible.
The Gemara reformulates Rabba: the father retracted after forgetting, and an explicit order shows he had not repaid.
Rava asks: must a dying man's admission be witnessed or written, and can he jest at death?
Rava rules a dying man does not jest, so his admission counts as if written and delivered.
Mishna: a loan by note collects from sold liened property; a loan by witnesses collects only from unsold property.

175b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a guarantor's uncollected note collects only from unsold property; Rabbi Yishmael permits that much.
Ben Nannas objects that a guarantor's debt cannot be collected at all, from sold or unsold property.
Ben Nannas explains: a rescuer who pays is exempt, but a guarantor who pledged before the loan is liable.
Rabbi Yishmael praises the study of monetary law and urges students to attend Shimon ben Nannas.
Ulla: by Torah law a loan, written or oral, collects from liened property sold later; oral loans are limited for purchasers' sake.
If so, a written loan should also not collect from purchasers, since that causes them loss.
Written loans are discoverable, so purchasers who did not investigate brought the loss on themselves.
Rabba: by Torah law collection is only from unsold property; sold liened property is allowed to avoid deterring lenders.
If so, why not let oral loans collect from sold liened property too?
Oral loans have no publicity, so purchasers cannot discover them even after investigation.
Did Rabba really say this, given his firstborn ruling that suggests land is liened by Torah law?
Reversing the attributions would conflict with Ulla's view that Torah law limits collection to inferior land.
Rabba was explaining the western sages' view, which he himself does not hold.
Rav and Shmuel: oral loans collect only from the borrower, not from heirs or purchasers, since no Torah lien exists.
Rabbi Yoḥanan and Resh Lakish: oral loans collect from heirs and purchasers, since Torah law liens the debtor's property.
Objection from a tosefta on a pit digger: the heirs must pay the ox owner, like a loan by oral contract.
Rabbi Ela: the baraita concerns a pit digger who was tried before dying, creating a written-type liability.
Objection: the baraita says the ox killed him, so no trial could occur before death.
Rav Adda bar Ahava: the ox made him a mortally wounded man who lived long enough to be tried.
Objection: another version says the ox buried him, so no trial was possible.
Judges sat at the pit's mouth and found the digger liable before he died.

176a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Pappa: an oral loan collects from heirs to avoid deterring lenders, but not from purchasers, who lack notice.
Mishna: a debtor's handwritten note without witnesses collects only from unsold property.
Rabba bar Natan asks Rabbi Yoḥanan: if the handwritten note was later ratified in court, does that change things?
Rabbi Yoḥanan: even a court-ratified handwritten note collects only from unsold property.
Rami bar Ḥama raises an objection from a mishna on three invalid bills of divorce.
The mishna: three invalid divorce bills still leave the offspring of a remarriage unflawed.
Rabbi Elazar: a bill handed over before two witnesses is valid, and collects even from sold liened property.
Mishna on a guarantor whose commitment was written after the note; Rav says collect only from unsold property.
Rav's other ruling: even if written before the note, collect only from unsold property.
There is a contradiction between Rav's two rulings on this point.
Resolved: the first ruling concerns a standalone guarantor clause; the second uses a conjunction tying it to the witnesses.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: in both cases collect only from unsold property, even with a conjunction.
Rava objects from a baraita: witnesses signing a greeting in a bill of divorce make it invalid.
Rabbi Abbahu: Rabbi Yoḥanan distinguished a standalone greeting from one joined by and, which ties the signatures in.
Objection: then Rabbi Yoḥanan agrees with Rav, though he was presented as disagreeing.
Mishna's incident with Rabbi Yishmael and Ben Nannas; Rabba bar bar Ḥana: the halakha follows Rabbi Yishmael's first view.
Would Rabbi Yishmael agree with Ben Nannas about a debtor being strangled, since the guarantee was under duress?
A teaching: Rabbi Yishmael disagreed with Ben Nannas also in the strangling case, so he holds that case valid.
Is the halakha according to Rabbi Yishmael even in the strangling case?
Ravin reports Rabbi Yoḥanan: the halakha follows Rabbi Yishmael in the strangling case too.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: a strangled debtor's guarantor is bound only if an act of acquisition is done, which conflicts with Rav Naḥman.

176b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A guarantor who undertakes a guarantee before a court needs no act of acquisition, unlike a guarantor generally.
The halakha: a guarantor pledged at the time of the loan, or before a court, needs no acquisition; later pledges do.
Closing formula ending the chapter Get Pashut and the tractate Bava Batra.
